metadata.title: AI
metadata.definition: Artificial Intelligence (AI) studies problems that are difficult or impractical to solve using traditional algorithmic methods.

metadata.title: AI Problem Characteristics
metadata.definition: The problems that AI studies are often reminiscent of those thought to require human intelligence, and AI solution strategies are often capable of generalizing across multiple classes of problems.

metadata.title: AI Ubiquity
metadata.definition: AI techniques are now widespread in computing, powering everyday applications such as email, social networks, photography, and financial markets.

metadata.title: Virtual Assistants
metadata.definition: AI systems assist users by understanding and executing requests, e.g. Siri, Alexa.

metadata.title: Autonomous Agents
metadata.definition: Autonomous agents are AI systems designed to perceive their environment and interact appropriately with it.

metadata.title: Self-Driving Cars
metadata.definition: An application of autonomous agents, where vehicles are capable of operating on their own without human intervention.

metadata.title: Robotics
metadata.definition: The field of research, design, manufacturing, operation and application of robots, including robots that operate as autonomous agents.

metadata.title: Symbolic AI
metadata.definition: One of the traditional approaches in AI, focuses on representing knowledge through symbols, logic and rules.

metadata.title: Subsymbolic AI
metadata.definition: One of the traditional approaches in AI, includes distributed processing models such as neural networks, where knowledge is not explicitly represented symbolically.

metadata.title: Knowledge Representation
metadata.definition: Methods and structures for encoding information and knowledge in a way that can be stored, accessed, and manipulated by AI systems.

metadata.title: Problem Solving
metadata.definition: The methods and strategies used by AI systems to find solutions to problems, often including search and inference.

metadata.title: Optimization
metadata.definition: Methods are used to find the best solution from a set of possible solutions, often to improve performance or achieve a specific goal.

metadata.title: Perception
metadata.definition: The aspect of AI that deals with the collection, processing, and interpretation of information from the environment.

metadata.title: Speech Recognition
metadata.definition: The ability of a computer to convert speech into text or other understandable formats.

metadata.title: NLU
metadata.definition: The ability of a computer to understand the meaning of text or speech in natural human language.

metadata.title: Computer Vision
metadata.definition: The field of AI enables computers to collect, process, analyze and understand images and videos from the real world.

metadata.title: AI Search
metadata.definition: Algorithmic techniques are used to explore the state space in search of a solution or a path from the initial state to the goal state.

metadata.title: AI Planning
metadata.definition: The field of AI is concerned with designing sequences of actions to achieve a specific goal or set of goals.

metadata.title: Generative AI
metadata.definition: The aspect of AI that involves generating new content, such as narratives, conversations, images, models or recommendations.

metadata.title: AI Action
metadata.definition: The aspect of AI that involves AI agents performing actions in their environment.

metadata.title: Task Automation
metadata.definition: The use of technology to perform routine or repetitive tasks without human intervention.

metadata.title: AI Control Systems
metadata.definition: Systems use AI techniques to manage, regulate and control the operation of devices, machines or processes.

metadata.title: AI Architecture
metadata.definition: The organizational structures and design of AI systems.

metadata.title: Single-agent System
metadata.definition: AI systems in which a single agent operates and interacts with its environment.

metadata.title: Multi-agent System
metadata.definition: AI systems consist of multiple agents that interact with each other and the environment to achieve common or individual goals.

metadata.title: Machine Learning
metadata.definition: A branch of artificial intelligence that allows systems to learn from data without being explicitly programmed, which can be used in all aspects of AI.

metadata.title: AI Approach Suitability
metadata.definition: The skill of determining when an AI approach is appropriate or most effective for solving a particular problem.

metadata.title: AI Representation & Reasoning
metadata.definition: Skill in selecting the most appropriate knowledge representation schemes and inference mechanisms for a specific AI problem.

metadata.title: AI System Deployment
metadata.definition: Skills to build and develop AI solutions based on selected representations and inference mechanisms.

metadata.title: AI Performance Evaluation
metadata.definition: Skills to evaluate the effectiveness and accuracy of deployed AI solutions.

metadata.title: AI Social Impact
metadata.definition: Skills to consider and evaluate the broader effects of AI systems on society, beyond technical performance.

metadata.title: AI Popularity
metadata.definition: Over the past decade, the term "artificial intelligence" has become popular in business circles, news articles, and everyday conversations.

metadata.title: Big Data in AI
metadata.definition: The widespread availability of large data sets is a key factor driving recent advances in AI, especially in machine learning.

metadata.title: AI Compute Power
metadata.definition: Increasing computing power is a key factor for the development of AI, allowing it to handle complex models and huge amounts of data.

metadata.title: AI Algorithm Advances
metadata.definition: Improvements in AI algorithms have contributed significantly to recent advances, making AI systems more efficient and powerful.

metadata.title: Learned Representations
metadata.definition: The trend in AI is a shift from knowledge representations manually designed by engineers to representations learned automatically through optimization on large data sets.

metadata.title: Neural Networks
metadata.definition: A machine learning model inspired by the structure and function of the human brain, consisting of interconnected layers of artificial neurons.

metadata.title: Deep Learning
metadata.definition: A branch of machine learning that uses neural networks with many hidden layers (deep neural networks) to learn complex representations of data.

metadata.title: AI: Tech Term vs. Marketing
metadata.definition: "Artificial intelligence" is now both a specialized technical term and a marketing keyword used by businesses to promote the added value of their services.

metadata.title: AI Interdisciplinary Applications
metadata.definition: AI techniques are increasingly widely used in many different fields such as biology, art, architecture and finance to solve specialized problems.

metadata.title: Public AI Access
metadata.definition: For the first time in history, the public has access to sophisticated AI-driven tools.

metadata.title: Generative AI Content
metadata.definition: apply AI in creating diverse types of content such as essays, poetry from suggestions, artwork from descriptions, and even fake images or videos (deepfakes) of real people.

metadata.title: AI Stock Trading
metadata.definition: Use AI technology to analyze the market, predict trends and automate stock trading transactions.

metadata.title: AI Content Curation
metadata.definition: Use AI to personalize and curate news streams and social media content for users.

metadata.title: AI Candidate Assessment
metadata.definition: apply AI to automatically analyze and evaluate job candidates' profiles and skills.

metadata.title: AI Medical Diagnosis
metadata.definition: Use AI to support diagnosis and early detection of diseases or health conditions based on medical data.

metadata.title: AI Recidivism Prediction
metadata.definition: applying AI to predict the likelihood that an individual will reoffend after being released can influence sentencing decisions.

metadata.title: AI Ethical Considerations
metadata.definition: Important ethical issues need to be understood and considered when developing and applying AI technology, given its potential for significant impact on society.

metadata.title: AI Terminology Shift
metadata.definition: Reflects common terminology changes within the AI ​​field and widespread usage outside the field.

metadata.title: Neural Net Focus
metadata.definition: Increased emphasis on neural networks to reflect recent advances in the field of AI.

metadata.title: Representation Learning
metadata.definition: Increased emphasis on representation learning to reflect recent advances in the field of AI.

metadata.title: Symbolic Methods
metadata.definition: Lighten the emphasis but retain symbolic methods in the AI ​​program due to its unique capabilities, practical applications, ensuring broad education and support for neurosymbolic methods.

metadata.title: Subsymbolic Methods
metadata.definition: Enhance understanding of parasymbolic methods.

metadata.title: Learned Representations
metadata.definition: Enhance understanding of learned representations.

metadata.title: Knowledge-based AI
metadata.definition: Knowledge-based methods are retained in the AI ​​program to ensure broad education and unique capabilities.

metadata.title: Neurosymbolic AI
metadata.definition: The methods integrate both learned and symbolic representations.

metadata.title: AI Applications
metadata.definition: Increased emphasis on practical applications of AI in a variety of fields (e.g., medicine, sustainability, social media).

metadata.title: Deep Generative Models
metadata.definition: Discusses tools that use deep generation models, how they work at a high level, their uses, and disadvantages.

metadata.title: ChatGPT
metadata.definition: An example of a widely used worm generation model, discussion of operation, uses, and disadvantages.

metadata.title: DALL-E
metadata.definition: An example of a widely used worm generation model, discussion of operation, uses, and disadvantages.

metadata.title: Midjourney
metadata.definition: An example of a widely used worm generation model, discussion of operation, uses, and disadvantages.

metadata.title: AI Societal Impact
metadata.definition: The importance of understanding and evaluating the broader societal impacts and implications of AI methods and applications.

metadata.title: AI Ethics
metadata.definition: An important issue in the social impact of AI, including in the curriculum.

metadata.title: AI Fairness
metadata.definition: An important issue in the social impact of AI, including in the curriculum.

metadata.title: AI Trust
metadata.definition: An important issue in the social impact of AI, including in the curriculum.

metadata.title: AI Explainability (XAI)
metadata.definition: An important issue in the social impact of AI, including in the curriculum.

metadata.title: AI & Data Science Link
metadata.definition: The AI ​​program includes connections to data science through cross-connections with Data Management and other fields, as well as a sample course in Data Science.

metadata.title: Basic AI Literacy
metadata.definition: The clear goal is to develop a basic understanding of AI for every computer science student.

metadata.title: AI Critical Thinking
metadata.definition: The clear goal is to develop critical thinking about AI in every computer science student.

metadata.title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
metadata.definition: New techniques became popular and were added to the curriculum.

metadata.title: AI Fundamentals
metadata.definition: The unit introduces the basic concepts of AI. Includes 2 hours of CS Core and 1 hour of KA Core.

metadata.title: Search (AI)
metadata.definition: Unit of knowledge on search methods in AI. Includes 2 hours of CS Core and 6 hours of KA Core. There are 3 additional CS Core hours shared with Algorithm Foundations (Search no information).

metadata.title: Fundamental KR&R
metadata.definition: Unit of knowledge on basic knowledge representation and inference. Includes 1 hour of CS Core and 2 hours of KA Core. There is an additional hour of CS Core shared with Mathematical Foundations (Probability).

metadata.title: Machine Learning (ML)
metadata.definition: Unit of knowledge on machine learning methods. Includes 4 hours of CS Core and 6 hours of KA Core.

metadata.title: AI Apps & Societal Impact
metadata.definition: Unit of knowledge on the practical applications and social impact of AI. Includes 3 hours of CS Core and 3 hours of KA Core.

metadata.title: Probabilistic KR&R
metadata.definition: Unit of knowledge on representation and inference based on probability.

metadata.title: Planning (AI)
metadata.definition: Unit of knowledge on planning techniques in AI.

metadata.title: Logical KR&R
metadata.definition: Unit of knowledge about logic-based representation and reasoning.

metadata.title: Agents & Cognitive Systems
metadata.definition: Unit of knowledge on types of agents and cognitive systems in AI.

metadata.title: Natural Language Processing (NLP)
metadata.definition: Unit of knowledge on natural language processing.

metadata.title: Robotics
metadata.definition: Unit of knowledge about robotics.

metadata.title: Perception & Computer Vision
metadata.definition: Unit of knowledge in cognition and computer vision.

metadata.title: Uninformed Search
metadata.definition: Part of the Search unit, shared with Algorithm Foundations.

metadata.title: Probability in AI
metadata.definition: Part of the Fundamental Knowledge Representation and Reasoning unit, shared with Mathematical Foundations.

metadata.title: AI Problem Overview
metadata.definition: An overview of the types of problems AI tries to solve.

metadata.title: Recent AI Successes
metadata.definition: Examples of how AI has been successfully applied in practice.

metadata.title: AI Agent Definition
metadata.definition: understand different definitions of agents in AI and specific examples.

metadata.title: Reactive Agents
metadata.definition: A type of agent that only reacts directly to the current environment without the ability to plan or complex reasoning.

metadata.title: Deliberative Agents
metadata.definition: A type of agent capable of planning, reasoning, and building models of the world to make decisions.

metadata.title: Intelligent Behavior
metadata.definition: Discuss the criteria and definitions of behavior considered intelligent.

metadata.title: Turing Test
metadata.definition: A method for evaluating a machine's ability to exhibit human-equivalent intelligent behavior.

metadata.title: Turing Test Limitations
metadata.definition: understand the weaknesses and criticisms of the Turing test as a measure of intelligence.

metadata.title: Multimodal I/O
metadata.definition: Ability to process and produce information through a variety of media (e.g., text, images, sound).

metadata.title: Intelligent Behavior Simulation
metadata.definition: Ways in which computers can simulate aspects of intelligent behavior.

metadata.title: Rational vs. Non-rational Reasoning
metadata.definition: The difference between making decisions based on optimal logic and data versus other forms of reasoning.

metadata.title: Problem Characteristics
metadata.definition: Understanding the different characteristics of a problem can influence the AI ​​approach.

metadata.title: Observable Problems
metadata.definition: Distinguish between problems where the agent can observe the entire state of the environment from problems where only a part can be observed.

metadata.title: Agent Problems
metadata.definition: Distinguish problems with only one agent from problems with many interacting agents.

metadata.title: Deterministic vs. Stochastic
metadata.definition: Distinguish between problems where the outcome of an action is certain from those where there is an element of chance.

metadata.title: Static vs. Dynamic Problems
metadata.definition: Distinguish between problems where the environment does not change during solution from problems where the environment changes independently of the agent.

metadata.title: Discrete vs Continuous Problems
metadata.definition: Distinguish between problems with a finite and countable number of states or actions from those with an infinite or continuously variable space of states or actions.

metadata.title: Nature of Agents
metadata.definition: Delve deeper into the properties, architecture, and functionality of AI agents.

metadata.title: Agent Autonomy Types
metadata.definition: Learn about the different levels of autonomy in AI systems, from fully automated to requiring human intervention, or a combination of both.

metadata.title: Reflex Agents
metadata.definition: Research on AI agents that operate based on simple reflex rules, responding directly to environmental signals without the need for complex planning.

metadata.title: Goal-based Agents
metadata.definition: Learn about AI agents acting to achieve one or more specific goals, often through planning and search.

metadata.title: Utility-based Agents
metadata.definition: The study of AI agents choosing actions to maximize their utility function, weighing desired and likely outcomes.

metadata.title: Decision Making Under Uncertainty
metadata.definition: Research methods and algorithms for AI agents to make optimal decisions when information about the environment or the results of actions are not completely clear.

metadata.title: Decision Making Incomplete Info
metadata.definition: Explore how AI agents process and make decisions with only partial information about the world state or available options.

metadata.title: Perception in AI
metadata.definition: analyze the role of the ability to acquire and interpret information from the environment (cognition) in the effective operation of AI agents.

metadata.title: Agent-Environment Interaction
metadata.definition: Learn about how AI agents interact with their environment, including influencing and responding to changes, to achieve their goals.

metadata.title: Learning-based Agents
metadata.definition: Research AI agents capable of improving their performance through experience, using machine learning algorithms.

metadata.title: Embodied Agents
metadata.definition: Learn about AI agents that have a physical existence in the real or simulated world, capable of physically interacting with the environment.

metadata.title: Embodied Agent Sensors
metadata.definition: Study the types of sensors that embodied agents use to collect information from the physical environment.

metadata.title: Embodied Agent Dynamics
metadata.definition: Learn about the laws of physics and motion behavior that govern embodied agents and their interactions with the environment.

metadata.title: Embodied Agent Actuators
metadata.definition: Study the parts of embodied agents that allow them to physically impact the environment (e.g., robotic arms, wheels).

metadata.title: AI Applications Overview
metadata.definition: Provides an overview of fields and how AI is applied in practice, from healthcare to finance to manufacturing.

metadata.title: AI Growth & Impact
metadata.definition: analyze the rapid growth of AI and its far-reaching effects on the economy, social structures, and ethical issues.

metadata.title: Problem Characterization Practice
metadata.definition: Practice skills in analyzing and characterizing an AI problem in specific situations, including environment, state, and goals.

metadata.title: Agent Nature (Advanced)
metadata.definition: Study in more detail the structure, types and operations of AI agents, accompanied by specific illustrative examples.

metadata.title: AI Impact (Advanced)
metadata.definition: A more in-depth analysis of the current and potential applications of AI, as well as its complex impacts on economic, social, ethical and security domains.

metadata.title: AI Philosophical Issues
metadata.definition: Explore deep philosophical questions related to AI, such as consciousness, intelligence, machine ethics, and the nature of intelligence.

metadata.title: History of AI
metadata.definition: Overview of important milestones, key figures and development of the field of artificial intelligence over time.

metadata.title: Turing Test
metadata.definition: understand the Turing test, a famous test proposed to evaluate the ability of a machine to exhibit intellectual behavior equivalent to or indistinguishable from humans.

metadata.title: Chinese Room Experiment
metadata.definition: A study of the 'Chinese Room' thought experiment and the philosophical debates it raises about the nature of understanding and consciousness in AI.

metadata.title: Optimal Reasoning/Behavior
metadata.definition: Distinguish and understand the behaviors or reasoning processes that achieve the best possible results based on established criteria.

metadata.title: Human-like Reasoning/Behavior
metadata.definition: Distinguish and understand behaviors or reasoning processes that simulate how humans think and act, often not necessarily optimally.

metadata.title: AI, ML, DL Distinction
metadata.definition: understand and clearly distinguish the concepts of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning and Deep Learning.

metadata.title: State Space Representation
metadata.definition: Learn to describe a search problem as a state space, where each state represents a configuration of the problem.

metadata.title: States, Goals, Operators
metadata.definition: Learn how to clearly define possible states, desired goal states, and possible actions (operators) to transition between states.

metadata.title: State Decomposition
metadata.definition: Learn to break down complex states into simpler representations or hypothesis spaces for more efficient searches.

metadata.title: Graph Search Problem Solving
metadata.definition: Study a problem-solving method by traversing a graph representing the state space to find the path from the initial state to the goal state.

metadata.title: Graph as Search Space
metadata.definition: understand how to represent the problem space as a graph, where vertices are states and edges are operators.

metadata.title: Tree Traversal Exploration
metadata.definition: Learn tree traversal techniques to explore the search space, considering it a subtree of a graph.

metadata.title: Dynamic Graph Construction
metadata.definition: Investigate how to build a state space graph dynamically during the search process, instead of having the entire graph from the beginning.

metadata.title: Uninformed Graph Search
metadata.definition: Overview of search algorithms that traverse the graph without using any additional information about the distance to the target (heuristics).

metadata.title: Breadth-first Search (BFS)
metadata.definition: Learn the BFS algorithm, traverse the graph by layer, ensuring to find the shortest path in the unweighted graph.

metadata.title: Depth-first Search (DFS)
metadata.definition: Learn the DFS algorithm, traversing the graph as deeply as possible before returning.

metadata.title: Iterative Deepening DFS (IDDFS)
metadata.definition: DFS variant research combines the benefits of BFS (optimality) with the benefits of DFS (memory efficiency).

metadata.title: Uniform Cost Search (UCS)
metadata.definition: Learn an optimal search algorithm for weighted graphs, always expanding the node with the smallest total path cost from the root.

metadata.title: Heuristic Graph Search
metadata.definition: Overview of search algorithms that use heuristic functions to estimate the distance to the target, helping to increase search efficiency.

metadata.title: Heuristic Design & Admissibility
metadata.definition: Learn how to design effective heuristic functions and understand the concept of heuristic feasibility to ensure algorithm optimization.

metadata.title: Hill-climbing Algorithm
metadata.definition: Study a simple local search algorithm that always moves to a better neighboring state, with the goal of reaching the peak (maximum).

metadata.title: Local Minima & Search Landscape
metadata.definition: understand the concept of local minima in search spaces and how they affect local search algorithms such as hill climbing.

metadata.title: Local vs Global Solutions
metadata.definition: Distinguish between solutions that are optimal only in a local region of the search space and solutions that are optimal over the entire space.

metadata.title: Greedy Best-First Search
metadata.definition: Learning search algorithms use heuristics to always expand the node believed to be closest to the target.

metadata.title: A* Search
metadata.definition: Research on widely used informative search algorithms, combining past path costs and heuristic estimation to find optimal paths.

metadata.title: Graph Search Space Complexity
metadata.definition: analyze the amount of memory that graph search algorithms require to operate, according to the number of vertices and edges.

metadata.title: Graph Search Time Complexity
metadata.definition: analyze the computational time required by graph search algorithms to find a solution, according to the number of vertices and edges.

metadata.title: Bidirectional Search
metadata.definition: Research algorithms that search simultaneously from the starting state and the goal state, hoping to meet in the middle to increase efficiency.

metadata.title: Beam Search
metadata.definition: Learn a variant of breadth-first search or best-first search, retaining only a limited number of nodes (beam width) at each level to reduce memory overhead.

metadata.title: Two-Player Games
metadata.definition: Research theories and algorithms for solving games involving two players with opposing goals.

metadata.title: Minimax Search
metadata.definition: Learning search algorithms are used in game theory to find the optimal move for a player assuming that the opponent also plays optimally.

metadata.title: Alpha-beta Pruning
metadata.definition: Research optimization techniques for the Minimax algorithm, helping to remove unnecessary branches in the search tree without affecting the final result.

metadata.title: Ply Cutoff
metadata.definition: understand the concept of limiting the depth of a search tree in Minimax and Alpha-beta pruning algorithms to manage computational resources.

metadata.title: A* Implementation
metadata.definition: Programming skills to implement the A* search algorithm in real-world problems, including the management of priority queues and related data structures.

metadata.title: Constraint Satisfaction (CSP)
metadata.definition: Study of constraint satisfaction problems (CSP), where the goal is to find a set of values ​​for variables such that all constraints are satisfied.

metadata.title: Search Space
metadata.definition: In-depth study of the structure and characteristics of the search space, including how it affects the effectiveness of algorithms.

metadata.title: Search Tree Construction
metadata.definition: Learn the techniques and challenges of building search trees to represent state space efficiently.

metadata.title: Dynamic Search Space
metadata.definition: The study of search spaces that change during problem solving, requires adaptive algorithms.

metadata.title: Combinatorial Explosion
metadata.definition: understand the problem where the size of the search space increases exponentially with the number of variables or choices, making it difficult to solve.

metadata.title: Search Space Topology
metadata.definition: Study the shape and characteristics of the search space 'landscape', including local minima, peaks, saddles, etc., and their impact on search.

metadata.title: Local Search
metadata.definition: Study of search algorithms that start from one solution and continuously move to better neighboring solutions, often used for optimization problems.

metadata.title: Tabu Search
metadata.definition: Learn a metaheuristic local search algorithm that uses memory (tabu lists) to avoid repeating explored solutions and escape local minima.

metadata.title: A* Variants
metadata.definition: Research advanced versions of the A* algorithm such as IDA*, SMA*, and RBFS that are designed to address memory or time constraints.

metadata.title: IDA* Search
metadata.definition: Informed Iterative Depth First Search, a variant of A* that minimizes memory requirements.

metadata.title: SMA* Search
metadata.definition: A* search simplifies memory, a variant of A* that can handle larger search spaces by eliminating the least promising nodes when memory runs out.

metadata.title: RBFS Search
metadata.definition: Recursive first-best search, a memory-friendly variant of A* uses recursion to perform a heuristic deepening search.

metadata.title: Horizon Effect
metadata.definition: Study the horizon effect in games, where the Minimax algorithm can ignore bad results that are outside the specified search depth.

metadata.title: Opening/Endgame Books
metadata.definition: Learn about using pre-planned strategies for the opening and late game stages of fighting games to improve AI performance.

metadata.title: Game Solved Meaning
metadata.definition: analyze what it means to find a perfect optimal strategy for a game (e.g., checkers), that guarantees never losing if the opponent makes no mistakes.

metadata.title: Minimax Implementation
metadata.definition: Programming skills to implement the Minimax search algorithm in fighting game applications.

metadata.title: Beam Search Implementation
metadata.definition: Programming skills to implement the Beam search algorithm in search problems that require memory efficiency.

metadata.title: Expectimax Search
metadata.definition: Research search algorithms used in games with random elements (chance nodes) or in the process of solving Markov decision making problems (MDP), combining optimization and expectations.

metadata.title: Stochastic Search
metadata.definition: Overview of search methods that use random elements to explore the solution space, especially useful for complex optimization problems.

metadata.title: Simulated Annealing
metadata.definition: Learn a metaheuristic optimization algorithm inspired by metallurgy, capable of escaping local minima.

metadata.title: Genetic Algorithms
metadata.definition: Study of a class of optimization algorithms inspired by natural selection and genetics, used to find approximate solutions to complex problems.

metadata.title: Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)
metadata.definition: Learn a heuristic search algorithm to make decisions in complex problems, especially in games, by randomly sampling from the search space.

metadata.title: A*/Beam Search Design
metadata.definition: Ability to design and implement A* search or beam search algorithms to solve a specific problem.

metadata.title: A*/Beam vs. Other Searches
metadata.definition: Compare the performance of the A* or beam search algorithm with other search algorithms based on solution cost, number of nodes expanded, and other criteria.

metadata.title: Minimax Search
metadata.definition: understand and apply the Minimax search algorithm to solve two-player fighting games.

metadata.title: Alpha-Beta Pruning
metadata.definition: apply alpha-beta pruning to reduce the search space in two-player fighting games (e.g., Connect Four).

metadata.title: Genetic Algorithms
metadata.definition: understand the concept and working mechanism of genetic algorithms.

metadata.title: GA vs. Other Optimizers
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast genetic algorithms with classical search techniques, explaining when to use genetic algorithms to learn a model versus other forms of optimization (e.g., gradient descent).

metadata.title: Heuristic Search Types
metadata.definition: understand and differentiate between different heuristic search techniques.

metadata.title: Heuristic Search Applicability
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast the applicability of different heuristic search techniques to a specific problem.

metadata.title: CSP Modeling
metadata.definition: Ability to model logic or Sudoku problems into a constraint satisfaction problem.

metadata.title: Backtrack Search for CSP
metadata.definition: apply backtracking search to solve constraint satisfaction problems.

metadata.title: Arc Consistency
metadata.definition: Determine the extent to which arc consistency can reduce the search space in the constraint satisfaction problem.

metadata.title: Knowledge Representation Types
metadata.definition: understand different types of knowledge representation in AI.

metadata.title: Symbolic/Logic KR
metadata.definition: Master the concept of symbolic and logical knowledge representation.

metadata.title: NLP to KR
metadata.definition: The ability to create a symbolic or logical representation from a problem statement in natural language.

metadata.title: Learned Subsymbolic KR
metadata.definition: Understanding learned symbolic sub-representations.

metadata.title: Graphical Models
metadata.definition: Introduction to graphical models such as Naive Bayes and Bayesian networks for knowledge representation and inference.

metadata.title: Probabilistic Inference Overview
metadata.definition: Overview of the fundamentals of probabilistic inference.

metadata.title: Bayes' Theorem
metadata.definition: Master Bayes' Theorem and its significance in probabilistic inference.

metadata.title: Bayesian Inference
metadata.definition: understand the fundamentals of Bayesian inference and how it works.

metadata.title: Random Variables & Distributions
metadata.definition: understand random variables and types of probability distributions.

metadata.title: Axioms of Probability
metadata.definition: Master the basic axioms of probability.

metadata.title: Probabilistic Inference
metadata.definition: Ability to perform probabilistic inference to draw conclusions based on data and models.

metadata.title: Deriving Bayes' Rule
metadata.definition: understand how to differentiate and prove the Bayes' Rule formula.

metadata.title: Bayesian Inference
metadata.definition: apply Bayesian inference to more complex examples and problems.

metadata.title: Probabilistic Independence
metadata.definition: understand the concept of independence of random variables in probability.

metadata.title: Conditional Independence
metadata.definition: understand the concept of conditional independence of random variables.

metadata.title: Markov Chains
metadata.definition: Introduction to Markov chains and their basic properties.

metadata.title: Markov Models
metadata.definition: An introduction to Markov models, including basic applications.

metadata.title: Utility & Decision Making
metadata.definition: understand the concept of value and how to make decisions under conditions of uncertainty.

metadata.title: ML Tasks
metadata.definition: understand definitions and diverse examples of machine learning tasks.

metadata.title: Supervised Learning
metadata.definition: Master the concept of supervised learning.

metadata.title: Classification
metadata.definition: Understanding the classification problem in supervised learning.

metadata.title: Regression
metadata.definition: Understanding the regression problem in supervised learning.

metadata.title: Reinforcement Learning
metadata.definition: Master the concept of reinforcement learning.

metadata.title: Unsupervised Learning
metadata.definition: Master the concept of unsupervised learning.

metadata.title: Clustering
metadata.definition: Understanding the clustering problem in unsupervised learning.

metadata.title: No Free Lunch Theorem
metadata.definition: understand the 'There is no free lunch' theorem and its implications in machine learning.

metadata.title: ML Error Sources
metadata.definition: understand sources of error and undecidability limits in machine learning systems.

metadata.title: Simple Statistical Supervised Learning
metadata.definition: Understanding how statistical supervised learning models work is simple enough to properly use existing implementations.

metadata.title: Linear Regression
metadata.definition: Master the fundamentals of linear regression as an example of supervised learning.

metadata.title: Decision Trees
metadata.definition: Master the fundamentals of decision trees as an example of supervised learning.

metadata.title: Overfitting
metadata.definition: Understanding the overfitting problem in machine learning.

metadata.title: Controlling Model Complexity
metadata.definition: Intuitively understand methods for controlling solution complexity such as regularization and pruning.

metadata.title: Bias-Variance Tradeoff
metadata.definition: understand the trade-off between bias (underfitting) and variance (overfitting) in machine learning.

metadata.title: Data Preprocessing
metadata.definition: understand the importance and pitfalls of data preprocessing choices.

metadata.title: Missing Value Handling
metadata.definition: Missing value handling techniques such as imputing or marking as missing, along with their consequences.

metadata.title: Feature Encoding
metadata.definition: Methods for encoding categorical variables and real-valued data for machine learning models.

metadata.title: Data Normalization/Standardization
metadata.definition: understand data normalization and standardization techniques.

metadata.title: Real-world Data ML
metadata.definition: The importance of using real data instead of textbook examples in machine learning.

metadata.title: Hypothesis Space & Complexity
metadata.definition: Understanding hypothesis spaces and their complexity in machine learning.

metadata.title: Simple Feature Expansion
metadata.definition: Basic feature expansion techniques are simple, such as squaring univariate features.

metadata.title: Learned Feature Representations
metadata.definition: Understanding feature representations learned through machine learning models.

metadata.title: ML Model Evaluation
metadata.definition: understand the fundamentals of machine learning model evaluation.

metadata.title: Train-Validation-Test Split
metadata.definition: understand the importance of dividing data into training, validation, and test sets.

metadata.title: Classification Metrics
metadata.definition: Common performance metrics for evaluating classification models (e.g. accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score).

metadata.title: Held-out Data Performance
metadata.definition: Method for estimating model performance on held-out data.

metadata.title: Hyperparameter Tuning
metadata.definition: Use a test set to fine-tune the parameters of a machine learning model.

metadata.title: Model Understanding & Limitations
metadata.definition: Master how a model works, its limitations and pitfalls, and the implications of the decisions the model makes.

metadata.title: Basic Neural Networks
metadata.definition: The fundamentals of how neural networks work and their training, without going into computational detail.

metadata.title: Basic Generative Neural Networks
metadata.definition: A basic introduction to generative neural networks, including large language models (LLMs).

metadata.title: ML Ethics
metadata.definition: Ethical issues related to machine learning, focusing on real data, real scenarios, and case studies.

metadata.title: Bias & Unintended Consequences
metadata.definition: understand bias in data sets, algorithms, evaluations, and their unintended consequences in machine learning.

metadata.title: ML as Optimization
metadata.definition: Describe how basic machine learning problems, such as linear regression or logistic regression, are defined and solved in terms of optimizing an objective function.

metadata.title: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)
metadata.definition: A linear regression method optimizes by minimizing the sum of squares of residuals between predicted and actual values.

metadata.title: Logistic Regression
metadata.definition: A classification algorithm uses the sigmoid function to model the probability of a class, often used for binary classification problems.

metadata.title: Objective Function
metadata.definition: Function that an optimization algorithm seeks to minimize (cost/loss function) or maximize (profit function) to achieve the machine learning goal.

metadata.title: Gradient Descent
metadata.definition: An iterative optimization algorithm that finds the local minimum (or maximum) of a function by moving against the function's gradient.

metadata.title: Regularization for Overfitting
metadata.definition: Techniques that add constraints or penalties to the model to reduce complexity, help the model generalize better on new data, and avoid overfitting to the training data.

metadata.title: Regularization Formulas
metadata.definition: The mathematical representation of the normalization terms (e.g., L1, L2) is added to the objective function to control the complexity of the model.

metadata.title: Ensemble Learning
metadata.definition: The technique combines multiple machine learning models to create a more powerful model, often delivering better overall performance than a single model.

metadata.title: Weighted Majority Vote Ensemble
metadata.definition: A method of combining output from component models in an ensemble by assigning weights to each model and taking a weighted majority decision.

metadata.title: Deep Learning
metadata.definition: A branch of machine learning that uses artificial neural networks with many layers (deep networks) to learn representations of data at different levels of abstraction.

metadata.title: Deep Feedforward Networks (Intuitive)
metadata.definition: understand the structure and basic operation of multi-layer feedforward neural networks, in which information only moves in one direction from the input layer to the output layer, without going into deep mathematical formulas.

metadata.title: CNN Intuition
metadata.definition: Understanding the basic structure and operation of CNNs, especially in image processing, which uses convolutional layers to automatically learn spatial features, without going into deep mathematical formulas.

metadata.title: Feature Visualization
metadata.definition: Techniques to visualize and understand what the layers of a deep neural network are learning or detecting in the input data, helping to explain the model.

metadata.title: Deep Architectures
metadata.definition: Overview of other types of neural network architectures beyond feedforward and convolutional networks, designed for specific types of data and tasks.

metadata.title: Generative Neural Networks
metadata.definition: A type of neural network that is capable of generating new data (e.g., images, text) that is similar to the training data it learned from.

metadata.title: Recurrent Neural Networks
metadata.definition: Neural networks are specifically designed to process sequential data (e.g. time series, text), capable of maintaining an internal 'memory' state.

metadata.title: Transformer Model
metadata.definition: A groundbreaking neural network architecture that uses attention mechanisms, which are especially effective in natural language processing and other sequential tasks.

metadata.title: Model Evaluation
metadata.definition: Methods and metrics are used to measure how well a machine learning model performs its task on unseen data.

metadata.title: Classification Metrics
metadata.definition: Metrics used to evaluate the performance of classification models, including error rate, accuracy, coverage, F1-score, etc.

metadata.title: Error Rate
metadata.definition: The proportion of false predictions (including false positives and false negatives) in the total number of predictions of a classification problem.

metadata.title: Precision
metadata.definition: The proportion of true positives among all cases predicted to be positive.

metadata.title: Recall
metadata.definition: Proportion of true positives among all true positives.

metadata.title: Regression Metrics
metadata.definition: Metrics used to evaluate the performance of regression models, such as mean absolute error (MAE), mean squared error (MSE), R-squared, etc.

metadata.title: Confusion Matrix
metadata.definition: A table summarizing the performance of a classification algorithm, showing the number of correct and incorrect predictions for each class.

metadata.title: Cross-validation
metadata.definition: A technique to more reliably evaluate model performance and minimize overfitting by dividing the data into multiple subsets for iterative training and testing.

metadata.title: Hyperparameter Tuning
metadata.definition: The process of finding optimal values ​​for the hyperparameters of a machine learning model to achieve the best performance.

metadata.title: Grid Search
metadata.definition: A method of fine-tuning hyper-parameters by trying all possible combinations of parameter values ​​in a predetermined grid.

metadata.title: Random Search
metadata.definition: A method for fine-tuning hyper-parameters by randomly sampling parameter combinations from a defined space.

metadata.title: Reinforcement Learning
metadata.definition: Introduces the basic principles and algorithms of reinforcement learning, where an agent learns to perform actions in an environment to maximize cumulative rewards.

metadata.title: ML Applications
metadata.definition: Practical domains and problems that machine learning algorithms can be applied to solve.

metadata.title: ML in Healthcare
metadata.definition: Examples include the use of machine learning for disease diagnosis, drug development, medical image analysis, and treatment personalization.

metadata.title: ML in Economics
metadata.definition: Examples of using machine learning are for market forecasting, consumer behavior analysis, and financial optimization.

metadata.title: ML in Computer Vision
metadata.definition: Examples of the use of machine learning in computer vision, such as object recognition, face detection, and image analysis.

metadata.title: ML in NLP
metadata.definition: Examples of the use of machine learning in natural language processing (NLP), such as machine translation, sentiment analysis, and text generation.

metadata.title: ML in Robotics
metadata.definition: Examples of using machine learning are for robot control, environmental perception, and motion planning.

metadata.title: ML in Gaming
metadata.definition: Examples of using machine learning are to develop gaming AI, create intelligent opponents, and optimize playing strategies.

metadata.title: ML Ethics
metadata.definition: Ethical issues related to the design, implementation, and use of machine learning systems, including privacy, fairness, accountability, and transparency.

metadata.title: ML Ethics: Real Scenarios
metadata.definition: Emphasizes the importance of considering the ethical implications of machine learning in real-life situations and with real data.

metadata.title: ML Ethics Case Studies
metadata.definition: analyze specific cases where ethical issues in machine learning have arisen and how they were or could be resolved.

metadata.title: ML Privacy
metadata.definition: Challenges and solutions related to protecting personal information when using data to train and deploy machine learning models.

metadata.title: ML Fairness
metadata.definition: Ensure that machine learning models do not create or perpetuate biased results that discriminate against specific groups of people.

metadata.title: ML Intellectual Property
metadata.definition: Legal and ethical issues related to ownership of data, models, algorithms, and other intellectual products in the field of machine learning.

metadata.title: Explainable AI (XAI)
metadata.definition: The ability to understand how a machine learning model makes decisions, or predictions, is especially important for 'black box' systems.

metadata.title: Statistical Learning
metadata.definition: Machine learning methods are grounded in statistical theory, using statistical models and principles to analyze data and make predictions.

metadata.title: Parameter Estimation
metadata.definition: The process of using sample data to estimate the unknown parameters of a probability distribution or statistical model.

metadata.title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)
metadata.definition: A method of parameter estimation by finding parameter values ​​that maximize the probability of observing the given data.

metadata.title: Supervised Learning
metadata.definition: A type of machine learning in which an algorithm is trained on a labeled data set, learning to map inputs to desired outputs.

metadata.title: Decision Tree
metadata.definition: A nonparametric prediction model uses a decision tree structure in which each internal node represents an attribute, each branch represents an attribute value, and each leaf node represents a class or value.

metadata.title: Nearest Neighbor Classification
metadata.definition: A non-parametric classification algorithm assigns a new data point to the class of the closest data point(s) in the training set.

metadata.title: Nearest Neighbor Regression
metadata.definition: A non-parametric regression algorithm uses the values ​​of the closest data points in the training set to predict the value for a new data point.

metadata.title: Simple Neural Networks
metadata.definition: Neural network models, with few layers and basic structure, are often used as an introductory step before learning more complex architectures.

metadata.title: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP)
metadata.definition: A type of feedforward neural network consisting of at least three layers of nodes (input layer, one or more hidden layers, and output layer), capable of learning nonlinear relationships.

metadata.title: Linear Regression
metadata.definition: A linear model predicts a continuous target variable from one or more independent variables by finding the best linear relationship.

metadata.title: Logistic Regression
metadata.definition: A statistical model is used to model the probability of a binary target variable (2-class classification) using a logistic function.

metadata.title: Support Vector Machines (SVM)
metadata.definition: A supervised learning algorithm is used for both classification and regression, which works by finding the best dividing hyperplane between data classes.

metadata.title: Kernel Functions (SVM)
metadata.definition: Functions are used in SVM to transform data into a higher dimensional space, allowing the search for nonlinear separating hyperplanes.

metadata.title: Gaussian Processes
metadata.definition: A non-parametric machine learning method based on multivariate Gaussian distribution, used for regression and classification problems.

metadata.title: Overfitting
metadata.definition: The phenomenon of a model overlearning the training data, including noise, leads to poor performance when faced with new, never-before-seen data.

metadata.title: Curse of Dimensionality
metadata.definition: Problems arise when analyzing and organizing data in high-dimensional space, as data becomes more sparse and algorithms become less efficient.

metadata.title: Regularization (Math)
metadata.definition: Deep dive into the mathematical formulas and calculations of normalization techniques, including L1 and L2, to control model complexity.

metadata.title: L2 Regularization
metadata.definition: A form of normalization that adds the square of the weight magnitude to the objective function (also called Ridge Regression or weight decay), which helps reduce large weights and avoid overfitting.

metadata.title: L1 Normalization
metadata.definition: A form of normalization that adds the absolute value of the weights to the objective function (also called Lasso Regression), which tends to bring some weights to zero, helping with feature selection.

metadata.title: Experiment Design
metadata.definition: create a systematic plan for performing machine learning experiments, including how to collect, prepare data, and evaluate models to ensure reliable results.

metadata.title: Data Preparation
metadata.definition: Steps to process raw data to make it suitable and efficient for a machine learning model, including cleaning, transforming, and encoding the data.

metadata.title: Data Standardization
metadata.definition: Adjusting data values ​​so they have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1, helps machine learning algorithms work more effectively.

metadata.title: Data Representation
metadata.definition: How the data is encoded or structured so that it can be used effectively by machine learning algorithms, e.g., feature vector format.

metadata.title: One-hot Encoding
metadata.definition: The technique converts categorical variables into a numeric format (binary vector) that can be used by a machine learning model, avoiding erroneous ordering of categories.

metadata.title: Hypothesis Space
metadata.definition: The set of all functions or models that a machine learning algorithm can choose from to solve a particular problem.

metadata.title: Bias (ML)
metadata.definition: Systematic errors or biases in data, algorithms, or machine learning decision-making processes, can lead to inaccurate or unfair results.

metadata.title: Algorithmic Bias
metadata.definition: Systematic bias in an algorithm, often due to biased training data or algorithm design, leads to unfair or inaccurate results for specific groups.

metadata.title: Search Bias
metadata.definition: Bias in the way an algorithm searches or explores the solution space, can cause optimal solutions or important regions of the space to be overlooked.

metadata.title: Data Splitting
metadata.definition: The process of dividing the overall data set into different subsets (training, validation, testing) to effectively train and evaluate the model.

metadata.title: Stratified Splitting
metadata.definition: Data partitioning technique to ensure that the scale distribution of important classes or attributes is preserved in all data subsets (training, validation, testing).

metadata.title: Training Set
metadata.definition: The data portion is used to train the machine learning model, where the model learns patterns and relationships from the data.

metadata.title: Validation Set
metadata.definition: The independent data section is used to fine-tune the model's hyper-parameters and to select the best model, avoiding overfitting during training.

metadata.title: Test Set
metadata.definition: A completely independent portion of the data is used to evaluate the final performance of the trained model, providing an unbiased estimate of generalization ability.

metadata.title: Hyperparameter Tuning
metadata.definition: The process of finding optimal values ​​for the hyperparameters of a machine learning model to achieve the best performance, usually through grid search or random search combined with cross-validation.

metadata.title: Grid Search
metadata.definition: A systematic method for fine-tuning hyper-parameters by trying all possible combinations of parameter values ​​within a predetermined grid, often combined with cross-validation.

metadata.title: Random Search
metadata.definition: An effective method for fine-tuning hyperparameters is by randomly sampling parameter combinations from a defined space, often combined with cross-validation.

metadata.title: Performance Evaluation
metadata.definition: Advanced methods and metrics are used to measure and compare the performance of machine learning models, including ROC and AUC curves.

metadata.title: Cross-Validation
metadata.definition: More advanced cross-validation techniques, including different variations (e.g., K-fold, leave-one-out) to evaluate model performance and robustly tune parameters.

metadata.title: Error Rate
metadata.definition: The basic evaluation metric for classification, measuring the misprediction rate, is considered in an advanced context along with other metrics.

metadata.title: Precision
metadata.definition: Index that evaluates the accuracy of positive predictions, used in advanced classification performance analytics.

metadata.title: Recall
metadata.definition: The metric evaluates the model's ability to find all actual positives, used in advanced classification performance analyses.

metadata.title: Confusion Matrix
metadata.definition: A detailed tool to analyze classifier performance, providing insight into the types of errors made, especially useful in complex classification scenarios.

metadata.title: ROC Curve
metadata.definition: A graph showing the model's classification performance at all possible classification thresholds, commonly used to evaluate binary classification models.

metadata.title: AUC
metadata.definition: An index that summarizes the overall performance of a classifier across all thresholds, with higher values ​​indicating a better classification model.

metadata.title: Bayesian Learning
metadata.definition: A machine learning approach based on Bayes' theorem, which combines prior knowledge with observational data to create posterior inference.

metadata.title: Naive Bayes
metadata.definition: A classification algorithm based on Bayes' theorem with the assumption of strong independence between features, commonly used in text classification.

metadata.title: Naive Bayes & Linear Models
metadata.definition: Study how Naive Bayes, although based on probability, can be understood and related to linear classification models.

metadata.title: Bayesian Networks
metadata.definition: Graphical models represent a set of variables and the conditional probability dependencies between them.

metadata.title: Prior Probability
metadata.definition: The initial belief about the probability of an event or parameter before any new data is observed.

metadata.title: Posterior Probability
metadata.definition: The probability of an event or parameter, after considering new data, is calculated by combining the prior probability and the data through Bayes' theorem.

metadata.title: Generative Models (Bayes)
metadata.definition: The models learn the joint probability distribution of data and labels, allowing the generation of new data samples and the estimation of label probabilities for a given input.

metadata.title: Deep Learning
metadata.definition: In-depth study of the theories, architecture, and applications of deep learning, including mathematical and technical aspects.

metadata.title: Deep Feedforward Networks
metadata.definition: A detailed study of the structure, operation, and mathematical aspects of deep feedforward neural networks (also known as MLPs), including activation functions, backpropagation, and optimization.

metadata.title: Neural Tangent Kernel
metadata.definition: A theoretical concept that helps understand the behavior of large neural networks (with an infinite number of neurons) during training, linking them to kernel models.

metadata.title: Neural Net Training
metadata.definition: Study the fundamentals and challenges of training neural networks, including weight initialization, optimization, learning rates, and normalization techniques.

metadata.title: Convolutional Neural Networks
metadata.definition: A detailed study of the structure, layers (convolution, pooling, fully connected) and operation of CNNs, including mathematical aspects and extensive applications in computer vision.

metadata.title: Autoencoders
metadata.definition: The neural network is trained to encode the input data into a lower-dimensional representation (encoding) and then decode that representation to reconstruct the original input.

metadata.title: Recurrent Neural Networks
metadata.definition: Deeper research on types of recurrent networks (e.g., RNNs, LSTMs, GRUs) and their ability to process sequential data, remember information over time, and applications in NLP and time series.

metadata.title: Deep Learning Representation
metadata.definition: How data is encoded or transformed by deep networks to create meaningful features, helping the model learn more complex patterns.

metadata.title: Transfer Learning
metadata.definition: Technique of using a model that has been trained on a large task or data set (e.g., pre-trained models) to improve performance on a new task or smaller data set.

metadata.title: Adversarial Training
metadata.definition: A technique for training models to become more robust against adversarial disturbances (adversarial examples), helping to improve model robustness and safety.

metadata.title: GANs
metadata.definition: A class of machine learning algorithms in which two neural networks (a generator and a discriminator) compete with each other to generate realistic new data and differentiate real/fake data.

metadata.title: Attention Mechanism
metadata.definition: A technique that allows a neural network to focus on the most important parts of the input data when processing information, especially useful in NLP and vision.

metadata.title: Representation (General)
metadata.definition: The study of how data is structured, encoded, or transformed into suitable formats so that machine learning algorithms can process and learn effectively.

metadata.title: Handcrafted Features
metadata.definition: Data features are designed by humans based on domain knowledge and experience, which often requires a high level of expertise and can be time-consuming.

metadata.title: Basis Expansion
metadata.definition: Technique that transforms data into a higher dimensional space by using basis functions (e.g., polynomial functions, spline functions) to model nonlinear relationships.

metadata.title: Learned Representation
metadata.definition: Data features are automatically discovered and extracted from raw data by the model (e.g., by a deep neural network), which is often more efficient and flexible than manual representation.

metadata.title: Deep Nets (Learned Rep.)
metadata.definition: Use deep neural networks as a powerful tool to automatically learn and extract meaningful, hierarchical representations from input data.

metadata.title: Unsupervised Learning
metadata.definition: A type of machine learning in which the algorithm looks for patterns, hidden structures, or relationships in unlabeled data, without a predetermined desired output.

metadata.title: Clustering
metadata.definition: The technique of grouping similar data points into clusters, or groups, based on some similarity measure, is a core task of unsupervised learning.

metadata.title: K-means Clustering
metadata.definition: An iterative clustering algorithm divides the data into k clusters, where each data point belongs to the cluster with the closest center.

metadata.title: Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM)
metadata.definition: A statistical model that represents data points as originating from a finite mixture of Gaussian (usually Gaussian) distributions, used for clustering and density estimation.

metadata.title: Expectation-Maximization (EM)
metadata.definition: An iterative algorithm for finding maximum likelihood estimates or maximum posterior estimates of parameters in statistical models with unobservable latent variables.

metadata.title: Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs)
metadata.definition: A type of artificial neural network belonging to the family of self-organizing neural networks, used to reduce data dimensionality and visualize complex relationships in data.

metadata.title: Graph Analysis
metadata.definition: Study the structure, properties, and relationships between nodes and edges in data represented as graphs, to discover patterns and useful information.

metadata.title: PageRank Algorithm
metadata.definition: An algorithm used by Google to rank web pages in search results, measuring the relative importance of a node (page) in a graph based on link structure.

metadata.title: Semi-Supervised Learning
metadata.definition: A type of machine learning that uses both labeled and unlabeled data to train a model, especially useful when labeling the data is expensive.

metadata.title: Graphical Models
metadata.definition: Mathematical structures represent conditional dependencies between variables through a graph, helping with probabilistic analysis and inference.

metadata.title: Ensemble Learning
metadata.definition: Research advanced model ensemble methods, including boosting, bagging, and random forest, to improve model performance and robustness.

metadata.title: Weighted Majority Vote
metadata.definition: The method combines output from component models by assigning weights to each model, especially useful in model ensembles.

metadata.title: Boosting
metadata.definition: A model ensemble technique that builds a strong classifier by combining multiple weak classifiers, training sequentially to focus on misclassified data samples.

metadata.title: Bagging
metadata.definition: A model ensemble technique that creates multiple versions of a model by resampling the training data (with replacement) and then combining the predictions.

metadata.title: Random Forest
metadata.definition: An ensemble learning algorithm uses multiple decision trees, each trained on a randomly sampled subset of data and a random feature subset, and then the predictions are aggregated.

metadata.title: Gated Ensembles
metadata.definition: A model ensemble architecture in which a 'gating' network learns to dynamically combine the output of component models based on the characteristics of the input.

metadata.title: Learning Theory
metadata.definition: An overview of the mathematical research on machine learning, focusing on understanding why machine learning algorithms work and their generalizability.

metadata.title: Learning Theory Overview
metadata.definition: Explain the fundamentals behind the ability of machine learning algorithms to learn and generalize from limited data, including the concepts of training error and generalization error.

metadata.title: VC Dimension
metadata.definition: A measure of the capacity or complexity of a class of functions (e.g. a machine learning model), indicating the maximum number of data points that the model can 'sort' in every possible way.

metadata.title: Generalization Bounds
metadata.definition: Mathematical bounds dictate how well a model can generalize on new, never-before-seen data, based on its performance on training data and the complexity of the model.

metadata.title: Reinforcement Learning
metadata.definition: A branch of machine learning that focuses on how intelligent agents should perform actions in an environment to maximize the concept of cumulative rewards over time.

metadata.title: Exploration-Exploitation Trade-off
metadata.definition: The balance between trying new actions to explore the potential for greater rewards (exploration) and leveraging existing knowledge to maximize immediate rewards (exploitation) in reinforcement learning problems.

metadata.title: Markov Decision Processes (MDPs)
metadata.definition: A mathematical framework for modeling decision making in situations where outcomes are partly random and partly under the control of the decision maker. This is the basis of many reinforcement learning algorithms.

metadata.title: Value & Policy Iteration
metadata.definition: Two basic algorithms in reinforcement learning to find optimal policies in Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). Value iteration finds the optimal value function, while policy iteration finds the optimal policy directly.

metadata.title: Policy Gradient Methods
metadata.definition: A class of reinforcement learning algorithms optimizes parametric policies directly by estimating the gradient of the objective function (usually the total reward) over the policy parameters.

metadata.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL)
metadata.definition: The combination of reinforcement learning and deep learning, using deep neural networks to represent value or policy functions, allows learning from complex, high-dimensional input data.

metadata.title: Learning from Demonstration (LfD)
metadata.definition: A method in machine learning that allows a system to learn a behavior by observing examples of that behavior performed by an agent (usually a human).

metadata.title: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL)
metadata.definition: A technique for inferring the hidden reward function that an agent is trying to optimize, based on observations of that agent's behavior.

metadata.title: Explainable AI (XAI)
metadata.definition: The field of research in machine learning aims to create models that are more understandable to humans, providing transparency into how decisions are made and the reasoning behind predictions.

metadata.title: Feature Importance
metadata.definition: The ability to determine how much each input feature contributes to the prediction or decision of a machine learning model, helps to better understand the model's behavior.

metadata.title: LIME
metadata.definition: An agnostic model explanation technique provides local explanations for the predictions of any classifier or regressor, by approximating the model's behavior around a particular example.

metadata.title: Shapley Values
metadata.definition: A method from game theory to allocate 'value' or equitable contribution to each feature in making predictions of a machine learning model.

metadata.title: Interpretable Models
metadata.definition: Machine learning models are designed to make it easier to understand how they operate or make decisions, with ways of representing data or knowledge that enhance interpretation.

metadata.title: Recommendation Systems
metadata.definition: Software systems that provide recommendations of items (products, movies, articles, etc.) to users, based on their interests, past behavior, and/or the behavior of similar users.

metadata.title: ML Hardware
metadata.definition: The physical components of computers and systems are designed or optimized to accelerate the complex and resource-intensive calculations of machine learning algorithms.

metadata.title: GPU
metadata.definition: Specialized processors were originally designed for graphics rendering, but with their powerful parallel architecture, they have become extremely effective for training deep learning models.

metadata.title: TPU
metadata.definition: Application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) were specifically developed by Google to accelerate neural network calculations, especially tensor operations in deep learning.

metadata.title: ML in Healthcare
metadata.definition: The use of machine learning algorithms to solve problems in the medical field, including disease diagnosis, drug development, medical image analysis, treatment personalization, and patient outcome prediction.

metadata.title: ML in Economics
metadata.definition: The application of machine learning techniques to analyze economic data, predict market trends, model consumer behavior, optimize economic policy, and detect financial fraud.

metadata.title: ML in Education
metadata.definition: The use of machine learning to improve the teaching and learning process, including intelligent tutoring systems, personalizing learning pathways, predicting student performance and analyzing educational data.

metadata.title: ML in Computer Vision
metadata.definition: The application of machine learning to enable computers to 'understand' and process images and videos, including object recognition, face detection, image segmentation and image description.

metadata.title: ML in NLP
metadata.definition: The use of machine learning to process and understand human language, including machine translation, sentiment analysis, text summarization, speech recognition, and text generation.

metadata.title: ML in Robotics
metadata.definition: Integrating machine learning into robots allows them to learn from experience, adapt to new environments, improve control, and perform complex tasks automatically.

metadata.title: ML in Gaming
metadata.definition: The use of machine learning to develop game agents (adversarial AI), generate game content, adjust difficulty, and analyze player behavior.

metadata.title: ML in Data Mining
metadata.definition: applying machine learning techniques to discover valuable patterns, trends, and insights from large data sets. (Refer also to DM/Data Analytics).

metadata.title: ML Ethics
metadata.definition: The study of ethical, social, and legal issues arising from the development and deployment of machine learning systems, including issues of bias, fairness, privacy, and accountability.

metadata.title: Real-world ML Ethics
metadata.definition: Focuses on analyzing real-life situations and concrete examples to better understand the ethical implications of real-world machine learning systems and methods to address them. (Refer to SEP-Context).

metadata.title: Dataset Bias
metadata.definition: The presence of bias or unrepresentation in the data used to train a machine learning model, resulting in the model making unfair or inaccurate predictions or decisions for certain groups.

metadata.title: Algorithmic Bias
metadata.definition: Systematic or unfair bias in the results of a machine learning algorithm, which may be due to the algorithm design, the training data set, or both.

metadata.title: Evaluation Bias
metadata.definition: The presence of bias in the process of evaluating the performance of a machine learning model, can lead to an incorrect assessment of the model's ability to generalize or be fair.

metadata.title: ML Data Privacy
metadata.definition: Issues related to protecting personal and sensitive information used in training and deploying machine learning models, ensuring compliance with regulations and individual rights. (Refer also to SEP-Privacy).

metadata.title: ML Fairness
metadata.definition: Ensure that machine learning systems make decisions or predictions that do not discriminate or disadvantage specific individuals or groups, regardless of their sensitive attributes.

metadata.title: ML Trust
metadata.definition: The level of confidence a user or stakeholder has in a machine learning system's ability to operate reliably, securely, and fairly, especially in mission-critical applications.

metadata.title: Ethical ML Explainability
metadata.definition: The ethical aspect of ensuring that machine learning model decisions and operations can be understood and explained by humans contributes to building trust and accountability. (Related to AI-009 but focusing on ethical aspects).

metadata.title: Supervised Learning
metadata.definition: A type of machine learning algorithm that learns a mapping from input to output based on pre-labeled input-output example pairs.

metadata.title: Unsupervised Learning
metadata.definition: A type of machine learning algorithm that looks for hidden patterns and structures in unlabeled data, such as clustering or dimensionality reduction.

metadata.title: Compare ML Paradigms
metadata.definition: Ability to distinguish and compare the characteristics, operating principles, and appropriate applications of supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning.

metadata.title: ML Paradigm Selection
metadata.definition: The ability to determine which machine learning style (supervised, reinforcement, unsupervised) is most appropriate to solve a specific problem based on the nature of the data and the goal.

metadata.title: AI
metadata.definition: The field of computer science specializes in creating intelligent machines that can perform tasks that typically require human intelligence.

metadata.title: ML
metadata.definition: A subset of artificial intelligence that enables systems to learn from data, identify patterns, and make decisions with minimal human intervention.

metadata.title: DL
metadata.definition: A subset of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers (deep neural networks) to learn representations of data with multiple levels of abstraction.

metadata.title: AI ML DL Distinction
metadata.definition: Ability to clearly differentiate the concepts of Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning and Deep Learning, understanding the hierarchical relationship and core differences between them.

metadata.title: Classification Problem Formulation
metadata.definition: The ability to structure a real-world problem so that it can be solved using classification techniques, including determining the input and output characteristics to be predicted.

metadata.title: ML Input Features
metadata.definition: Attributes or independent variables of data are used as input to a machine learning model to make predictions or decisions.

metadata.title: ML Output Prediction
metadata.definition: The value or label that a machine learning model is trained to produce based on input features.

metadata.title: Classification Problem
metadata.definition: A type of supervised learning problem in which the goal is to predict a discrete label or category for an input data point.

metadata.title: Simple Statistical Learning
metadata.definition: Basic machine learning algorithms are based on statistical principles, used to solve classification or regression problems, such as logistic regression, k-NN, or simple decision trees.

metadata.title: Classifier Accuracy
metadata.definition: Technique that quantifies the performance of a classifier by calculating the proportion of correct predictions it makes on a test data set.

metadata.title: Overfitting
metadata.definition: A situation in machine learning where a model overlearns details and noise from training data to the point that it performs poorly on new, unseen data.

metadata.title: Learning Curve
metadata.definition: Histograms show model performance (e.g., accuracy, error) as a function of the amount of training data or number of training iterations, used to diagnose overfitting or underfitting.

metadata.title: Overfitting Solutions
metadata.definition: Techniques used to minimize overfitting include regularization, data augmentation, choosing a simpler model, or using early stopping techniques.

metadata.title: ML as Optimization
metadata.definition: understand that training a machine learning model often involves minimizing a loss function or maximizing an objective function by adjusting model parameters through optimization algorithms.

metadata.title: ML as Search
metadata.definition: The concept of machine learning involves searching the space of models or parameters to find the model that best fits the given data and goals.

metadata.title: Implement Statistical Learning
metadata.definition: Ability to code and configure statistical learning algorithms to build models from data, often using specialized libraries and frameworks.

metadata.title: Classifier Training

metadata.title: Predict New Data

metadata.title: NN Training Process

metadata.title: NN Learned Representations

metadata.title: ML Performance Evaluation

metadata.title: Visualize NN Training

metadata.title: Compare ML Techniques

metadata.title: evaluate Simple ML System

metadata.title: Current ML Theory
metadata.definition: Describes the current state of machine learning theory, including its achievements and limitations.

metadata.title: Overfitting

metadata.title: Triple Tradeoff

metadata.title: ML Ethical Issues
metadata.definition: Describe ethical issues related to data selection, preprocessing steps, algorithm selection, and visualization/presentation of results in a practical Machine Learning application.

metadata.definition: Research and apply artificial intelligence in many different fields such as medicine, health, sustainability, social media, economics, education, and robotics.

metadata.title: AI Problem Evaluation
