metadata.title: Ill-defined Problems

metadata.title: Data Availability & Scarcity
metadata.definition: Issues related to data availability to train AI models, including cases where data is abundant or scarce.

metadata.title: Data Quality
metadata.definition: Importance and techniques to ensure high quality data, free of errors or noise, for AI applications.

metadata.title: Basic Data Cleaning

metadata.title: Data Preprocessing

metadata.title: Dataset Bias
metadata.definition: The existence of biases or unfair representation in the training data set, leading to potentially biased AI models.

metadata.definition: Bias in the results or decisions of an AI algorithm due to algorithm design, training data, or implementation.

metadata.title: Evaluation Bias

metadata.title: Deep Image Generative Models
metadata.definition: The operating mechanism of deep learning models capable of creating new images, including structure and principles.

metadata.title: DALL-E

metadata.title: Midjourney

metadata.title: Stable Diffusion

metadata.title: Attention (Image Generative Models)
metadata.definition: The role and how the attention mechanism works in deep image generation models to focus on important parts of the data.

metadata.title: How LLMs Work

metadata.title: ChatGPT
metadata.definition: Example of a large language model, designed for dialogue and the generation of contextually relevant text.

metadata.title: Bard

metadata.title: Attention (LLMs)
metadata.definition: The role and how attention mechanisms work in large language models to process and produce coherent text.

metadata.title: Foundational Models
metadata.definition: The concept of large models is trained on vast data and can be adapted for a variety of tasks.

metadata.title: Using Foundational Models
metadata.definition: Methods and techniques for applying and customizing platform models for specific applications.

metadata.title: Benefits of Large Data Pre-training
metadata.definition: The advantages of using large amounts of data to train underlying models include generalization and high performance.

metadata.title: Challenges of Large Data Pre-training
metadata.definition: Challenges and difficulties encountered when training underlying models on big data, such as cost, bias, and privacy issues.

metadata.title: AI Fairness

metadata.title: AI Trustworthiness

metadata.title: Explainable AI (XAI)

metadata.title: AI Data Privacy

metadata.title: Human Autonomy in AI

metadata.title: AI Sustainability

metadata.title: Propositional Logic
metadata.definition: Review basic concepts of propositional logic, including syntax, semantics, and logical operations.

metadata.title: Predicate Logic
metadata.definition: Review the basic concepts of predicate logic, including predicates, variables, quantifiers, and inference rules.

metadata.title: Propositional Resolution
metadata.definition: Deductive technique for proving the unsatisfactoriness of a set of propositions in propositional logic.

metadata.title: Propositional Theorem Proving
metadata.definition: Use deductive methods, such as solution, to prove the correctness of a theorem in propositional logic.

metadata.title: Forward Chaining
metadata.definition: An inference strategy starts from known facts and applies rules to infer new facts until the goal is achieved.

metadata.title: Backward Chaining
metadata.definition: An inference strategy starts from a goal and looks for rules that can lead to that goal, tracing back to the necessary conditions.

metadata.title: Knowledge Representation Issues
metadata.definition: Discuss the challenges and difficulties in representing knowledge effectively so that computers can process and reason.

metadata.title: Description Logics (DLs)
metadata.definition: A family of knowledge representation languages ​​used to model concepts and the relationships between them.

metadata.title: Ontology Engineering
metadata.definition: The process of building and developing ontologies, i.e. models that formalize concepts and relationships in a knowledge domain.

metadata.title: Semantic Web
metadata.definition: An extension of the World Wide Web where data is given semantic meaning, allowing computers to understand and process information more effectively.

metadata.title: Non-monotonic Reasoning
metadata.definition: Type of inference in which conclusions can be revoked when new information is added.

metadata.title: Non-classical Logics
metadata.definition: Logic systems extend or modify the principles of classical logic to handle problems such as inconsistency, uncertainty, or nonmonotonicity.

metadata.title: Default Reasoning
metadata.definition: A form of nonmonotonic inference where conclusions are drawn based on default assumptions in the absence of conflicting information.

metadata.title: Argumentation
metadata.definition: The study of how to construct, analyze and evaluate logical arguments, especially in multi-agent systems.

metadata.title: Action & Change Reasoning
metadata.definition: Techniques and models for representing and reasoning about how actions change the state of the world.

metadata.title: Situation Calculus
metadata.definition: A first-order predicate logic language is used to represent knowledge about actions and their effects.

metadata.title: Event Calculus
metadata.definition: A logic-based knowledge representation method used to reason about time and occurrences.

metadata.title: Temporal Reasoning
metadata.definition: Reason about temporal relationships between events and states, including concepts such as before, after, and concurrent.

metadata.title: Spatial Reasoning
metadata.definition: Infer spatial relationships between objects, including location, shape, and orientation.

metadata.title: Logic Programming
metadata.definition: A style of programming based on formal logic, in which programs are written as logical statements and execution is a process of proving theorems.

metadata.title: Prolog
metadata.definition: A popular logic programming language, commonly used in AI applications involving knowledge representation and inference.

metadata.title: Answer Set Programming (ASP)
metadata.definition: A form of non-monotonic logic programming, used to solve search and optimization problems by finding 'solution sets'.

metadata.title: Rule-based Expert Systems
metadata.definition: AI systems simulate human decision-making using a set of 'IF-THEN' rules.

metadata.title: Semantic Networks
metadata.definition: A method of representing knowledge as a graph, where nodes represent concepts and edges represent relationships between them.

metadata.title: Model-based Reasoning
metadata.definition: An inference method uses a qualitative or quantitative model of a system to predict or explain its behavior.

metadata.title: Case-based Reasoning
metadata.definition: A method of inference that solves new problems by adapting solutions used in similar cases before.

metadata.title: Clausal Form
metadata.definition: A standard form of logic formulas, commonly used in theorem solutions and proofs, consisting of clauses containing only selection operators.

metadata.title: Planning Systems
metadata.definition: AI systems are capable of generating a sequence of actions to achieve a specific goal from an initial state.

metadata.title: Planning as Search
metadata.definition: View planning as a search problem in state space or plan space.

metadata.title: Operator-based Planning
metadata.definition: The planning method uses operator (action) definitions to transition world states.

metadata.title: Propositional Planning
metadata.definition: A type of planning that uses propositional logic to represent states and goals, often involving conversion to a Boolean satisfaction problem.

metadata.title: Monotonic Inference
metadata.definition: A type of inference in which conclusions drawn are never revoked when new information becomes available.

metadata.title: Non-monotonic Inference
metadata.definition: A type of inference in which conclusions may change or be revoked as new information is added, as opposed to monotonic inference.

metadata.title: Conditional Independence
metadata.definition: Review the concept of two variables being conditionally independent of each other when the value of a third variable is known.

metadata.title: Probabilistic Knowledge Representation
metadata.definition: Methods for representing knowledge in probabilistic models, including how to represent uncertainty and stochastic relationships.

metadata.title: Bayesian Networks
metadata.definition: The probabilistic graphical model represents a set of variables and the conditionally independent relationships between them.

metadata.title: Exact Bayesian Inference
metadata.definition: Algorithms to calculate exact probability distributions of variables in a Bayesian Network given observational information.

metadata.title: Bayesian Inference Complexity
metadata.definition: An analysis of the computational cost and factors affecting the complexity of exact inference algorithms in Bayesian Networks.

metadata.title: Markov Blankets
metadata.definition: The set of nodes in a Bayesian Network such that, knowing their value, a node becomes independent of all other nodes in the network.

metadata.title: d-separation
metadata.definition: A graphical criterion for determining conditional independence between sets of variables in Bayesian Networks.

metadata.title: Monte Carlo Sampling
metadata.definition: Simulation techniques rely on random sampling to estimate quantities in complex probability models.

metadata.title: Gibbs Sampling
metadata.definition: A Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling algorithm is used to sample from a multivariate probability distribution that is difficult to sample directly.

metadata.title: Markov Networks
metadata.definition: The undirected probability graph model represents dependency relationships between variables through potential functions on subgroups of variables.

metadata.title: Relational Probabilistic Models
metadata.definition: Probabilistic models extend probabilistic graph theory to represent relationships between entities, allowing inference and learning in complex domains.

metadata.title: Hidden Markov Models (HMM)
metadata.definition: A statistical model in which the system being modeled is assumed to be a Markov process with hidden states that are not directly observable, but can only be inferred from available observations.

metadata.title: Decision Theory
metadata.definition: The study of the decisions of agents when the consequences of their choices are not known with certainty, including probabilistic and utility inference methods.

metadata.title: Preferences and Utility Functions
metadata.definition: Concepts in decision theory for quantifying the degree of desirability or value that an agent assigns to various outcomes or states.

metadata.title: Expected Utility Maximization
metadata.definition: A principle in decision theory according to which a rational agent should choose the action that maximizes the total expected value (utility) of all possible outcomes.

metadata.title: Game Theory
metadata.definition: Study mathematical models of conflict and cooperation between intelligent and rational decision-making agents.

metadata.title: Propositional & First-Order Logic
metadata.definition: Review the fundamentals of propositional and first-order logic, used as the foundation for knowledge representation and reasoning in AI.

metadata.title: Planning Operators & State Representation
metadata.definition: How to identify possible actions (operators) and how to describe states of the world in AI planning problems.

metadata.title: Total Order Planning
metadata.definition: A planning method in which all actions in the plan are arranged in a specific linear order.

metadata.title: Partial Order Planning
metadata.definition: A planning method in which only the necessary ordering constraints between actions are specified, allowing unrelated actions to be performed in parallel or in any order.

metadata.title: Plan Graphs & GraphPlan
metadata.definition: Techniques for representing planning problems in graph form to find effective solutions, such as the GraphPlan algorithm.

metadata.title: Hierarchical Planning
metadata.definition: A planning method that divides a large problem into smaller, more abstract sub-problems and solves them in a hierarchical structure.

metadata.title: Planning Languages & Representation
metadata.definition: Standard languages ​​and methods for describing planning problems, including states, goals, and operators.

metadata.title: PDDL
metadata.definition: A standardized language used to describe planning domains and problems in AI, allowing different planners to work on the same problem definition.

metadata.title: Multi-agent Planning
metadata.definition: Plan for systems that include multiple interacting agents, where each agent may have its own goals and need to coordinate actions.

metadata.title: MDP-based Planning
metadata.definition: Planning in uncertain environments using a Markov Decision Process framework to find optimal action policies.

metadata.title: Planning, Execution & Replanning
metadata.definition: The study of how plans are created, implemented, and continuously adjusted in changing or uncertain environments.

metadata.title: Conditional Planning
metadata.definition: A type of planning that creates plans with ramifications, allowing the agent to react to uncertain outcomes of actions.

metadata.title: Continuous Planning
metadata.definition: Plan in environments where time and actions can occur continuously rather than discretely.

metadata.title: Probabilistic Planning
metadata.definition: Planning in environments where the outcomes of actions are uncertain and described by probability distributions.

metadata.title: Agent Architectures
metadata.definition: Frameworks, or structural designs for building intelligent agents, dictate how they process information, make decisions, and perform actions.

metadata.title: Reactive Agent Architectures
metadata.definition: Simple agent architectures respond directly to environmental stimuli without the need to plan or maintain internal models.

metadata.title: Layered Agent
metadata.definition: Agent architectures include multiple layers to handle behaviors at different levels of abstraction, combining reaction and planning.

metadata.title: Cognitive Agent
metadata.definition: Agent architectures simulate human cognitive abilities such as reasoning, learning, planning, and knowledge maintenance.

metadata.title: Agent Theory
metadata.definition: Theoretical study of intelligent agents, including mathematical formulas to describe their behavior, goals, and interactions.

metadata.title: Agent Rationality
metadata.definition: The concept of rational agent behavior, where the agent acts to achieve its goals in the most efficient manner, based on available information.

metadata.title: Game Theory
metadata.definition: The study of strategies and interactions of intelligent and rational agents in competitive or cooperative situations, especially in the context of multi-agent systems.

metadata.title: Decision-Theoretic Agent
metadata.definition: Agents make decisions based on the principles of decision theory, considering the utility and probability of different outcomes.

metadata.title: Agent MDP
metadata.definition: Use Markov Decision Processes to model and solve agent decision-making problems in dynamic and uncertain environments.

metadata.title: Bandit Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms are used for explore-exploit problems, where an agent must make repeated choices from a set of options (arm) to maximize the reward.

metadata.title: Software Agent
metadata.definition: Computer programs perform autonomous tasks on behalf of users or other programs in a digital environment.

metadata.title: Personal AI Assistant
metadata.definition: Software agents are designed to assist users in daily tasks, providing information and automating activities.

metadata.title: Info Retrieval Agent
metadata.definition: Agents specialize in searching, retrieving, and filtering information from different sources for users.

metadata.title: Collaborative Agent
metadata.definition: Agents work together to achieve a common goal or share information to improve each other's performance, applicable in both software agents and multi-agent systems.

metadata.title: Information Gathering Agent
metadata.definition: Agents are designed to automatically collect and synthesize information from their environment.

metadata.title: Trustworthy Agent
metadata.definition: Agents are designed to exhibit human-like characteristics or emotions to enhance user trust and engagement.

metadata.title: Agent Emotion Modeling
metadata.definition: Techniques and methods for AI agents to recognize, express, and react to emotions, to create more natural interactions.

metadata.title: Learning Agent
metadata.definition: Agents have the ability to improve their performance over time by learning from experience or data.

metadata.title: Cognitive Systems
metadata.definition: AI systems are designed to simulate and replicate human cognitive abilities such as learning, reasoning, memory, problem solving, and decision making.

metadata.title: Cognitive Architectures
metadata.definition: Frameworks or theories about the overall structure of a cognitive system, integrating different information processing capabilities.

metadata.title: ACT-R Architecture
metadata.definition: A cognitive architecture developed at Carnegie Mellon University, focused on modeling human cognition and learning, including memory components and modules.

metadata.title: SOAR Architecture
metadata.definition: An artificial intelligence synthesis and cognitive architecture designed to solve problems by searching the state space and using 'chunking' to learn.

metadata.title: ICARUS Architecture
metadata.definition: A cognitive architecture focuses on high-level cognitive modeling, conceptual learning, and goal-based planning.

metadata.title: FORR Architecture
metadata.definition: A cognitive architecture designed to model decision making and learning, especially in strategically demanding tasks.

metadata.title: Cognitive Perception
metadata.definition: The ability of a cognitive system to collect, interpret, and process information from the environment through sensors or input data.

metadata.title: Cognitive Decision Making
metadata.definition: The process by which the cognitive system chooses between different actions or outcomes, often based on goals, knowledge, and available information.

metadata.title: Cognitive Prediction
metadata.definition: The ability of a cognitive system to estimate future events or states based on current and past information.

metadata.title: Cognitive Knowledge Maintenance
metadata.definition: Processes and techniques for updating, modifying, and managing the knowledge base of a cognitive system over time.

metadata.title: Cognitive Knowledge Representation
metadata.definition: How knowledge is encoded and stored so that cognitive systems can use it to reason and make decisions.

metadata.title: Cognitive Knowledge Organization
metadata.definition: Methods for structuring and organizing knowledge to optimize retrieval and use in cognitive systems.

metadata.title: Cognitive Knowledge Utilization
metadata.definition: How the cognitive system applies existing knowledge to solve problems, make decisions, or perform tasks.

metadata.title: Cognitive Knowledge Acquisition
metadata.definition: Methods and processes for capturing new knowledge from the environment, data, or people and integrating it into cognitive systems.

metadata.title: Cognitive Knowledge Refinement
metadata.definition: The process of improving the accuracy, completeness, and efficiency of knowledge in a cognitive system through learning or feedback.

metadata.title: Cognitive System Evaluation
metadata.definition: Practical use cases of cognitive systems and methods to evaluate their performance, efficiency, and rationality.

metadata.title: Multi-Agent Systems
metadata.definition: Systems consist of multiple agents that interact with each other and with the environment to achieve their own goals or common goals.

metadata.title: Agent Teams
metadata.definition: A collection of collaborating actors with assigned roles and responsibilities to perform more complex tasks.

metadata.title: Competitive Agents
metadata.definition: Agents in a multi-agent system have conflicting goals and compete with each other to maximize their own utility or reward.

metadata.title: MAS Auctions
metadata.definition: Application of auction mechanisms to allocate resources or tasks among competing agents in a multi-agent system.

metadata.title: MAS Voting
metadata.definition: Voting methods and algorithms for aggregating the preferences or decisions of multiple agents into a common choice.

metadata.title: Swarm Intelligence
metadata.definition: Multi-agent systems simulate the collective behavior of populations of organisms (such as ants, birds) to solve problems.

metadata.title: MAS Learning
metadata.definition: The field that studies how agents in a multiagent system learn and adapt in their interacting environments.

metadata.title: Human-Agent Interaction
metadata.definition: The study of how humans and AI agents interact, including interface design, communication, and trust.

metadata.title: HAI Communication Methods
metadata.definition: The ways in which humans and AI agents exchange information, including both verbal and nonverbal communication.

metadata.title: HAI Verbal Communication
metadata.definition: The techniques and challenges of using spoken or written language for AI agents to interact with humans.

metadata.title: HAI Nonverbal Communication
metadata.definition: Research on how AI agents can use or interpret non-verbal signals such as gestures, facial expressions, and tone of voice to interact with humans.

metadata.title: HAI Practical Issues
metadata.definition: Practical challenges and considerations in designing, implementing, and maintaining AI human-agent interaction systems.

metadata.title: Transactional Agents
metadata.definition: AI agents are designed to carry out buying, selling, auctioning or negotiating activities in financial markets or e-commerce.

metadata.title: Agent-based Supply Chain
metadata.definition: apply AI agents to automate, optimize and manage supply chain processes.

metadata.title: Ethical AI Interaction
metadata.definition: Ethical concerns arise from AI systems' interactions with humans, including privacy, responsibility, bias, and fairness.

metadata.title: AI Interaction Regulations
metadata.definition: Legal and regulatory frameworks govern the design, deployment, and use of human-interactive AI systems to ensure safety, security, and fairness.

metadata.title: NLP
metadata.definition: The field of AI focuses on enabling computers to understand, interpret, and generate natural human language.

metadata.title: Deterministic & Stochastic Grammar
metadata.definition: understand and distinguish between deterministic grammars (which always produce the same result for the same input) and stochastic grammars (which use probability to choose between options).

metadata.title: Parsing Algorithms
metadata.definition: Research methods and algorithms to analyze the syntactic structure of a sentence in natural language.

metadata.title: CFG & CYK Parser
metadata.definition: Learn about Context-Free Grammar (CFG) and graph parsing algorithms like CYK, which are used to determine whether a string belongs to a specific grammar.

metadata.title: PCFG & Weighted CYK
metadata.definition: Research on Probabilistic Context-Free Grammar (PCFG) and how the CYK algorithm can be extended to handle probabilities in grammars.

metadata.title: Semantic Representation
metadata.definition: Explore methods for representing the semantic meaning of natural language, a core task in Natural Language Processing.

metadata.title: Logic Knowledge Representation
metadata.definition: Learn how to use formal logic to represent and reason on knowledge from natural language.

metadata.title: Semantic Roles
metadata.definition: Study how entities in a sentence play different roles (e.g., agent, object, tool) in an event or action.

metadata.title: Temporal Representation
metadata.definition: Explore methods for representing and reasoning about temporal information extracted from text.

metadata.title: BDI Model
metadata.definition: The study of cognitive models for representing the beliefs, desires, and intentions of agents, especially in the context of language processing and social reasoning.

metadata.title: Corpus-based Methods
metadata.definition: Learn about using large data sets (corpora) to analyze, model, and develop NLP applications.

metadata.title: N-gram & HMM
metadata.definition: Study statistical models such as N-grams (sequences of words) and Hidden Markov Models (HMM) to predict and analyze sequences in natural language.

metadata.title: Smoothing & Backoff
metadata.definition: Learn smoothing and redundancy techniques for handling invisible events (sparse data) in statistical language models.

metadata.title: POS Tagging & Morphology
metadata.definition: Study practical applications of NLP such as word-class tagging (assigning word-class labels to each word) and morphology (studying word structure).

metadata.title: Information Retrieval
metadata.definition: Learn about methods and systems for searching and retrieving relevant information from a document collection.

metadata.title: Vector Space Model
metadata.definition: Study the vector space model, where documents and queries are represented as vectors to calculate similarity.

metadata.title: TF-IDF
metadata.definition: Learn about the TF (Term Frequency) and IDF (Inverse Document Frequency) statistics used to evaluate the importance of a word in a document and in a collection of documents.

metadata.title: Precision & Recall
metadata.definition: Study important performance metrics such as precision and recall in information retrieval and classification tasks.

metadata.title: Information Extraction
metadata.definition: Learn about techniques for automatically extracting structured information from unstructured text.

metadata.title: Machine Translation
metadata.definition: Research methods and models to automatically translate text from one language to another.

metadata.title: Text Classification & Clustering
metadata.definition: Learn about methods for assigning predefined labels or categories to text.

metadata.title: Bag-of-Words Model
metadata.definition: Study the bag of words model, a simple representation in NLP and information retrieval, where word order is ignored and only word frequency is considered.

metadata.title: Deep Learning for NLP
metadata.definition: Learn advanced deep learning techniques applied in the field of Natural Language Processing.

metadata.title: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs)
metadata.definition: Research Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), a type of neural network suitable for processing sequence data such as text.

metadata.title: Transformer Model
metadata.definition: Learn about the Transformer architecture, an advanced model based on self-attention, revolutionizing NLP tasks.

metadata.title: Multimodal Embeddings
metadata.definition: Study how to represent data from multiple modalities (e.g., text, images) into a common vector space to understand multimodal context.

metadata.title: Generative Language Models
metadata.definition: Learn about language models that produce new, coherent, and meaningful text.

metadata.title: Robotics Overview
metadata.definition: Overview of current challenges, unsolved problems, and significant advances in the field of robotics.

metadata.title: Modern Robotic Systems & Sensors
metadata.definition: Explore the most advanced robotic systems, the types of sensors they use, and how sensor data is processed for decision making.

metadata.title: Robot Control Architectures
metadata.definition: Study different ways to design robot control systems, including proactive (planning) and reactive (sensor-based) architectures, along with the Braitenberg vehicle concept.

metadata.title: Robotics World Models
metadata.definition: Learn how robots build and maintain internal representations of their surroundings (world models) to plan and navigate.

metadata.title: Robotics Uncertainty
metadata.definition: Explores the nature of uncertainties in sensor data and in the implementation of robot control actions, as well as methods for managing them.

metadata.title: Robotics Sensors & Actuators
metadata.definition: Learn about the input devices (sensors) and output devices (actuators) that robots use to interact with the physical world.

metadata.title: Robotics Sensors
metadata.definition: Study specific types of sensors used in robotics, including LIDAR, sonar, vision systems, depth sensors, stereoscopic, event cameras, microphones, and tactile sensors.

metadata.title: Robotics Actuators
metadata.definition: Learn about the types of actuators that robots use to move, manipulate, or physically interact, such as wheels, robotic arms, and grippers.

metadata.title: Robotics Coordinate Systems
metadata.definition: Study how to represent the position and orientation of a robot and its components using coordinate systems, translations and rotations in 2D and 3D space.

metadata.title: Configuration Space & Maps
metadata.definition: Learn about the configuration space (the set of all possible positions and orientations of the robot) and the types of environment maps used to plan the robot's movements.

metadata.title: Uncertain Sensor Data Interpretation
metadata.definition: Study methods and algorithms for processing and interpreting data from robotic sensors, which often contain uncertainty and noise.

metadata.title: SLAM in Robotics
metadata.definition: Learn about the Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) problem, where a robot builds a map of its environment while simultaneously tracking its own position within that map.

metadata.title: Robotics Navigation & Control
metadata.definition: Study of algorithms and strategies that allow robots to move through their environment autonomously and perform the necessary control actions.

metadata.title: Forward & Inverse Kinematics
metadata.definition: Learn about forward kinematics (determining the final position based on joint angles) and inverse kinematics (determining joint angles to achieve the desired final position) of a robot arm.

metadata.title: Motion Planning & Trajectory Opt.
metadata.definition: Research algorithms to find safe and effective paths for robots to move in environments with obstacles, as well as optimize trajectories according to criteria such as time or energy.

metadata.title: Robotics Manipulation & Grasping
metadata.definition: Learn about techniques and strategies for robots to manipulate and grasp various objects in physical environments.

metadata.title: Joint Control & Dynamics
metadata.definition: Study how to control each individual joint of the robot and understand how the dynamics (force, torque) affect the robot's movements.

metadata.title: Vision-based Robot Control
metadata.definition: Learn about robot control systems that use data from visual sensors (cameras) to guide movement and interaction.

metadata.title: Multi-Robot Coordination
metadata.definition: Research methods for multiple robots to work together effectively to complete a common task, including task assignment and communication.

metadata.title: Human-Robot Interaction (HRI)
metadata.definition: Explore the research field of how humans and robots can interact naturally and effectively.

metadata.title: Shared Workspace HRI
metadata.definition: Learn about scenarios and designs where humans and robots share a physical space to perform tasks.

metadata.title: Human-Robot Teaming & Physical HRI
metadata.definition: Research on how humans and robots can form teams to complete tasks, including direct physical interaction between the two.

metadata.title: Socially Assistive Robots

metadata.title: HRI Intent Prediction
metadata.definition: Research methods for robots to predict human actions, tasks or goals to improve coordination in HRI.

metadata.title: HRI Collaboration & Communication
metadata.definition: Learn diverse forms of human-robot communication and cooperation, from explicit commands to nonverbal signals, to achieve common goals.

metadata.title: Robot-Human Trust

metadata.title: Robotics Impact

metadata.title: Robot Labor Impact
metadata.definition: Research the broader impacts of robotics on society, the economy and the labor market, including right-to-work issues.

metadata.title: Robot Privacy Ethics

metadata.title: Autonomous Robot Liability
metadata.definition: Research legal frameworks and challenges in determining liability when autonomous robots cause damage or accidents.

metadata.title: Autonomous Weapons Ethics
metadata.definition: Discusses the ethical and social issues involved in the development and use of fully autonomous weapons systems capable of making killing decisions without human intervention.

metadata.title: Human Supervision Robotics
metadata.definition: Research the importance and methods to ensure humans can still effectively monitor and control autonomous robotic systems.

metadata.title: Robot Navigation Strategies
metadata.definition: Study different methods and algorithms for robots to move in environments with complete or incomplete information, including path planning, obstacle avoidance, and positioning.

metadata.title: Robot Navigation Analysis
metadata.definition: evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of different robot navigation strategies, considering their effectiveness, reliability, and applicability in specific situations.

metadata.title: Multi-Robot Coordination
metadata.definition: Methods and algorithms for synchronizing and managing the actions of a group of robots to complete a common task.

metadata.title: Multi-Robot Sensor Fusion
metadata.definition: Methods for robots to share and integrate sensor data from multiple sources to gain a more comprehensive view of the environment and support common missions.

metadata.title: Multi-Robot vs. HRI
metadata.definition: analyze the differences in goals, methods, and challenges between collaborative autonomous robotic systems and robotic systems that work alongside humans.

metadata.title: Multi-Robot vs. HRI Contexts
metadata.definition: Study how requirements, constraints, and characteristics of the task environment shape different approaches to multi-robot coordination and human-robot collaboration.

metadata.title: Robot Social Impact
metadata.definition: analyzes the impacts of robotics on society, including employment, social interaction, and cultural change.

metadata.title: Robot Economic Impact
metadata.definition: analyze the economic impacts of robotics, including productivity, production costs, and resource distribution.

metadata.title: Robot Ethics
metadata.definition: analyze ethical issues related to robot design, deployment, and use, such as privacy, responsibility, and fairness.

metadata.title: Computer Vision
metadata.definition: The field that studies how computers can 'understand' and process images and videos from the real world, including methods of image acquisition, representation and analysis.

metadata.title: Image Acquisition
metadata.definition: Methods and technologies for collecting image data from sensor devices such as cameras.

metadata.title: Image Representation
metadata.definition: Ways to store and structure image data for computer processing, such as pixel matrices, histograms, or feature-based descriptions.

metadata.title: Image Processing
metadata.definition: Techniques for transforming, enhancing, or extracting information from digital images, including filtering, transforming, and restoring images.

metadata.title: Image Properties
metadata.definition: Image characteristics and properties such as brightness, contrast, color, texture, and shape.

metadata.title: Shape Representation
metadata.definition: Methods for describing and encoding the shape of an object in an image, such as by contour, region, or geometric feature.

metadata.title: Object Recognition
metadata.definition: The process of identifying and classifying specific objects in an image or video.

metadata.title: Image Segmentation
metadata.definition: Technique of dividing a digital image into segments (sets of pixels) to simplify or change the image representation, making analysis easier.

metadata.title: Motion Analysis (CV)
metadata.definition: Techniques for detecting, tracking, and estimating object or camera motion in an image or video sequence.

metadata.title: Generative Models (CV)
metadata.definition: Machine learning models are capable of generating new image data similar to training data, which is used in image synthesis, quality enhancement, and style transformation.

metadata.title: Audio Recognition
metadata.definition: The computer process of identifying and classifying different types of sounds (e.g., environmental noise, animal sounds, music).

metadata.title: Speech Recognition
metadata.definition: Technology that converts spoken language into text, allowing computers to understand and respond to human speech.

metadata.title: Tactile Sensing
metadata.definition: Research on how AI systems process and interpret information from tactile sensors to physically interact with the environment.

metadata.title: Proprioception
metadata.definition: The ability of a robot or AI system to sense the position, orientation, and movement of its own body parts.

metadata.title: AI Olfaction & Others
metadata.definition: Explore other non-visual or auditory sensory modalities that AI can use, such as sensing smell (olfactory).

metadata.title: Modular Recognition
metadata.definition: Design identity systems into independent, exchangeable or reusable components, to improve flexibility and maintainability.

metadata.title: Pattern Recognition Methods
metadata.definition: Techniques and algorithms for finding and identifying patterns in data, often used for classification or clustering.

metadata.title: Classification Algorithms
metadata.definition: Machine learning algorithms are used to assign category labels to data points based on features learned from the training data set.

metadata.title: Classification Metrics
metadata.definition: Metrics and statistics used to evaluate the performance of a classification algorithm, such as accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1-score.

metadata.title: Statistical Pattern Recognition
metadata.definition: apply statistical methods such as Bayesian analysis and support vector machines (SVM) to build pattern recognition models.

metadata.title: Deep Learning (PR)
metadata.definition: Use deep neural networks, such as convolutional networks (CNN) and recurrent networks (RNN), to automatically learn features and perform high-performance pattern recognition.

metadata.title: Thresholding Segmentation
metadata.definition: A simple image segmentation method based on choosing a threshold value to separate pixels into two or more groups (e.g., foreground and background).

metadata.title: Edge-based Segmentation
metadata.definition: Image segmentation techniques are based on detecting boundaries and edges in images, where pixel intensities change suddenly.

metadata.title: Region-based Segmentation
metadata.definition: Image segmentation methods group neighboring pixels with similar properties (e.g., color, texture) into larger regions.

metadata.title: Contour Shape Representation
metadata.definition: A way to represent the shape of an object by describing its outer boundary (contour).

metadata.title: Region Shape Representation
metadata.definition: A way of representing the shape of an object by describing the properties of the region it occupies (e.g. area, center, moment).

metadata.title: Speaker Recognition
metadata.definition: The technology determines a speaker's identity from their voice, as opposed to recognizing speech content.

metadata.title: Cross-Modal Data Conversion
metadata.definition: Technique that transforms data from one type of sensor (e.g., tactile) into a format that can be processed by another sensory domain (e.g., visual).

metadata.title: Feature Extraction Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms are used to extract salient and meaningful features from raw data (e.g., images, sounds) to reduce data dimensionality and improve machine learning performance.

metadata.title: Edge Detection
metadata.definition: An image processing technique for identifying points in an image that have abrupt changes in pixel intensity, often representing the boundaries of objects.

metadata.title: Corner Detection
metadata.definition: An image processing technique for finding special points in an image where two edges intersect, often used as feature points for tracking or image registration.

metadata.title: Audio Fourier Coefficients
metadata.definition: apply Fourier transform to analyze the frequency spectrum of audio signals, extracting coefficients representing the frequency components of the signal.

metadata.title: High-Level Perception Fusion
metadata.definition: The process of synthesizing low-level features (e.g., edges, corners) into more complex perceptual concepts (e.g., contours, objects, phonemes).

metadata.title: Contour/Polygon Construction
metadata.definition: Algorithms combine basic visual features (such as line segments or points) to form more complex geometric structures such as contours or polygons of objects.

metadata.title: Phoneme Hypothesis
metadata.definition: The process of analyzing audio signals to make predictions about the phonemes (the smallest meaningful units of sound) present in speech.

metadata.title: AI Fundamentals
metadata.definition: Overview of the fundamental areas of Artificial Intelligence and the ability to understand, develop, and apply techniques in each area.

metadata.title: AI Search
metadata.definition: Ability to solve problems using search techniques in Artificial Intelligence.

metadata.title: KRR

metadata.title: ML Fundamentals
metadata.definition: understand and apply simple machine learning methods to solve problems in Artificial Intelligence.

metadata.title: Bayesian Reasoning
metadata.definition: Knowledge of probability and ability to apply basic Bayesian reasoning to solve problems in AI.

metadata.title: AI Ethics
metadata.definition: Understanding of various applications of AI and related ethical and social impacts. This topic is integrated throughout the AI ​​course.

metadata.title: ML Learning Types
metadata.definition: Ability to understand, develop, and apply mechanisms for supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning.

metadata.title: ML KRR
metadata.definition: Knowledge of knowledge representation and inference methods in the context of Machine Learning applications.

metadata.title: Selected NLP Topics
metadata.definition: Selected topics in Natural Language Processing, including TF-IDF, bag of words, and text classification.

metadata.title: TF-IDF
metadata.definition: TF-IDF technique to evaluate the importance of a word in a document compared to the entire document set.

metadata.title: Bag of Words
metadata.definition: Bag of Words model to represent text as a vector of word frequency counts, ignoring grammar and word order.

metadata.title: Text Classification
metadata.definition: Techniques for classifying text into defined categories.

metadata.title: ML Ethics
metadata.definition: Ability to explain the ethical and social implications of applying machine learning to real-world problems. This topic is integrated throughout the course.

metadata.title: ML Algorithm Selection
metadata.definition: Ability to select the most suitable machine learning algorithm for a specific problem.

metadata.title: ML Data Preprocessing
metadata.definition: Ability to appropriately preprocess data to prepare it for machine learning algorithms.

metadata.title: ML Evaluation Techniques
metadata.definition: Ability to apply appropriate evaluation techniques to measure machine learning model performance.

metadata.title: ML Model Interpretability
metadata.definition: Ability to explain trained machine learning models, including understanding their strengths and limitations.

metadata.title: Detecting Data Bias & Errors
metadata.definition: Ability to identify biased data sets and other sources of error that can affect machine learning results.

metadata.title: Data Bias Mitigation
metadata.definition: Ability to apply methods to compensate for biased data sets and minimize their impact.

metadata.title: Supervised Learning
metadata.definition: understand and apply the basic mechanisms and principles of supervised learning.

metadata.title: Unsupervised Learning
metadata.definition: understand and apply the basic mechanisms and principles of unsupervised learning.

metadata.title: Reinforcement Learning
metadata.definition: understand and apply the basic mechanisms and principles of reinforcement learning.

metadata.title: Robotics Fundamentals
metadata.definition: Ability to understand and use robotics techniques to perceive the world using sensors, position the robot, plan paths, and navigate in simple robotics applications.

metadata.title: Robotics Hardware
metadata.definition: Knowledge focuses on the robot's hardware, including components and structures.

metadata.title: Robotics Constraints
metadata.definition: Knowledge of important constraints and considerations in robot design, operation and programming.

metadata.title: Robotics Software Architecture
metadata.definition: Knowledge of software architectures used to develop and control robots.

metadata.title: Robotics Search Techniques
metadata.definition: Selected search topics are well integrated with robotics, e.g. A* algorithm and path search.

metadata.definition: understand and apply the A* search algorithm to plan optimal paths for robots.

metadata.title: Robotics Pathfinding
metadata.definition: Ability to plan paths and navigate robots in simple environments.

metadata.title: Machine Learning in Robotics
metadata.definition: Selected machine learning topics are well integrated with robotics, e.g. neural networks for object recognition.

metadata.title: Object Recognition NNs
metadata.definition: applying neural networks to object recognition tasks in robotics applications.

metadata.title: Robotics Ethics
metadata.definition: Focus on social impact and specific, integrated robotics applications throughout the robotics course.

metadata.title: Robot Sensor Perception
metadata.definition: Ability to use robotic techniques to collect and process information from sensors to perceive the environment.

metadata.title: Robot Localization

metadata.title: Robotics Computer Vision Basics
metadata.definition: Ability to understand and apply simple computer vision techniques in robotics applications.

metadata.title: Robotics Motion Planning
metadata.definition: Ability to understand and apply motion planning techniques for robots.

metadata.title: Forward Kinematics

metadata.title: Inverse Kinematics
metadata.definition: Ability to understand and apply inverse kinematics techniques to determine the joint angle required for a desired end position and orientation.

metadata.title: Data Visualization Types
metadata.definition: Understanding of different types of charts and graphs for data visualization.

metadata.title: Data Visualization Libraries
metadata.definition: Knowledge of popular software libraries used to create data visualizations.

metadata.title: Data Visualization Fundamentals
metadata.definition: The fundamentals and theoretical foundations behind designing and creating effective data visualizations.

metadata.title: Ethical Data Visualization
metadata.definition: Understanding of ethical issues related to the presentation and interpretation of data through visualization.

metadata.title: Parallel Data Processing
metadata.definition: Concepts and techniques for parallel data processing in data management systems.

metadata.title: Distributed Data Processing
metadata.definition: Distributed data processing concepts and techniques, including frameworks such as MapReduce and cloud frameworks.

metadata.title: MapReduce
metadata.definition: MapReduce programming model and framework for processing and generating large data sets with distributed algorithms.

metadata.title: Cloud Data Processing Frameworks
metadata.definition: Cloud-based frameworks and platforms are used for large-scale data processing and analysis.

metadata.title: Graph Data Modeling
metadata.definition: Knowledge of how to represent data in graph form and applications in data modeling.

metadata.title: Entity Resolution
metadata.definition: Techniques for identifying and merging records referencing the same entity in different data sources.

metadata.title: SQL
metadata.definition: Ability to use SQL to query, manage, and manipulate data in relational databases.

metadata.title: Query Building
metadata.definition: Skills in building effective and accurate queries to extract desired information from data.

metadata.title: Graph Database (NoSQL)
metadata.definition: Knowledge of graph databases and how they are used in NoSQL systems.

metadata.title: Data Lakes
metadata.definition: Concepts and applications of data lakes for storing large amounts of raw, unstructured or semi-structured data.

metadata.title: NoSQL Data Consistency
metadata.definition: Issues and solutions related to data consistency in NoSQL database environments.

metadata.title: Data Privacy
metadata.definition: Knowledge of principles, regulations and techniques to protect the privacy of personal data.

metadata.title: PII
metadata.definition: Understanding Personally Identifiable Information (PII) and the importance of protecting it.

metadata.title: PII Protection
metadata.definition: Techniques and measures to protect Personally Identifiable Information from unauthorized access or misuse.

metadata.title: Data Discovery Techniques
metadata.definition: Techniques and methods for exploring, analyzing, and summarizing key characteristics of data sets.

metadata.title: Data Science Lifecycle
metadata.definition: Understanding of the different stages in the lifecycle of a data science project, from collection to deployment.

metadata.title: Data Provenance
metadata.definition: Understanding the origin, history and transformation of data.

metadata.title: Machine Learning for Data Science
metadata.definition: Machine learning techniques are applied in data science, including data preprocessing, missing data filling, supervised/semi-supervised/unsupervised learning, text analysis, graph analysis, PageRank, empirical methodology, evaluation, and ethics.

metadata.title: ML Data Preprocessing
metadata.definition: Specific data preprocessing techniques are needed to prepare data for machine learning models in data science.

metadata.title: Missing Data Imputation
metadata.definition: Methods and techniques for handling and filling in missing data values ​​in a data set.

metadata.title: Supervised Learning
metadata.definition: apply supervised learning methods to solve problems in data science, such as classification and regression.

metadata.title: Semi-Supervised Learning
metadata.definition: Learning methods use both labeled and unlabeled data to train the model.

metadata.title: Unsupervised Learning
