metadata.title: Text Analysis
metadata.definition: Techniques for analyzing and extracting meaningful information from text data in data science.

metadata.title: Graph Analysis
metadata.definition: Methods and tools for analyzing data represented as graphs in data science.

metadata.title: PageRank Algorithm
metadata.definition: understand and apply the PageRank algorithm to rank nodes in a graph, especially web pages.

metadata.title: Experimental Methodology (ML/DS)
metadata.definition: Methods and processes for designing, performing, and analyzing experiments in machine learning and data science.

metadata.title: ML Model Evaluation
metadata.definition: Techniques and criteria for evaluating machine learning model performance in data science projects.

metadata.title: ML/DS Ethics
metadata.definition: Ethical issues related to the development, deployment, and use of machine learning and data science systems.

metadata.title: DS Societal & Ethical Responsibility (SEP)
metadata.definition: Specific ethical and social impacts of data science applications, integrated throughout the course.

metadata.title: Statistical Analysis
metadata.definition: Statistical analysis techniques to understand data, draw conclusions, and support decisions.

metadata.title: Hypothesis Testing
metadata.definition: Statistical hypothesis testing methods for evaluating claims about a data set or population.

metadata.title: Statistical Experimental Design
metadata.definition: Principles and methods for designing experiments to collect statistically significant data and control extraneous variables.

metadata.title: Formulating Data Analysis Problems
metadata.definition: Ability to convert business or research questions into solvable problems using data analysis.

metadata.title: Data Storage Techniques
metadata.definition: Ability to understand and use data management techniques to store data effectively in current systems.

metadata.title: Algorithm Foundations
metadata.definition: Area of ​​knowledge that focuses on the nature of computation, including the concepts and skills needed to design and analyze algorithms to solve real-world computational problems.

metadata.title: Algorithm
metadata.definition: Structured computational processes that operate on data elements are the foundation of all theoretical calculations and applied programs.

metadata.title: Data Structures
metadata.definition: Ways of organizing data to allow efficient storage and access, are the foundation of all theoretical calculations and applied programs.

metadata.title: Theory of Computation
metadata.definition: The study of mathematical models of computation and problems that can be solved using algorithms.

metadata.title: Algorithm Capabilities & Limits
metadata.definition: Understanding of what algorithms can and cannot achieve, as well as the factors that influence their performance and applicability.

metadata.title: Algorithm Societal & Environmental Impact
metadata.definition: evaluate the ethical, social, and environmental consequences of algorithm development and implementation in real-world applications.

metadata.title: Nature of Computation
metadata.definition: understand the fundamentals and underlying theories that govern how computing works, independent of language or hardware.

metadata.title: Computational Problems
metadata.definition: Problems can be solved using computer algorithms, often defined in terms of inputs and desired outputs.

metadata.title: Computational Problem Solving
metadata.definition: Techniques and approaches for designing and implementing algorithmic solutions to real-world computational problems.

metadata.title: Algorithm Design
metadata.definition: The process of creating new algorithms or adapting existing algorithms to solve specific problems, taking into account efficiency and correctness.

metadata.title: Algorithm Analysis
metadata.definition: The process of estimating the resources (time, memory) required for an algorithm and evaluating its correctness under different circumstances.

metadata.title: Computational Complexity
metadata.definition: Research on the amount of resources (time, space) needed to solve computational problems, providing a theoretical basis for evaluating algorithm performance.

metadata.title: Computability
metadata.definition: The study of which problems can be solved by an algorithm, and which problems cannot, through formal computational models.

metadata.title: Foundational Data Structures & Algorithms
metadata.definition: The unit focuses on fundamental data structures and algorithms, providing an essential foundation for every computer science student. (Total hours CS Core: 11, KA Core: 6)

metadata.title: Algorithm Strategies
metadata.definition: The unit focuses on general methods and techniques for algorithm design, such as divide and conquer, dynamic programming, and more. (Total KA Core hours: 6)

metadata.title: Complexity Analysis
metadata.definition: The unit focuses on methods for quantifying the efficiency of algorithms in time and space. (Total hours CS Core: 6, KA Core: 3)

metadata.title: Computational Models & Formal Languages
metadata.definition: The unit focuses on theoretical models of computation and the formal languages ​​used to describe them. (Total hours CS Core: 9, KA Core: 23)

metadata.title: AL Societal, Ethical & Professional (SEP)
metadata.definition: The unit of knowledge ensures that the social, ethical and professional implications of computing are addressed throughout the AL area topics.

metadata.title: Linear Search
metadata.definition: A simple search algorithm that examines each element in a list or array in turn until the target is found or the list is exhausted.

metadata.title: Big O Notation
metadata.definition: A mathematical notation used to describe the worst-case behavior of a function when the argument goes to infinity, often used to classify the performance of an algorithm.

metadata.title: O(n) Complexity
metadata.definition: Linear time or space complexity, which means the time or space required to execute the algorithm increases linearly with the input size (n).

metadata.title: Brute-Force Strategy
metadata.definition: A simple problem-solving strategy by systematically trying out all possible possibilities or solutions until a solution is found.

metadata.title: Abstract Data Type (ADT)
metadata.definition: A mathematical model for a data structure that defines the operations allowed on the data without specifying how the data is stored internally.

metadata.title: ADT Operations
metadata.definition: Functions or methods are defined as part of an Abstract Data Type's interface, allowing interaction with the data it represents (e.g. add, delete, search).

metadata.title: Dictionary/Map
metadata.definition: A data structure that stores key-value pairs, allowing the value to be retrieved by its unique key.

metadata.title: Dictionary Add
metadata.definition: The operation adds a new key-value pair to the dictionary data structure.

metadata.title: Dictionary Remove
metadata.definition: The operation removes a key-value pair from a dictionary data structure based on its key.

metadata.title: Dictionary Search
metadata.definition: The operation retrieves the value associated with a specific key in a dictionary data structure.

metadata.title: Arrays
metadata.definition: A set of data elements of the same type stored in contiguous memory locations, accessible by an index.

metadata.title: Numeric Array
metadata.definition: Arrays contain data elements with numeric values ​​(e.g. integers, floats).

metadata.title: Non-Numeric Array
metadata.definition: Arrays contain data elements with non-numeric values ​​(for example, characters, strings, objects).

metadata.title: String as Array
metadata.definition: A sequence of characters is represented as an array, where each character occupies a position in the array and is accessed by index.

metadata.title: 1D Array (Vector)
metadata.definition: An array whose elements are arranged in a single dimension, often called a vector.

metadata.title: Multi-dimensional Array (Matrix)
metadata.definition: An array whose elements are arranged in multiple dimensions, often used to represent matrices or grids.

metadata.title: Record/Struct/Tuple
metadata.definition: Aggregate data structures allow fields or attributes of different data types to be grouped into a single unit.

metadata.title: Object (Data Structure)
metadata.definition: In object-oriented programming, an instance of a class, including both data (properties) and methods (behavior) that operate on that data.

metadata.title: Linked Lists
metadata.definition: A linear data structure where elements are not stored in contiguous memory locations but are linked by pointers or references.

metadata.title: Singly Linked List
metadata.definition: A linked list in which each node points to the next node in the chain, but there is no link back.

metadata.title: Doubly Linked List
metadata.definition: A linked list in which each node points to both the next and previous node in the chain, allowing two-way traversal.

metadata.title: Linear Linked List
metadata.definition: A linked list has a clear start (head) and end (tail) point, where the nodes are arranged in a linear sequence.

metadata.title: Circular Linked List
metadata.definition: A linked list in which the last node points back to the first node (or another node), forming a continuous loop.

metadata.title: Stacks
metadata.definition: An abstract data structure that operates on the LIFO (Last In, First Out) principle, with the main operations being push and pop.

metadata.title: Queues
metadata.definition: An abstract data structure that operates on the FIFO (First In, First Out) principle, with the main operations being insert (enqueue) and remove (dequeue).

metadata.title: Deques
metadata.definition: A double-ended queue allows elements to be added and removed from both ends of the queue efficiently.

metadata.title: Heap Priority Queue
metadata.definition: A priority queue is implemented using a heap data structure, where elements are retrieved based on their priority instead of order of arrival.

metadata.title: Hash Table/Map
metadata.definition: A data structure that maps keys to values ​​using a hash function to calculate an index or 'hash' into an array of buckets or slots.

metadata.title: Hash Collision Resolution
metadata.definition: Techniques used to handle the situation when two different keys hash to the same index in the hash table, such as probing or chaining.

metadata.title: Hash Collision Complexity
metadata.definition: analyze the performance of hash collision resolution methods, typically with respect to the time required to find, add, or delete elements when there is a collision.

metadata.title: Linear Probing
metadata.definition: A hash collision resolution method in which alternative locations are searched sequentially or according to a specific pattern (e.g., squared) in a hash table.

metadata.title: Chaining
metadata.definition: A method of hash collision resolution in which each location in a hash table contains a linked list or other data structure for all elements hashed to that location.

metadata.title: Rehashing
metadata.definition: A technique used to resolve hash collisions or when the load factor becomes too high, in which the hash table is rebuilt with a larger size and a new hash function.

metadata.title: Graphs
metadata.definition: A non-linear data structure consisting of nodes/vertices and edges connecting them, used to model complex relationships.

metadata.title: Undirected Graph
metadata.definition: A graph in which edges are undirected, meaning the connection between two vertices is symmetric (if A goes to B, then B goes to A).

metadata.title: Directed Graph
metadata.definition: A graph in which edges are directed, meaning the connection from one vertex to another is not necessarily symmetric.

metadata.title: Acyclic Graph
metadata.definition: A graph does not contain any cycles (a path that starts and ends at the same vertex) like a Tree.

metadata.title: Cyclic Graph
metadata.definition: A graph contains at least one cycle (a path that starts and ends at the same vertex).

metadata.title: Disconnected Graph
metadata.definition: A graph in which at least one pair of vertices has no path between them, i.e. it is made up of many connected components.

metadata.title: Connected Graph
metadata.definition: A graph in which there is a path between every pair of vertices, i.e. all vertices are connected.

metadata.title: Unweighted Graph
metadata.definition: A graph in which edges have no value (weight) associated with them, representing only the existence of a connection.

metadata.title: Weighted Graph
metadata.definition: A graph in which each edge has a numerical value (weight) associated with it, typically representing cost, distance, or strength of the relationship.

metadata.title: Graph Representation
metadata.definition: Different ways of storing graph structures in computer memory, such as adjacency lists or adjacency matrices, affect the efficiency of graph operations.

metadata.title: Adjacency List
metadata.definition: A method of representing a graph in which each vertex has a list (usually a linked list or array) of its neighbors.

metadata.title: Adjacency Matrix
metadata.definition: A method of representing a graph using a square matrix, whose elements indicate whether there are any edges between two vertices (usually 0 or 1, or an edge weight).

metadata.title: Trees
metadata.definition: A non-linear, hierarchical data structure consisting of nodes and edges without cycles, with a single root node.

metadata.title: Binary Tree
metadata.definition: A type of tree in which each node has at most two children, often called left children and right children.

metadata.title: N-ary Tree
metadata.definition: A type of tree in which each node can have at most N children, extended from the concept of a binary tree.

metadata.title: Search Tree
metadata.definition: A type of tree in which values ​​are stored in a particular order (e.g., smaller keys are in the left subtree, larger keys in the right subtree) to allow efficient searches, insertions, and deletions.

metadata.title: Balanced Tree
metadata.definition: A binary search tree is structured so that the height of the tree is kept to a minimum or approximately balanced, ensuring best performance for search, insert, and delete operations.

metadata.title: AVL Tree
metadata.definition: A self-balancing binary search tree, where the difference in height between the left and right subtrees of any node is at most 1.

metadata.title: Red-Black Tree
metadata.definition: A self-balancing binary search tree, uses a 'color' attribute (red or black) for each node along with strict rules to maintain balance after modification operations.

metadata.title: Heap (Data Structure)
metadata.definition: A complete binary tree organized to satisfy the heap property (e.g. max-heap: largest element at the root; min-heap: smallest element at the root), commonly used to implement priority queues.

metadata.title: Sets
metadata.definition: A data structure that stores unique, unordered elements and supports operations such as union, intersection, and difference.

metadata.title: Search Algorithms
metadata.definition: Methods used to locate a specific item or set of items in a data structure.

metadata.title: O(n) Complexity
metadata.definition: Linear time complexity representation, which states that the execution time of the algorithm increases proportionally to the input size (n).

metadata.title: Linear Search
metadata.definition: The simplest search algorithm, examines each element in the list in order until the target is found or the list is exhausted. Has O(n) complexity.

metadata.title: O(log n) Complexity
metadata.definition: A representation of logarithmic time complexity, which indicates that an algorithm's execution time increases significantly more slowly than the input size, typically involves bisecting the search space.

metadata.title: Binary Search
metadata.definition: An efficient search algorithm for sorted data works by repeatedly bisecting the search space. Has O(log n) complexity.

metadata.title: O(log_b n) Complexity
metadata.definition: Logarithmic time complexity with base b, typically applied to search algorithms on tree or hierarchical data structures (e.g., binary trees, B-trees).

metadata.title: Depth-First Search
metadata.definition: The algorithm searches the tree or graph, exploring as deeply as possible along each branch before backtracking and exploring another branch. It is a form of non-informational search.

metadata.title: Breadth-First Search
metadata.definition: The algorithm searches a tree or graph, exploring all nodes at the same level before moving on to the next level. It is a form of non-informational search.

metadata.title: Sorting Algorithms
metadata.definition: Systematic methods are used to arrange a set of items in a specific order (e.g., numbers, letters).

metadata.title: Stable Sort
metadata.definition: A property of a sorting algorithm that ensures that the relative order of elements with equal keys is maintained in the sorted output.

metadata.title: Unstable Sort
metadata.definition: A property of sorting algorithms, which does not guarantee that the relative order of elements with equal keys is maintained in the sorted output.

metadata.title: O(n^2) Complexity
metadata.definition: Represents the squared time complexity, which indicates that the execution time of the algorithm increases with the square of the input size (n).

metadata.title: Insertion Sort
metadata.definition: A simple sorting algorithm constructs the final sorted array or list element by element by inserting each unsorted element into its correct position. Has O(n^2) complexity.

metadata.title: Selection Sort
metadata.definition: The sorting algorithm is simple, iteratively finding the smallest (or largest) element from the unsorted section and placing it at the beginning of the sorted section. Has O(n^2) complexity.

metadata.title: O(n log n) Complexity
metadata.definition: The time complexity is common for efficient sorting algorithms, representing a trade-off between linear and logarithmic performance.

metadata.title: Quicksort
metadata.definition: The sorting algorithm is based on the divide and conquer method, selecting a pivot element and partitioning the array around it. Has average complexity O(n log n).

metadata.title: Mergesort
metadata.definition: The sorting algorithm is based on the divide-and-conquer method, which divides the list into smaller sublists, sorts them recursively, and then merges them. Has complexity O(n log n).

metadata.title: Timsort
metadata.definition: The hybrid sort algorithm, which combines insertion sort and merge sort, is designed to work efficiently on many types of real-world data and is the default sorting algorithm in Python and Java.

metadata.title: Graph Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms are designed to solve problems related to graph structure, such as path finding, spanning tree finding, connectivity analysis, etc.

metadata.title: Shortest Path Algorithms
metadata.definition: A set of algorithms used to find the path with the least weighted sum between two vertices or between a vertex and all other vertices in the graph.

metadata.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm
metadata.definition: The algorithm finds the shortest path from a source vertex to all other vertices in a graph with non-negative edge weights.

metadata.title: Floyd-Warshall Algorithm
metadata.definition: The algorithm finds the shortest path between all pairs of vertices in a graph with weight (can be negative, but has no negative cycles). apply dynamic planning.

metadata.title: Minimum Spanning Tree Algorithms
metadata.definition: Set of algorithms used to find a subtree of a weighted undirected graph, including all vertices, with the smallest possible total edge weights.

metadata.title: Prim's Algorithm
metadata.definition: Greedy algorithm to find the minimum spanning tree for a weighted undirected graph, starting from a vertex and expanding the tree by adding the least weighted edge connecting the new vertex to the existing tree.

metadata.title: Kruskal's Algorithm
metadata.definition: Greedy algorithm to find the minimum spanning tree for a weighted undirected graph, by continuously adding edges with the least weight without forming cycles.

metadata.title: Heapsort
metadata.definition: The sorting algorithm is based on the binary heap data structure. It sorts by building a max-heap and continuously extracting the largest element. Has complexity O(n log n).

metadata.title: Pseudo-linear O(n) Complexity
metadata.definition: Algorithms that have nearly linear complexity O(n) under some specific conditions (e.g., limited range of input values), typically do not rely on comparison.

metadata.title: Bucket Sort
metadata.definition: The non-comparison sorting algorithm works by distributing elements into a finite number of 'bins', then sorting each bin individually. Effective when data is evenly distributed.

metadata.title: Counting Sort
metadata.definition: The comparison-free sorting algorithm works by counting the number of occurrences of each key value in the array. Suitable for integers in a small range.

metadata.title: Radix Sort
metadata.definition: The non-comparison sorting algorithm sorts numbers by processing individual digits (or bits) from least significant position to most significant position.

metadata.title: Transitive Closure
metadata.definition: In graph theory, transitive closure of a directed graph is a new graph that contains an edge from vertex u to vertex v if there is a path from u to v in the original graph.

metadata.title: Warshall's Algorithm
metadata.definition: Algorithm to find transitive closure of a directed graph. It uses dynamic programming to identify all pairs of vertices that have a path between them.

metadata.title: Topological Sort
metadata.definition: The algorithm arranges the vertices of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) in a linear order such that for each edge directed from u to v, vertex u appears before vertex v in the order.

metadata.title: Pattern Matching
metadata.definition: Techniques and algorithms for finding similar patterns, subsequences, or structures in data, commonly used in text processing and biology.

metadata.title: Efficient String Matching
metadata.definition: Algorithms are designed to quickly find occurrences of one or more patterns in a large text string.

metadata.title: Boyer-Moore Algorithm
metadata.definition: Efficient string matching algorithm, often one of the fastest string matching algorithms in practice. It works by skipping parts of the text based on 'bad character' and 'good suffix' rules.

metadata.title: KMP Algorithm
metadata.definition: Efficient string matching algorithm, avoids rechecking characters in the text by using information about the prefixes and suffixes of the pattern. Has linear complexity.

metadata.title: Longest Common Subsequence
metadata.definition: The problem is to find the longest subsequence of both input strings. Usually solved by dynamic programming.

metadata.title: Regex Matching
metadata.definition: The process of searching and matching strings according to patterns defined by regular expressions, widely used in text processing.

metadata.title: Cryptographic Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms and techniques used to secure information and communication, including encryption, hashing, digital signatures, and more.

metadata.title: SHA-256
metadata.definition: Cryptographic hash functions belong to the SHA-2 family, which produces a unique 256-bit (32-byte) hash value from input data. Widely used in information security and blockchain.

metadata.title: Parallel Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms are designed to perform calculations simultaneously on multiple processors or threads, to speed up execution of large problems.

metadata.title: Consensus Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms enable a distributed group of agents to reach agreement on a single data value or system state, even in the presence of errors or malicious behavior.

metadata.title: Blockchain
metadata.definition: A distributed ledger technology that records transactions in a secure and immutable way through the use of cryptographically linked blocks. Usually based on a consensus algorithm.

metadata.title: Proof of Work (PoW)
metadata.definition: A consensus mechanism used in distributed systems (e.g., Bitcoin) to prevent service abuse and validate transactions, requires a certain amount of computational work.

metadata.title: Proof of Stake (PoS)
metadata.definition: A consensus mechanism in distributed systems where validators are chosen based on the amount of cryptocurrency they own and 'stake', to secure the network.

metadata.title: Quantum Algorithms
metadata.definition: The algorithms are designed to run on quantum computers, exploiting quantum mechanical phenomena such as superposition and entanglement to solve complex problems.

metadata.title: Oracle-based Quantum Algorithms
metadata.definition: Quantum algorithms use an 'oracle' (black box) to evaluate a function, often with significantly fewer queries than classical computers.

metadata.title: Deutsch-Jozsa Algorithm
metadata.definition: One of the earliest quantum algorithms, demonstrating that quantum computers can solve some problems faster than classical computers under certain circumstances.

metadata.title: Bernstein-Vazirani Algorithm
metadata.definition: Quantum algorithms can find a hidden binary string (or linear binary function) with just one oracle query, while classical algorithms need many more queries.

metadata.title: Simon's Algorithm
metadata.definition: The quantum algorithm searches for a hidden 'cycle' of a function, demonstrating a superpolynomial speed-up compared to the best classical algorithm.

metadata.title: QFT Superpolynomial Speedup
metadata.definition: The concept of using quantum Fourier transform to achieve a significant (better than polynomial) speedup in algorithm runtime compared to classical algorithms.

metadata.title: Shor's Algorithm
metadata.definition: The famous quantum algorithm for factoring large integers and calculating discrete logarithms, has the potential to break many existing public cryptosystems.

metadata.title: Amplitude Amplification
metadata.definition: The concept of using amplitude amplification techniques in quantum computing to achieve polynomial (e.g., square root) speedups over classical algorithms, often in search problems.

metadata.title: Grover's Algorithm
metadata.definition: Quantum algorithm for searching in unstructured or unsorted databases, providing quadratic speed-up compared to classical search.

metadata.title: Fast Fourier Transform
metadata.definition: Efficient algorithm for computing the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) and inverse Fourier transform of a series, which has wide applications in signal and image processing.

metadata.title: Differential Evolution
metadata.definition: A metaheuristic optimization algorithm belongs to the family of evolutionary algorithms, used to solve continuous optimization problems using mutation, hybridization, and selection operators.

metadata.title: Algorithm Paradigms
metadata.definition: Generic design methods for building efficient algorithms provide a framework for solving different types of problems.

metadata.title: Brute-Force
metadata.definition: A simple algorithm design model that examines all possible possibilities directly to find a solution to a problem.

metadata.title: Traveling Salesperson Problem
metadata.definition: The famous optimization problem, finding the shortest path through a list of cities and back to the starting point, each city is visited only once. Is an example of an NP-hard problem.

metadata.title: Knapsack Problem
metadata.definition: Optimization problem, choose a set of items with different weights and values ​​to maximize the total value without exceeding the weight limit of a bag. Can be solved by exhaustive, greedy or dynamic programming.

metadata.title: Decrease-and-Conquer
metadata.definition: The algorithm design model solves a problem by transforming it into a smaller version of itself, solving the smaller version, and then expanding the solution.

metadata.title: Decrease-by-Constant
metadata.definition: A variation of the Reduce and Conquer model, where the size of the problem decreases by a constant (usually 1) at each step, for example in insertion sort.

metadata.title: Decrease-by-Constant Factor
metadata.definition: A variation of the Reduce and Conquer model, where the size of the problem decreases by a constant factor (e.g., bisection) at each step, for example in binary search.

metadata.title: Decrease-by-Variable Size
metadata.definition: A variation of the Reduce and Conquer model, where the size of the problem is reduced by a variable amount at each step, depending on the input data.

metadata.title: Euclidean Algorithm
metadata.definition: An efficient algorithm for calculating the greatest common divisor (GCD) of two integers, which is an example of a variable dimensionality reduce-and-conquer model.

metadata.title: Divide-and-Conquer
metadata.definition: The algorithm design model solves a problem by dividing it into smaller, independent sub-problems of the same type, solving them recursively, and then combining the solutions.

metadata.title: Strassen Algorithm
metadata.definition: The matrix multiplication algorithm is faster than the standard algorithm, using a divide-and-conquer method to reduce the number of multiplications. Has complexity O(n^log2 7).

metadata.title: Greedy Algorithm
metadata.definition: The algorithm design model makes a locally optimal choice at each step in the hope that this sequence of choices will lead to a globally optimal solution.

metadata.title: Transform-and-Conquer
metadata.definition: The algorithm design model solves a problem by transforming it into another instance whose solution is known, then solving for the new instance and transforming the result back.

metadata.title: Instance Simplification
metadata.definition: Techniques in the transform and conquer paradigm that transform a complex representation of a problem into a simpler representation that is easier to solve, often by preprocessing the data.

metadata.title: Duplicate Detection by Sorting
metadata.definition: Technique for finding duplicate elements in a list by first sorting the list, then traversing adjacent elements to detect similar values.

metadata.title: Change of Representation
metadata.definition: Techniques in the transform and conquer paradigm that change the representation of data or a problem so that solving becomes easier or more efficient (e.g., using heap for heapsort).

metadata.title: Problem Reduction
metadata.definition: Engineering in the transform and conquer model transforms a problem into another problem that already has an algorithm to solve, then applies that algorithm.

metadata.title: Least Common Multiple
metadata.definition: Mathematical concept, the smallest positive integer that is divisible by both (or more) given integers. Usually calculated by reducing to the greatest common divisor.

metadata.title: Linear Programming
metadata.definition: Mathematical technique for optimizing (maximizing or minimizing) a linear objective function, subject to linear constraints. There are many applications in resource optimization.

metadata.title: Dynamic Programming
metadata.definition: The algorithm design model solves complex problems by dividing them into overlapping subproblems and storing the results of the subproblems to avoid recomputation.

metadata.title: Bellman-Ford Algorithm
metadata.definition: The algorithm finds the shortest path from a source to all other vertices in a graph with (possibly negative) edge weights and is capable of detecting negative cycles.

metadata.title: Space-Time Tradeoff
metadata.definition: Concept in algorithm design where an algorithm can be designed to use less time but more storage space, or vice versa, to achieve desired performance.

metadata.title: Hashing
metadata.definition: Technique of mapping input data of arbitrary size to a fixed-sized value (hash value), commonly used for fast searches, data integrity checking, and in hash tables for storage.

metadata.title: Exponential Growth Handling
metadata.definition: Techniques and algorithms are used to solve problems whose search space or complexity increases exponentially, often by pruning or estimation.

metadata.title: A* Algorithm
metadata.definition: The algorithm searches for the optimal path in the graph, using a heuristic function to estimate the cost from the current node to the goal, combined with the actual cost from the starting point, to find an efficient path.

metadata.title: Branch-and-Bound
metadata.definition: General algorithm design method for finding optimal solutions to discrete and combinatorial optimization problems, by dividing the search space into branches and eliminating non-potential (near) branches.

metadata.title: Backtracking
metadata.definition: Algorithmic techniques recursively solve problems by attempting to construct a solution step by step, eliminating options that do not lead to a valid solution, and backtracking to try other options.

metadata.title: Iteration and Recursion
metadata.definition: Two basic methods for repeating a block of code or a process. Iteration uses loops (for, while), while recursion uses functions that call themselves.

metadata.title: Factorial
metadata.definition: Mathematical function that calculates the product of all positive integers less than or equal to a given positive integer. Often used as an example to illustrate the concepts of iteration and recursion.

metadata.title: Tree Search
metadata.definition: General concept of algorithms that explore nodes and branches of a tree data structure to search for a specific node or gather information.

metadata.title: Approximation Algorithms
metadata.definition: The algorithms are designed to find an approximate solution to NP-hard optimization problems in polynomial time, when finding an optimal solution is not feasible.

metadata.title: Iterative Improvement
metadata.definition: Algorithms start with a feasible solution and then continuously improve it by taking small steps until a stopping criterion is reached (e.g., no further improvement is possible).

metadata.title: Ford-Fulkerson Algorithm
metadata.definition: Algorithm to calculate maximum flow in flow network. It works by finding paths that increase the flow from the source to the destination until there are no more paths that can be increased.

metadata.title: Simplex Algorithm
metadata.definition: A popular algorithm for solving linear programming problems, finding the optimal solution by moving between vertices of a polyhedral feasible region.

metadata.title: Randomized Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms use randomness as part of their logic, often to find efficient solutions to problems that the algorithm determines are difficult to solve, or to achieve good average performance.

metadata.title: Max-Cut Problem
metadata.definition: Optimization problem on graph: find a partition of vertices into two sets such that the number of edges going between the two sets is maximum. It is an NP-hard problem.

metadata.title: Balls and Bins Problem
metadata.definition: A classic probability problem, often used to analyze the performance of random algorithms and data structures such as hash tables and load distribution.

metadata.title: Quantum Computing
metadata.definition: Field of research that uses quantum mechanical phenomena to perform calculations, with the potential to solve some problems faster than classical computers.

metadata.title: Algorithm Paradigm Characteristics
metadata.definition: Ability to explain the defining characteristics of various algorithmic models and illustrate them with concrete examples, showing how those examples satisfy the model's characteristics.

metadata.title: Algorithm Paradigm Evaluation
metadata.definition: Ability to evaluate and select appropriate algorithm models for practical problems, and analyze the advantages, disadvantages and trade-offs between selected models and algorithms.

metadata.title: Iterative Algorithms
metadata.definition: Concepts and examples of algorithms that use iterative structures to solve problems.

metadata.title: Recursive Algorithms
metadata.definition: Concepts and examples of algorithms that use recursive (calling itself) structures to solve problems.

metadata.title: Iteration vs. Recursion
metadata.definition: analyze the advantages, disadvantages and appropriate use cases of iterative and recursive algorithms.

metadata.title: Greedy Method
metadata.definition: Concept of the greedy method in algorithm design, including how it works and the conditions to ensure an optimal solution.

metadata.title: Greedy Optimality
metadata.definition: evaluate when a greedy algorithm can provide an optimal solution to a problem and when it cannot.

metadata.title: Exponential Complexity Handling
metadata.definition: Techniques and strategies for solving or approximating problems of exponential algorithmic complexity, in search of more feasible solutions.

metadata.title: Complexity Analysis Framework
metadata.definition: Conceptual framework used to evaluate algorithm performance, including basic factors and methods.

metadata.title: Algorithm Performance Cases
metadata.definition: Methods for evaluating the performance of an algorithm based on different input scenarios: best, average, and worst.

metadata.title: Empirical & Asymptotic Measurement
metadata.definition: Methods for measuring algorithm performance, including actual measurement and evaluation based on the growth rate of the complexity function.

metadata.title: Input Size & Basic Operations
metadata.definition: Basic factors to analyze algorithm complexity: input data size and number of primitive operations performed.

metadata.title: Time-Space Efficiency
metadata.definition: There are two main aspects of algorithm performance: the amount of time and the amount of memory space the algorithm requires.

metadata.title: Asymptotic Complexity Analysis
metadata.definition: Method for analyzing algorithm performance as input size approaches infinity, focusing on upper and lower bounds for the average and worst case.

metadata.title: Big-O, Big-Omega, Big-Theta
metadata.definition: Formal mathematical notation used to describe the upper bound (Big-O), lower bound (Big-Omega), and strict bound (Big-Theta) of algorithmic complexity.

metadata.title: Basic Complexity Classes
metadata.definition: Groups classify algorithms based on the growth rate of the time or space complexity function.

metadata.title: O(1) Complexity
metadata.definition: Complexity class whose execution time is constant, independent of input size (e.g. array access).

metadata.title: O(log n) Complexity
metadata.definition: A class of complexity whose execution time increases as a logarithm of the input size (e.g., binary search).

metadata.title: O(n) Complexity
metadata.definition: Complexity class where execution time increases linearly with input size (e.g. linear search).

metadata.title: O(n log n) Complexity
metadata.definition: Complexity class whose execution time increases as n multiplied by the logarithm of n (e.g., mergesort).

metadata.title: O(n^2) Complexity
metadata.definition: A class of complexity whose execution time increases as the square of the input size (e.g. selection sort).

metadata.title: O(n^c) Complexity
metadata.definition: Complexity class where execution time increases as a power of the input size (e.g. O(n^3) Gauss elimination).

metadata.title: O(2^n) Complexity
metadata.definition: The class of complexity whose execution time increases exponentially with the input size, typically hard problems (e.g. Knapsack, SAT, TSP).

metadata.title: O(n!) Complexity
metadata.definition: A class of complexity whose execution time increases with the factorial of the input size, commonly encountered in problems that list all permutations (e.g., Hamiltonian Cycles, all permutations).

metadata.title: Empirical Performance Measurement
metadata.definition: The technique measures the actual performance of an algorithm by running it with different input data sets.

metadata.title: Feasibility & Intractability
metadata.definition: Classify problems into those that can be solved in polynomial time (feasible) and those that cannot (or are very difficult) to solve in polynomial time (impossible).

metadata.title: P, NP, NP-Complete Classes
metadata.definition: Important problem classes in computational complexity theory: P (solvable in polynomial time), NP (verifiable in polynomial time) and NP-Complete (is NP and the most difficult of NP).

metadata.title: NP-Complete Problems
metadata.definition: Problems in the NP-Complete class, have the characteristic that if a polynomial time algorithm is found for one problem, all other problems in the NP class can be solved in polynomial time (e.g. SAT, Knapsack, TSP).

metadata.title: Reduction
metadata.definition: The technique of converting one problem into another problem, often used to prove the NP-hardness or NP-completeness of a problem.

metadata.title: Time-Space Trade-off
metadata.definition: Algorithm design principle where reducing time requirements can increase space requirements and vice versa.

metadata.title: Little-o, Little-Omega, Little-Theta
metadata.definition: Additional mathematical notations to more strictly describe the asymptotic bounds of the complexity function (e.g., Little-o for a non-tight upper bound).

metadata.title: Formal Recurrence Analysis
metadata.definition: Techniques for analyzing the complexity of recursive algorithms using formal mathematical tools such as recursive equations.

metadata.title: Amortized Analysis
metadata.definition: Technique that analyzes the performance of a sequence of operations, where the high cost of some operations is offset by the low cost of other operations, yielding a low average cost per operation.

metadata.title: Turing Machine Complexity Models
metadata.definition: Theoretical models for defining and analyzing computational complexity are based on the concept of Turing machines.

metadata.title: Turing Time Complexity
metadata.definition: Define time complexity in the context of the Turing machine model.

metadata.title: P, NP, NP-C, EXP (Turing)
metadata.definition: The complexity classes P, NP, NP-Complete and EXP are defined based on the execution time of a Turing machine.

metadata.title: Cook-Levin Theorem
metadata.definition: The fundamental theorem in complexity theory proves that the SAT problem is NP-Complete.

metadata.title: Turing Space Complexity
metadata.definition: Define space complexity in the context of the Turing machine model.

metadata.title: NSpace & PSpace Classes
metadata.definition: Space complexity classes are defined by Turing machines: NSpace (non-deterministic polynomial space) and PSpace (deterministic polynomial space).

metadata.title: Savitch's Theorem
metadata.definition: The theorem proves that any language that can be recognized by a non-deterministic Turing machine with space S(n) can also be recognized by a deterministic Turing machine with space S(n)^2.

metadata.title: BST Balance Impact
metadata.definition: Explain how the balanced structure of a binary search tree affects the time complexity of operations such as search, insertion, deletion.

metadata.title: NP-Hard, NP, NP-Complete Relation
metadata.definition: Explain the relationship between the complexity classes NP, NP-Hard, and NP-Complete, where NP-Hard is the set of problems at least as difficult as the NP-Complete problem, and NP is the set of problems that are verifiable in polynomial time.

metadata.title: Recurrence Relations for Time Complexity
metadata.definition: The technique uses recursive equations to model and solve the time complexity of recursively defined algorithms.

metadata.title: Master Theorem
metadata.definition: Theorems used to solve recursive equations have a certain form, often appearing when analyzing the complexity of divide-and-conquer algorithms.

metadata.title: P and NP Complexity Classes
metadata.definition: Explain the definition and meaning of the P (polynomial time) and NP (nondeterministic polynomial time) complexity classes, including the relationship between them and their significance in computational theory.

metadata.title: NP-Complete & Reduction Proofs
metadata.definition: Prove that a problem is NP-Complete by attributing a known canonical NP-Complete problem (e.g., 3SAT and Clique) to it.

metadata.title: P-space & EXP Relation
metadata.definition: Explain the P-space (polynomial space) complexity class and its relationship to the EXP (exponential time) class.

metadata.title: Formal Automata Models
metadata.definition: An overview of formal automaton models used to describe language recognition and computation processes.

metadata.title: Finite State Automaton (FSA)
metadata.definition: Concepts, operations, and applications of finite-state automatons, including deterministic and non-deterministic variants.

metadata.title: Pushdown Automaton (PDA)
metadata.definition: Concept, operation and applications of stack automaton, a computational model more powerful than FSA, capable of processing context-free language.

metadata.title: Linear Bounded Automaton (LBA)
metadata.definition: Concepts, operations and applications of linear edge automatons, computational models involving context-sensitive languages.

metadata.title: Turing Machine
metadata.definition: Basic concept, structure, and operation of a Turing Machine, a universal computational model that represents any algorithm.

metadata.title: Formal Language, Grammar, Chomsky Hierarchy
metadata.definition: An overview of formal languages, the grammar used to describe them, and the Chomsky hierarchy that classifies language types based on the expressive power of the grammar.

metadata.title: Regular Language (Type-3)
metadata.definition: Definition, properties and representations of formal languages, corresponding to finite state automatons.

metadata.title: Regular Expression (Regex)
metadata.definition: Syntax, semantics, and applications of regular expressions for describing and matching patterns in regular languages.

metadata.title: Context-Free Language (Type-2)
metadata.definition: Definition, properties, and representations of context-free languages, corresponding to stack automatons.

metadata.title: Context-Sensitive Language (Type-1)
metadata.definition: Definition, properties, and representations of context-sensitive languages, corresponding to linear boundary automatons.

metadata.title: Recursively Enumerable Language (Type-0)
metadata.definition: Definition, properties, and representations of recursive enumeration languages, corresponding to Turing Machines.

metadata.title: Chomsky Hierarchy Relations
metadata.definition: analyze the correspondence relationship between automaton types (FSA, PDA, LBA, Turing Machine), language types (regular, context-free, context-sensitive, recursively enumerable) and grammar types in the Chomsky hierarchy.

metadata.title: Decidability, Computability, Halting Problem
metadata.definition: The concepts of problem determinism, function computability, and Halting Problem along with their meaning in computational theory.

metadata.title: Church-Turing Thesis
metadata.definition: Explain the Church-Turing Thesis, which asserts that a Turing Machine can compute any function that an algorithm can compute, and what it means for computer science.

metadata.title: Algorithm Correctness
metadata.definition: Methods and techniques for proving the correctness of an algorithm, ensuring the algorithm behaves as expected for all valid inputs.

metadata.title: Invariants (Loop, Recursion)
metadata.definition: Use invariants (e.g. loop invariants) to prove the correctness of algorithms in iterative, recursive, or tree search structures.

metadata.title: DFA vs NFA
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast the capabilities of deterministic and non-deterministic automatons in models such as FSA and PDA, including parity in computational power.

metadata.title: Pumping Lemma Proofs
metadata.definition: apply Pumping Lemma to prove that a language does not belong to a certain class of formal languages.

metadata.title: Pumping Lemma for Regular Languages
metadata.definition: Use Pumping Lemma to prove the limits of finite-state automatons and regular languages, i.e. prove that a language is not regular.

metadata.title: Pumping Lemma for CFL
metadata.definition: Use Pumping Lemma to demonstrate the limits of stack automaton and context-free languages, i.e. prove a language is not context-free.

metadata.title: Advanced Decidability (Arithmetization, Diagonalization)
metadata.definition: Advanced techniques for decidability analysis, including arithmetic and diagonalization, to prove undecidable problems, such as the Stationarity Problem.

metadata.title: Arithmetization & Diagonalization for Halting Problem
metadata.definition: apply arithmetic and diagonalization techniques to prove that the Stopping Problem for Turing Machines is undecidable.

metadata.title: Reducibility
metadata.definition: The concept of reducibility between problems and different types of reducibility is used to classify the difficulty of problems.

metadata.title: Time Complexity (Turing Machine)
metadata.definition: Algorithm time complexity analysis based on the Turing Machine model, including asymptotic notations and classification of time complexity classes.

metadata.title: Space Complexity (Pspace, Savitch's Theorem)
metadata.definition: Concept of space complexity (amount of memory required), space complexity classes such as Pspace and Savitch's Theorem.

metadata.title: Equivalent Computation Models
metadata.definition: Study of different computational models with power equivalent to Turing Machines, demonstrating that they can simulate each other.

metadata.title: Turing Machine Variants
metadata.definition: Study the standard Turing Machine and its variants such as the multiband Turing Machine, the Deterministic Turing Machine, and demonstrate their equivalence in computational power.

metadata.title: Lambda Calculus
metadata.definition: Introduction to Lambda Calculus as a formal computational model, especially important in functional programming.

metadata.title: Mu-Recursive Functions
metadata.definition: Introduction to Recursive Functions Mu as another formal computational model, equivalent to a Turing Machine.

metadata.title: Quantum Computing
metadata.definition: An overview of the field of quantum computing, its basic principles and potential.

metadata.title: Quantum Mechanics Postulates
metadata.definition: Study the basic postulates of quantum mechanics that underlie quantum computing.

metadata.title: Quantum State Space
metadata.definition: The concept of the state space that qubits can exist in in quantum computing.

metadata.title: Quantum State Evolution
metadata.definition: Rules and how quantum states change over time or due to the effects of quantum operations.

metadata.title: Quantum State Composition
metadata.definition: How the states of multiple qubits combine to form the states of a larger quantum system.

metadata.title: Quantum State Measurement
metadata.definition: The process of measuring quantum states and the associated wave function collapse.

metadata.title: Qubit Column Vector Representation
metadata.definition: How to represent the state of qubits (quantum bits) using column vectors in linear algebra.

metadata.title: Quantum Operation Matrix Representation
metadata.definition: The way to represent quantum operations (quantum gates) uses matrices to influence the qubit state.

metadata.title: Basic Quantum Gates (XNOT, CNOT)
metadata.definition: Introduce and explain basic quantum gates such as XNOT gate (Pauli-X) and CNOT gate (Controlled-NOT).

metadata.title: Universal Turing Machine
metadata.definition: Explain the concept of a Universal Turing Machine, its ability to simulate any other Turing Machine, and its operation as a model of a programmable computer.

metadata.title: Regex vs Type-3 Regular Expressions
metadata.definition: Explain the difference between regular expressions used in programming languages ​​(which often have extended features beyond Type-3 regular languages) and formal regular expressions that correspond to Type-3 acceptors.

metadata.title: Rice's Theorem
metadata.definition: Explain Rice's Theorem, an important result in the theory of computation about the undecidability of non-trivial properties of computable functions.

metadata.title: Proof of Uncomputability by Reduction
metadata.definition: Explain an example of proving a problem to be non-computable by reducing it to a known non-computable problem.

metadata.title: Primitive Recursive Functions
metadata.definition: Explain primitive recursive functions, their meaning, and their implementation on a Turing Machine.

metadata.title: General Recursive Functions
metadata.definition: Explain general recursive functions, their meaning, and their implementation on a Turing Machine.

metadata.title: Recursive Function Components
metadata.definition: Explain the basic components that make up recursive functions: zero function, successor, selection, primitive recursion, composition, and the Mu operator.

metadata.title: Recursive Functions on Turing Machine
metadata.definition: Explain how primitive and general recursive functions can be implemented or simulated on a Turing Machine model.

metadata.title: Lambda Calculus Computation
metadata.definition: Explains how calculations are performed in Lambda Calculus, including concepts such as Alpha transformation and Beta reduction.

metadata.title: Alpha Conversion (Lambda Calculus)
metadata.definition: Explain the process of renaming bound variables in Lambda Calculus without changing the meaning of the expression.

metadata.title: Beta Reduction (Lambda Calculus)
metadata.definition: Explain the function application process in Lambda Calculus, replacing parameters with arguments.

metadata.title: Quantum State Space
metadata.definition: Explain the state space of a quantum system, represented as a unit vector in Hilbert space.

metadata.title: Quantum State Evolution (Unitary Operators)
metadata.definition: Explain the state evolution of a quantum system through the use of unitary operators.

metadata.title: Quantum State Composition (Tensor Product)
metadata.definition: Explain how to combine the states of multiple quantum systems through the use of tensor products.

metadata.title: Quantum Measurement (Probabilistic Outcome)
metadata.definition: Explain the probabilistic measurement results of a quantum state.

metadata.title: Pauli-X Gate
metadata.definition: Explain the operation of a quantum XNOT gate (also called Pauli-X) on a quantum bit represented by a matrix and column vector.

metadata.title: CNOT Gate
metadata.definition: Explain the operation of a CNOT (Controlled-NOT) quantum gate on a quantum bit represented by a matrix and column vector.

metadata.title: Qubit Representation (Matrix/Vector)
metadata.definition: Explain how a quantum bit is represented as a matrix and column vector in quantum computing.

metadata.title: Ethical & Safe Algorithms

metadata.title: Algorithmic Fairness
metadata.definition: understand the concept and importance of fairness in algorithm design and implementation.

metadata.title: Anonymity

metadata.title: Differential Privacy
metadata.definition: Explain how differential privacy protects personal information in a data set.

metadata.title: Algorithmic Accountability
metadata.definition: understand accountability regarding algorithmic decisions and outcomes.

metadata.title: Algorithmic Transparency
metadata.definition: understand the need for transparency in algorithmic operations and decisions.

metadata.title: Responsible Algorithms
metadata.definition: understand the principles of designing and implementing algorithms responsibly, considering social and ethical impact.

metadata.title: Inefficient Algorithm Impact

metadata.title: Algorithmic Sustainability
metadata.definition: evaluate algorithms for sustainability aspects, including long-term environmental and social impacts.

metadata.title: Context-Aware Computing
metadata.definition: understand systems and algorithms that collect and use contextual information to provide appropriate services or decisions.

metadata.title: Algorithmic Social Solutions
metadata.definition: Develop algorithmic solutions to solve real-world social problems, for example routing ambulances to hospitals.

metadata.title: Algorithm Environmental Impact
metadata.definition: Explain the impact an algorithm can have on the environment when used to solve a real-world problem.

metadata.title: Algorithm Social Impact

metadata.title: Data Structure & Algorithm Selection
metadata.definition: Prepare a presentation to justify the choice of the appropriate data structure and/or algorithm to solve a given practical problem.

metadata.title: Algorithm Design Choices
metadata.definition: Explain the effects of design choices related to algorithm design.

metadata.title: Proof-of-Work Algorithm
metadata.definition: Explain Proof-of-Work algorithms, especially the trade-offs associated with them.

metadata.title: Proof-of-Stake Algorithm
metadata.definition: Explain Proof-of-Stake algorithms, especially the trade-offs associated with them.

metadata.title: PoW vs PoS Trade-offs
metadata.definition: Explain the trade-offs involved when comparing Proof-of-Work and Proof-of-Stake algorithms.

metadata.title: Big-O Complexity Analysis
metadata.definition: Introducing the method of analyzing algorithm complexity using Big-O notation.

metadata.title: Graph Algorithms
metadata.definition: Learn about algorithms that work on graph data structures, such as finding the shortest path or traversing a graph.

metadata.title: Backtracking Algorithm
metadata.definition: Learn about the backtracking algorithm, a technique for solving problems by systematically trying each solution.

metadata.title: Array
metadata.definition: Array data structure and basic operations with arrays.

metadata.title: String
metadata.definition: Character string data structure and basic operations with strings.
