metadata.title: Linear Search O(n)
metadata.definition: Linear search algorithm with O(n) time complexity.

metadata.title: Algorithmic SEP Basic
metadata.definition: Social, ethical, and professional issues related to algorithmic platforms, are presented at a basic level during SEP hours.

metadata.title: Brute Force Strategy Basic
metadata.definition: A strategy that solves a problem by trying every possible possibility directly, for example in linear search. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: under 1 hour)

metadata.title: Linear Search Algorithm
metadata.definition: A search algorithm iterates through each element in a list sequentially until the desired element is found or the list is exhausted. (Example for exhaust and repeat)

metadata.title: Iteration Strategy Basic
metadata.definition: Technique that solves a problem by repeating a set of instructions until a certain condition is achieved, a typical example is linear search. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: under 1 hour)

metadata.title: Basic Complexity Classes
metadata.definition: The basic classifications of algorithm complexity are based on the computational resources (time or space) they consume. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: under 1 hour)

metadata.title: O(1) Constant Time
metadata.definition: The runtime complexity of the algorithm does not vary with input size. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: under 1 hour)

metadata.title: O(n) Linear Time
metadata.definition: The runtime complexity of the algorithm increases proportionally to the input size. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: under 1 hour)

metadata.title: Abstract Data Types (ADTs)
metadata.definition: The concept of a data type is defined by behavior from the user's perspective, not the internal implementation. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Binary Search
metadata.definition: An efficient search algorithm for finding an item in a sorted list by repeatedly bisecting the search space. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Multidimensional Arrays
metadata.definition: Array data structures have more than one index to access elements, such as matrices. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Linked List
metadata.definition: A linear data structure consists of a sequence of 'nodes', where each node contains data and a pointer to the next node. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Hash Map & Collision Strategies
metadata.definition: A data structure that maps keys to values ​​using a hash function, including methods for dealing with two keys hashing into the same location. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Records, Structs, Tuples
metadata.definition: Composite data types allow data items of different types to be grouped under a single name. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Object
metadata.definition: An entity in object-oriented programming that combines data and methods that operate on that data. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Set
metadata.definition: A data structure that stores a unique set of values, in no particular order. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Stack
metadata.definition: The data structure follows the LIFO principle (Last-In, First-Out). (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Queue
metadata.definition: The data structure follows the FIFO principle (First-In, First-Out). (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Deque
metadata.definition: Double-ended queue, allowing elements to be added and removed from both ends. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Binary Tree
metadata.definition: Tree data structure in which each node has at most two child nodes. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Ordered Tree
metadata.definition: A tree data structure whose child nodes are arranged in a certain order (e.g., binary search tree). (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
metadata.definition: The tree or graph traversal algorithm starts from the root node and explores all neighboring nodes at the current level before moving on to deeper levels. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Depth-First Search (DFS)
metadata.definition: The tree or graph traversal algorithm starts at the root node and explores as far each branch as possible before backtracking. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Search Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms are designed to search for an item or a set of items with specific properties in a data structure. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Selection Sort O(n²)
metadata.definition: An in-place sorting algorithm compares the elements in the list to find the smallest (or largest) element and swaps it with the element in the first unsorted position. Runtime complexity is O(n²). (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Binary Search O(log n)
metadata.definition: Efficient search algorithm in sorted list, has logarithmic running time complexity O(log₂ n). (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Sorting Algorithms Intermediate
metadata.definition: Algorithms are designed to arrange the elements of a list in a certain order. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Merge Sort O(n log n)
metadata.definition: A sorting algorithm based on the divide-and-conquer principle, with running time complexity O(n log n). (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Tree Search O(log b n)
metadata.definition: A search algorithm on a tree data structure with logarithmic runtime complexity, often used for balanced trees or search trees. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 12 hours)

metadata.title: Brute Force
metadata.definition: A strategy that solves a problem by trying every possible possibility directly, such as a selection sort algorithm. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Decrease-and-Conquer
metadata.definition: An algorithmic strategy that solves a problem by transforming it into a smaller version of the same problem, for example searching a tree by depth or breadth. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Divide-and-Conquer
metadata.definition: An algorithmic strategy divides the problem into smaller subproblems, solves the subproblems independently, and then combines the solutions. For example: merge sort, quick sort. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Quicksort
metadata.definition: A sorting algorithm based on the divide and conquer principle, which usually has good performance in practice. (An example for Divide-and-Conquer)

metadata.title: Iteration vs Recursion
metadata.definition: Compare and differentiate between two basic programming techniques for solving problems, including for example factorials or tree searches. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Space-Time Tradeoff
metadata.definition: Concept in algorithm design where memory resources are used to reduce execution time, or vice versa, a typical example is hashing. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Complexity Analysis Framework
metadata.definition: Systematic structure for evaluating algorithm performance in time and space. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Intermediate Complexity Classes
metadata.definition: Basic classifications of algorithm complexity, advanced above the foundation level, include logarithmic, linear logarithmic, and quadratic classes. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Logarithmic Time O(log n)
metadata.definition: The runtime complexity of an algorithm increases with the logarithm of the input size, for example binary search. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Linearithmic Time O(n log n)
metadata.definition: The runtime complexity of the algorithm increases as n multiplied by the logarithm of n, for example merge sort. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Quadratic Time O(n²)
metadata.definition: The runtime complexity of an algorithm increases with the square of the input size, for example in select sort. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Time-Space Tradeoff
metadata.definition: Algorithm design considerations regarding optimization between execution time and amount of memory space required. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Algorithmic SEP
metadata.definition: Enhance and refine understanding of the impact of algorithm design and use on society, presented at an intermediate level during SEP hours.

metadata.title: Graph
metadata.definition: A nonlinear data structure consists of a set of vertices (nodes) and edges (links) connecting those vertices. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Graph Algorithms (Advanced)
metadata.definition: Algorithms are designed to solve problems on graph data structures, such as finding the shortest path or traversing the graph. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Asymptotic Complexity Analysis
metadata.definition: Method for analyzing the performance of an algorithm when the input size approaches infinity, using the notation Big O, Big Omega, Big Theta. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Advanced Complexity Classes
metadata.definition: The basic classifications of algorithmic complexity, considered at a more advanced level, include higher complexity classes such as exponential and factorial. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Exponential Time O(2^n)
metadata.definition: The runtime complexity of an algorithm increases exponentially with the input size, often indicating intractable problems. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Factorial Time O(n!)
metadata.definition: The runtime complexity of an algorithm increases with the factorial of the input size, which often occurs in permutation or all-instance problems. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Empirical Performance Measurement
metadata.definition: The methods realistically measure the runtime and memory consumption of algorithms by running them against specific data sets. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Tractability
metadata.definition: The likelihood that a problem can be solved by an algorithm in a reasonable amount of time (usually polynomial time). (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Intractability
metadata.definition: The concept of problems for which there are no known polynomial time algorithms to solve them, often requiring exponential or factorial time. (As part of the AL-Complexity unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Brute Force (Advanced)
metadata.definition: The strategy of solving problems by trying every possible possibility directly, is often applied to difficult problems such as the delivery man problem or the bag problem. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Traveling Salesperson Problem
metadata.definition: An optimization problem in which a salesperson must visit a set of cities and return to the starting point, finding the shortest possible route that passes through each city exactly once. (An example of Brute Force)

metadata.title: Knapsack Problem
metadata.definition: An optimization problem in which a set of items, each with a weight and value, must be placed into a bag of limited capacity such that the total value is maximized. (An example of Brute Force)

metadata.title: Decrease-and-Conquer (Advanced)
metadata.definition: An algorithmic strategy that solves a problem by transforming it into a smaller version of the same problem, for example topological sorting. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Topological Sort
metadata.definition: Linearize the vertices of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) such that for every directed edge u -> v, vertex u comes before vertex v in the sort order. (An example for Decrease-and-Conquer)

metadata.title: Divide-and-Conquer (Advanced)
metadata.definition: An algorithmic strategy divides the problem into smaller subproblems, solves the subproblems independently, and then combines the solutions. For example, Strassen's algorithm for matrix multiplication. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Strassen's Algorithm
metadata.definition: An algorithm for multiplying two n x n matrices that is faster than the standard matrix multiplication algorithm, using the principle of divide and conquer. (An example for Divide-and-Conquer)

metadata.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm (Greedy)
metadata.definition: An algorithmic strategy makes a locally optimal choice at each step in the hope of finding a globally optimal solution, such as Dijkstra's algorithm for finding the shortest path. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm
metadata.definition: Algorithm to find the shortest path between nodes in a graph with positive edge weights. (An example for Greedy)

metadata.title: Kruskal's Algorithm (Greedy)
metadata.definition: An algorithmic strategy makes a locally optimal choice at each step in the hope of finding a globally optimal solution, for example the Kruskal algorithm for finding a minimum spanning tree. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Kruskal's Algorithm
metadata.definition: Algorithm to find the minimum spanning tree for a weighted undirected graph. (An example for Greedy)

metadata.title: Transform-and-Conquer: Heapsort
metadata.definition: An algorithmic strategy solves a problem by transforming it into a version that a known algorithm can solve, such as heap sorting. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: 2-3 Tree
metadata.definition: A type of balanced search tree, where each node can have 2 or 3 child nodes, ensuring a logarithmic tree height. (An example for Transform-and-Conquer/Reduction)

metadata.title: AVL Tree
metadata.definition: A type of self-balancing binary search tree that maintains height balance of two subtrees to ensure logarithmic search, insertion, and deletion performance. (An example for Transform-and-Conquer/Reduction)

metadata.title: Red-Black Tree
metadata.definition: A type of self-balancing binary search tree that uses color attributes (red/black) to ensure logarithmic tree height and efficient operations. (An example for Transform-and-Conquer/Reduction)

metadata.title: Warshall's Algorithm (DP)
metadata.definition: An algorithmic technique that solves problems by dividing them into overlapping subproblems and optimization subproblems, storing the results to avoid recalculation. For example, Warshall's algorithm for finding transitive closure. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Floyd's Algorithm (DP)
metadata.definition: An algorithmic technique that solves problems by dividing them into overlapping subproblems and optimization subproblems, storing the results to avoid recalculation. For example, Floyd's algorithm to find all shortest paths. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Floyd's Algorithm
metadata.definition: The algorithm finds the shortest path between all pairs of vertices in a directed, weighted graph, which can handle negative weights. (An example for Dynamic Programming)

metadata.title: Bellman-Ford Algorithm (DP)
metadata.definition: An algorithmic technique that solves problems by dividing them into overlapping subproblems and optimization subproblems, storing the results to avoid recalculation. For example, the Bellman-Ford algorithm for finding the shortest path from a source in a graph has negative edge weights. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Bellman-Ford Algorithm
metadata.definition: The algorithm finds the shortest path from a source vertex to all other vertices in a directed graph with negative edge weights, detecting negative cycles. (An example for Dynamic Programming)

metadata.title: A* Algorithm
metadata.definition: Techniques used to solve problems of exponential complexity using approximation or intelligent search methods, such as the A* search algorithm. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: A* Algorithm
metadata.definition: A best path finding algorithm prioritizes finding a path from a source vertex to a destination vertex in a graph, using a heuristic function to estimate the lowest cost from the current vertex to the destination. (An example for Handling Exponential Growth)

metadata.title: Branch-and-Bound
metadata.definition: Techniques used to solve problems of exponential complexity using approximation or intelligent search methods, such as the branch-and-bound method. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Backtracking
metadata.definition: Techniques used to solve problems of exponential complexity using approximation or intelligent search methods, such as backtracking algorithms. (As part of the AL-Strategies unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Formal Models of Computation
metadata.definition: Abstract mathematical models are used to study computation, including theoretical constructs such as Turing machines, grammars, and languages. (As part of AL-Models unit: 9 hours)

metadata.title: Formal Grammars
metadata.definition: System of rules for creating or analyzing strings in a formal language, often used in formal language theory. (As part of AL-Models unit: 9 hours)

metadata.title: Formal Languages
metadata.definition: A finite set of strings constructed from a set of symbols (alphabet), defined by a formal grammar. (As part of AL-Models unit: 9 hours)

metadata.title: Turing Machine
metadata.definition: An abstract mathematical model of a computer, used to define algorithms and study the limits of computation. (As part of AL-Models unit: 9 hours)

metadata.title: Halting Problem Undecidability
metadata.definition: The theorem proves that no algorithm can determine in general terms whether an arbitrary computer program stops (terminates) or runs forever. (As part of AL-Models unit: 9 hours)

metadata.title: AL-SEP: Ethics & Society
metadata.definition: Improve your understanding and ability to analyze the far-reaching impact of algorithm design and use on society, presented at an advanced level in SEP hours.

metadata.title: Graph Algorithms (Advanced)
metadata.definition: In-depth study of graph data structures and the complex algorithms used to process them, within the context of a 4-course framework. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Sorting Algorithms (Advanced)
metadata.definition: Algorithms designed to sort the elements of a list in a certain order, including more efficient algorithms and algorithms with pseudo-linear complexity. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Heap Sort O(n log n)
metadata.definition: The sorting algorithm is based on a heap data structure, which has a runtime complexity of O(n log n). (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Pseudo-Linear Complexity O(n)
metadata.definition: Sorting algorithms have near-linear complexity O(n) under some specific conditions, such as bin sorting. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Bucket Sort
metadata.definition: The sorting algorithm divides elements into a finite number of 'buckets', then sorts each bucket separately. Effective with evenly distributed data. (An example for Pseudo O(n) complexity)

metadata.title: Pseudo-Linear Complexity O(n)
metadata.definition: Sorting algorithms have near-linear complexity O(n) under some specific conditions, such as counting sort. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Counting Sort
metadata.definition: The sorting algorithm uses the frequency of occurrence of elements to place them in their correct position. Effective when the value range is small. (An example for Pseudo O(n) complexity)

metadata.title: Pseudo-Linear Complexity O(n)
metadata.definition: Sorting algorithms have near-linear complexity O(n) under some specific conditions, such as radix sorting. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Radix Sort
metadata.definition: The sorting algorithm is not based on comparison, sorting elements by grouping them by individual digits or characters. (An example for Pseudo O(n) complexity)

metadata.title: Transitive Closure (Warshall)
metadata.definition: An algorithm that calculates all pairs of vertices (u,v) such that there is a path from u to v in a directed graph, such as Warshall's algorithm. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Graph Matching
metadata.definition: In graph theory, a set of edges with no vertices in common, often used in pairwise assignment or search problems. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Efficient String Matching
metadata.definition: Efficient search algorithms for finding the occurrence of a pattern (substring) in a text (mainstring), for example the Boyer-Moore algorithm. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: Boyer-Moore Algorithm
metadata.definition: An efficient string search algorithm, often the fastest standard string search algorithm, by ignoring parts of the text that are unlikely to contain a pattern. (An example for Efficient String Matching)

metadata.title: Efficient String Matching
metadata.definition: Efficient search algorithms for finding the occurrence of a pattern (substring) in a text (mainstring), for example the Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm. (As part of an AL-Foundational unit: 3 hours)

metadata.title: KMP Algorithm
metadata.definition: An efficient string search algorithm that avoids rechecking previously checked text characters. (An example for Efficient String Matching)

metadata.title: Longest Common Subsequence
metadata.definition: The ability to find the longest common substring between two or more given strings, a fundamental problem in dynamic programming and computational biology.

metadata.title: Regular Expression Matching
metadata.definition: Ability to use and understand regular expressions to search, match, and manipulate text based on specific patterns.

metadata.title: Algorithm Complexity
metadata.definition: Study of the computational resources (time, space) an algorithm requires to complete a task. Includes asymptotic analysis and basic complexity classes.

metadata.title: Asymptotic Complexity Analysis
metadata.definition: Mathematical method for describing the bounded behavior of an algorithm as input size increases, using Big O, Big Omega, and Big Theta notation.

metadata.title: Fundamental Complexity Classes
metadata.definition: Standard categories for classifying computational problems based on the resources required to solve them, such as O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2).

metadata.title: Exponential Complexity O(2^n)
metadata.definition: The complexity class represents an exponential growth of computational time or space with input size, often appearing in NP-hard problems with no known polynomial algorithm.

metadata.title: Factorial Complexity O(n!)
metadata.definition: The complexity class represents very rapid growth of computational time or space, typical for algorithms that iterate over all permutations, as in some brute-force methods.

metadata.title: Empirical Performance Measurement
metadata.definition: Practical techniques for evaluating the performance of algorithms by running them on real data and measuring runtime, memory usage, and other metrics.

metadata.title: Feasibility & Intractability
metadata.definition: Distinguish between problems that can be solved efficiently (in polynomial time) and problems that cannot be solved efficiently (in superpolynomial runtime), often involving the P and NP classes.

metadata.title: Algorithm Strategies
metadata.definition: Algorithm design and development methods to solve different types of computational problems, including exhaustion, divide and conquer, greed, etc.

metadata.title: Brute Force Strategy
metadata.definition: A method of solving problems by systematically trying every possible possibility until the right solution is found, often the simplest but ineffective method.

metadata.title: Traveling Salesperson Problem
metadata.definition: An optimization problem in which the goal is to find the shortest path through a set of cities and back to the starting point, a classic example of an NP-hard problem often illustrated by exhaustion.

metadata.title: Knapsack Problem
metadata.definition: An optimization problem in which the goal is to select items with different weights and values ​​to maximize the total value while not exceeding the bag's weight limit, another example of a problem that can be solved by brute force or dynamic programming.

metadata.title: Decrease-and-Conquer
metadata.definition: A strategy for designing an algorithm by reducing the size of a problem instance to a smaller instance, solving the smaller problem, and then expanding the solution to the solution of the original problem.

metadata.title: Topological Sort
metadata.definition: The algorithm sorts the vertices of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) in a linear order such that for every directed edge from u to v, u comes before v in the sort order.

metadata.title: Divide-and-Conquer Strategy
metadata.definition: A robust algorithmic strategy consists of three steps: dividing the larger problem into smaller subproblems, recursively solving the subproblems, and combining the subsolutions to form the solution of the original problem.

metadata.title: Strassen Algorithm
metadata.definition: A more efficient matrix multiplication algorithm than the standard algorithm, using a divide-and-conquer strategy to reduce the number of multiplications needed, especially useful for large matrices.

metadata.title: Greedy Strategy
metadata.definition: An algorithm design method in which a locally optimal choice is made at each step in the hope that it will lead to a globally optimal solution.

metadata.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm
metadata.definition: An algorithm for finding the shortest path between nodes in a graph with positively weighted edges, commonly used in network routing.

metadata.title: Kruskal's Algorithm
metadata.definition: An algorithm to find the Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) for a weighted undirected graph, by adding the edges with the least weight without forming a cycle.

metadata.title: Transform-and-Conquer
metadata.definition: An algorithmic strategy involves transforming a given problem into another (usually simpler or already solved) instance, solving the transformed instance, and then transforming the solution back.

metadata.title: Heapsort Algorithm
metadata.definition: A sorting algorithm based on the heap data structure, where the sorting problem is transformed into building and maintaining a heap.

metadata.title: 2-3 Tree
metadata.definition: A type of balanced search tree (B-tree) can contain 2 or 3 keys in each node and have all leaves at the same level, used to maintain efficient insertion, deletion, and search operations.

metadata.title: AVL Tree
metadata.definition: A type of self-balancing binary search tree, where the difference in height of the left and right subtrees of any node cannot be greater than 1.

metadata.title: Red-Black Tree
metadata.definition: Another type of self-balancing binary search tree, ensuring search, insertion, and deletion operations have O(log n) time complexity.

metadata.title: Dynamic Programming
metadata.definition: A mathematical optimization technique and algorithm design method that solves complex problems by dividing them into simpler subproblems and storing their results to avoid recalculation.

metadata.title: Warshall's Algorithm
metadata.definition: Algorithm to find transitive closure of a directed graph, indicating which pairs of vertices have a path between them.

metadata.title: Floyd's Algorithm
metadata.definition: An algorithm to find the shortest path between all pairs of vertices in a weighted graph, which can handle negative edge weights (but no negative cycles).

metadata.title: Bellman-Ford Algorithm
metadata.definition: An algorithm to find the shortest path from a source vertex to all other vertices in a weighted graph, which can handle negative edge weights and detect negative cycles.

metadata.title: Handling Exponential Growth
metadata.definition: Techniques and approaches for managing and solving problems of exponentially growing time complexity, often by finding approximate solutions or using heuristics.

metadata.title: A* Heuristic
metadata.definition: A best path search algorithm prioritizes the expansion of nodes by estimating the lowest cost from the current node to the destination, commonly used in artificial intelligence and pathfinding.

metadata.title: Branch-and-Bound
metadata.definition: An algorithmic strategy for finding optimal solutions to complex optimization problems, by dividing the search space into branches and eliminating unpromising branches using upper/lower bounds.

metadata.title: Backtracking
metadata.definition: A problem-solving technique by trying to construct a solution step by step; When a potential solution is no longer valid or does not lead to a solution, the algorithm backtracks and tries another option.

metadata.title: P, NP, NP-Complete
metadata.definition: Computational complexity theory models use Turing Machines to define and classify the P, NP, and NP-Complete problem classes, which are central to the Theory of Computation.

metadata.title: Class P
metadata.definition: The set of decision problems that can be solved by a deterministic polynomial Turing machine.

metadata.title: Class NP
metadata.definition: The set of decision problems whose solutions can be verified by a non-deterministic polynomial Turing machine.

metadata.title: Class NP-Complete

metadata.title: Unstructured Data

metadata.title: Structured/Streaming Data Systems

metadata.title: Data Modeling
metadata.definition: The process of creating an abstract and consistent model of the data used in an information system.

metadata.title: Relational Data Model
metadata.definition: A data model organizes data into tables (relations) with rows and columns, based on mathematical predicate logic.

metadata.title: Conceptual Models
metadata.definition: High-level data models are used to describe the overall data structure and relationships between entities, independent of the specific DBMS.

metadata.title: E-R Diagram
metadata.definition: A graphical tool for representing entities, attributes, and relationships between them in a conceptual database model.

metadata.title: UML Data Modeling
metadata.definition: Use Unified Modeling Language (UML) diagrams, especially class diagrams, to describe data structures and relationships.

metadata.title: Semi-structured Data Model
metadata.definition: The data models used to represent data do not have a strict fixed structure as in relational databases, but have some organization through tags or tree structures, e.g. XML, JSON.

metadata.title: DTD
metadata.definition: A markup language used to define the valid structure of an XML or SGML document.

metadata.title: XML
metadata.definition: A markup language used to encode documents in a format that can be read by both humans and machines.

metadata.title: JSON Schema
metadata.definition: A JSON-based standard for describing the structure and format of JSON data.

metadata.title: Spreadsheet Model
metadata.definition: Use spreadsheets to organize, store, and analyze data, often for simple applications or personal data analysis.

metadata.title: Object-Oriented Model
metadata.definition: Data models are based on the concept of objects, inheritance, encapsulation, and polymorphism, often used in object databases or object-relational mappings.

metadata.title: GraphQL
metadata.definition: A server-side runtime and query language for executing queries using a data type system defined by the provider.

metadata.title: New SQL Features
metadata.definition: Explore new features and enhancements introduced in recent versions of the SQL language, which expand query and data management capabilities.

metadata.title: Time-Series Data
metadata.definition: Data collected or recorded in chronological order, often used to track changes in a metric over time.

metadata.title: Time-Series Data Aggregation
metadata.definition: Aggregation techniques (e.g., averaging, summing, counting) on ​​time series data to extract meaningful information from different time periods.

metadata.title: Time-Series Data Joining
metadata.definition: Methods for combining different time series data sets based on time points or related attributes.

metadata.title: Graph Data
metadata.definition: Data is represented as nodes (entities) and edges (relationships) between them, commonly used in social networks, recommendation systems.

metadata.title: Graph Traversal
metadata.definition: The process of moving through relationships (edges) in a graph data structure to discover related entities or find paths.

metadata.title: Efficient Data Access Techniques
metadata.definition: Methods to optimize query performance by avoiding direct access and reprocessing of raw data, often including the use of special data structures and aggregation tools.

metadata.title: Materialized Views
metadata.definition: Database views whose results are physically stored in the database, allowing faster queries for complex or frequent queries.

metadata.title: Efficient Data Structures
metadata.definition: Data structures are specifically designed to optimize data access and processing, especially in big data situations, to improve performance.

metadata.title: HyperLogLog
metadata.definition: An algorithm that estimates the number of unique elements in a large data set with little error and low memory consumption.

metadata.title: Bitmap (Data Structure)
metadata.definition: A data structure used to represent a set of values ​​using a string of bits, where each bit represents the presence or absence of an element.

metadata.title: Geospatial Data
metadata.definition: Data describing objects, events or phenomena located on Earth, including spatial and non-spatial attributes.

metadata.title: GIS Database

metadata.title: Entity Integrity
metadata.definition: The rule ensures that each row (record) in a table has a unique primary key and is not empty.

metadata.title: Referential Integrity
metadata.definition: The rule ensures that foreign key values ​​in one table refer to existing primary key values ​​in another table or are null.

metadata.title: Candidate Key
metadata.definition: An attribute or set of attributes in a table that uniquely identifies each row and contains no child attributes that also uniquely identify the rows.

metadata.title: Superkey
metadata.definition: An attribute or set of attributes that uniquely identifies a row in a table. A candidate key is a minimal superkey.

metadata.title: Relational Database Design
metadata.definition: The process of creating an efficient and consistent relational database structure that adheres to the principles of normalization and data integrity.

metadata.title: Conceptual to Relational Mapping
metadata.definition: The process of converting a conceptual data model (for example, an E-R diagram) into a concrete relational data model, including creating tables, columns, and key definitions.

metadata.title: Physical Database Design
metadata.definition: The process of designing the actual data storage structures on disk, including the selection of file structures, indexing methods, and data organization to optimize performance.

metadata.title: File Structures & Storage
metadata.definition: The methods and techniques used to organize and store data on physical storage devices, including file formats, indexes, and how the data is organized.

metadata.title: Functional Dependencies Intro
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of functional dependencies in relational databases, describing binding relationships between attributes.

metadata.title: Normalization Theory
metadata.definition: Deep dive into relational database normalization principles and techniques to eliminate data redundancy and improve data integrity, based on functional dependencies.

metadata.title: Schema Decomposition
metadata.definition: The process of dividing a large relational schema into smaller schemas to achieve higher normal forms.

metadata.title: Lossless Join Decomposition
metadata.definition: A property of schema decomposition ensures that when child tables are reconnected, no information is lost or spurious information is created.

metadata.title: Dependency Preserving Decomposition
metadata.definition: A property of schema decomposition ensures that all original functional dependencies can be tested by testing only the functional dependencies in the decomposed child tables.

metadata.title: Database Normal Forms
metadata.definition: Rules for evaluating the degree of normalization of a relational table, with Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) being one of the higher normal forms, eliminating more data anomalies than previous normal forms.

metadata.title: BCNF
metadata.definition: A standard form in relational database design, stricter than 3NF, that eliminates functional dependencies where a non-key attribute depends on part of a candidate key.

metadata.title: Denormalization (Performance)
metadata.definition: The process of intentionally introducing data redundancy into a normalized database schema to improve query performance, often by reducing the number of joins required.

metadata.title: Advanced Functional Dependencies
metadata.definition: In-depth study of functional dependencies, including properties and how they are used in database normalization.

metadata.title: Attribute Closure
metadata.definition: The set of all attributes that can be determined from an initial set of attributes through the given functional dependencies.

metadata.title: Canonical Cover
metadata.definition: A minimal set of functional dependencies is equivalent to a given set of functional dependencies, no functional dependencies can be inferred from other functional dependencies in that set.

metadata.title: Advanced Normalization Theory
metadata.definition: In-depth study of normalization theory, including higher normal forms and more complex types of dependencies.

metadata.title: Multivalued Dependency (MVD)
metadata.definition: A type of dependency in a relational database that describes a constraint in which one set of attributes defines a different set of values ​​for another attribute, independent of the other attributes.

metadata.title: Fourth Normal Form (4NF)
metadata.definition: A higher standard form than BCNF, resolving anomalies caused by multivalued dependencies.

metadata.title: Join Dependency (JD)
metadata.definition: A constraint in a relational database ensures that a table can be decomposed into smaller tables and then rejoined without losing or adding information.

metadata.title: Project-Join Normal Form (PJNF)
metadata.definition: A higher normal form than 4NF, resolving anomalies caused by connection dependencies. (Equivalent to 5NF)

metadata.title: Fifth Normal Form (5NF)
metadata.definition: The highest standard in relational databases, resolving join dependencies to ensure that all dependencies are inferred from candidate keys. (Equivalent to PJNF)

metadata.title: Representation Theory (Database)
metadata.definition: Study of how information and knowledge are represented in various database models, including the theories underlying data and relational representation.

metadata.title: Conceptual to Relational Schema Design
metadata.definition: Ability to build a relational schema from a conceptual schema, including handling 1:1, 1:n, and n:m relationships.

metadata.title: File Structure to Relation Mapping
metadata.definition: Ability to map appropriate file structures to relations and indexes in the database management system.

metadata.title: Functional Dependency Theory
metadata.definition: Describe how functional dependency theory generalizes the concept of locking in databases.

metadata.title: Lossless & Dependency Preserving Decomposition
metadata.definition: The ability to define and protect a given decomposition as lossless and/or dependency-preserving.

metadata.title: Decomposition Normal Form Identification
metadata.definition: The ability to detect the normal form that a given decomposition achieves (e.g., 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF).

metadata.title: Denormalization Reasons
metadata.definition: Gives the rationale and context for denormalizing a relationship in the database, often to improve performance.

metadata.title: SQL Query Formulation
metadata.definition: understand and implement the steps to build an effective SQL query.

metadata.title: Interactive SQL Execution
metadata.definition: Ability to execute SQL queries interactively via command line interface or GUI tool.

metadata.title: Programmatic SQL Execution
metadata.definition: Ability to execute SQL queries through program code, for example using APIs or database drivers.

metadata.title: Relational Algebra
metadata.definition: understand and use relational algebra operators (selection, projection, connect, union, intersection, difference) as the theoretical foundation for SQL.

metadata.title: SQL Data Definition Language (DDL)
metadata.definition: Use SQL to define relational schemas, including table creation, integrity constraints, and other specifications.

metadata.title: SQL Integrity Constraints
metadata.definition: understand and define data integrity constraints (e.g. primary key, foreign key, NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE) in SQL.

metadata.title: SQL Data Manipulation Language (DML)
metadata.definition: Use the SQL update language subsection (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) to add, modify, or delete data in the database.

metadata.title: Relational Algebra
metadata.definition: Learn about relational algebra, a non-procedural query language based on first-order predicate logic.

metadata.title: Query By Example (QBE)
metadata.definition: Introduction to QBE, a visual query language for relational databases.

metadata.title: 4th-Generation Environments
metadata.definition: Learn about fourth-generation programming environments and tools, often bundled with high-level query and productivity languages.

metadata.title: Non-Procedural Query Invocation
metadata.definition: Various methods for calling non-procedural queries (like SQL) from within common programming languages.

metadata.title: Other Query Languages (XPATH, SPARQL)
metadata.definition: An introduction to important query languages ​​other than SQL, such as XPATH (for XML documents) and SPARQL (for RDF data).

metadata.title: Stored Procedures
metadata.definition: Learn about stored procedures, SQL scripts stored in a database to perform repetitive or complex tasks.

metadata.title: SQL SELECT Queries
metadata.definition: Ability to build SQL queries using SELECT clauses to select data.

metadata.title: SQL PROJECT Queries
metadata.definition: Ability to build SQL queries to project (select specific columns) data.

metadata.title: SQL JOIN Queries
metadata.definition: Ability to build SQL queries using JOIN clauses to join data from multiple tables.

metadata.title: SQL UNION Queries
metadata.definition: Ability to build SQL queries that use the UNION operator to combine result sets.

metadata.title: SQL INTERSECT Queries
metadata.definition: Ability to build SQL queries that use the INTERSECTION operator to find common rows between result sets.

metadata.title: SQL EXCEPT Queries
metadata.definition: Ability to build SQL queries that use the SET DIFFERENCE (subtract) operator to find row differences between result sets.

metadata.title: SQL SET DIVISION Queries
metadata.definition: Ability to build SQL queries using the SET DIVISION operator to resolve 'all' or 'every' queries.

metadata.title: Correlated vs. Uncorrelated Subqueries
metadata.definition: Ability to differentiate and understand the difference between correlated and uncorrelated nested SQL queries.

metadata.title: Programmatic SQL Data Iteration
metadata.definition: Ability to process and iterate through data result sets programmatically retrieved from an SQL query.

metadata.title: SQL Schema Definition with Constraints & Triggers
metadata.definition: Ability to define entire relational schema in SQL, including all integrity constraints and delete/update triggers.

metadata.title: Page Structures
metadata.definition: understand the structure and organization of data pages in a database management system and how they are stored on disk.

metadata.title: Index Structures
metadata.definition: understand the different types of index structures and their importance in speeding up database queries.

metadata.title: B+ Trees
metadata.definition: Research on the structure and operation of B+ trees, a popular type of index in database management systems.

metadata.title: Static Hash Indexes
metadata.definition: Study static hash indexes and how they provide fast access to data based on fixed hash values.

metadata.title: Dynamic Hash Indexes
metadata.definition: Study dynamic hash indexes and how they self-adjust to handle growth or decrease in the size of data.

metadata.title: SQL Index Creation
metadata.definition: How to use SQL commands to create and manage different types of indexes on database tables.

metadata.title: File Structures
metadata.definition: Learn about the basic file structures used to store data on disk in a database management system.

metadata.title: Heap Files
metadata.definition: Learn about heap files, a way of storing data in no particular order where records are added wherever there is free space.

metadata.title: Hash Files
metadata.definition: Learn about hash files and how they use hash functions to organize and access data quickly based on hash keys.

metadata.title: Query Operator Algorithms
metadata.definition: Study the basic algorithms used to implement query operators such as select, projection, and join.

metadata.title: External Sorting
metadata.definition: Learn about the external sort algorithm, used when the data to be sorted is too large to fit in main memory.

metadata.title: Selection Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms are used to perform selection (row filtering) operators during query processing.

metadata.title: Projection Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms are used to perform projection (column selection) operations, including handling the removal of duplicate records.

metadata.title: Natural Join Algorithms
metadata.definition: Study the algorithms used to perform natural joins between tables.

metadata.title: Nested Loop Join
metadata.definition: Learn about the nested loop join algorithm, one of the basic connection algorithms, traversing each pair of records.

metadata.title: Sort-Merge Join
metadata.definition: Learn about the sort-merge join algorithm, which requires tables to be sorted before merging.

metadata.title: Hash Join
metadata.definition: Learn about the hash join algorithm, which uses hash functions to group and connect records.

metadata.title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis
metadata.definition: analyze the efficiency and complexity of query processing algorithms, often measured by the number of I/O operations.

metadata.title: Query Transformations
metadata.definition: Techniques for converting a query from its original form to an equivalent form that can be executed more efficiently by the database management system.

metadata.title: Query Optimization
metadata.definition: understand the process and techniques that a database management system uses to select the optimal execution plan for a query.

metadata.title: Access Paths
metadata.definition: The different ways the query optimizer can access data (e.g., table scans, using indexes).

metadata.title: Query Plan Construction
metadata.definition: The process of building a detailed execution plan for a query, including the order of operations and access methods.

metadata.title: Selectivity Estimation
metadata.definition: Methods that estimate the number of records that will be returned by a query operator, important for optimization.

metadata.title: Index-Only Plans
metadata.definition: Query plans can be executed entirely using indexes without accessing the original data table.

metadata.title: Parallel Query Processing
metadata.definition: Learn about parallel query processing to speed up query execution by dividing work across multiple processors or nodes.

metadata.title: Parallel Scan
metadata.definition: Parallel data scanning technique across multiple devices or streams to speed up retrieval.

metadata.title: Parallel Join
metadata.definition: Technique for performing parallel connections between tables to speed up processing.

metadata.title: Parallel Aggregation
metadata.definition: Technique for performing aggregate operations (e.g., SUM, COUNT, AVG) in parallel on data partitions.

metadata.title: Database Tuning & Performance
metadata.definition: Methods and techniques to tune and improve overall database performance.

metadata.title: Index Selection
metadata.definition: The process of deciding which indexes should be created or modified to optimize the performance of executing a set of queries.

metadata.title: Index Performance Impact
metadata.definition: analyze the impact of using indexes on query speed, update costs, and storage capacity.

metadata.title: Denormalization for Performance
metadata.definition: apply denormalization as a tuning technique to improve query performance by reducing the number of joins, although it may increase data redundancy.

metadata.title: DB Buffer Management
metadata.definition: understand how database management systems manage caches in main memory to optimize data access from disk.

metadata.title: Transaction Isolation Levels
metadata.definition: Learn about different isolation levels for database transactions (e.g., Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable) and their impact on consistency and performance.

metadata.title: ACID Properties
metadata.definition: Master the four basic properties of transactions in database management systems: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability.

metadata.title: Serializability
metadata.definition: understand the principles and methods of ensuring that the result of the simultaneous execution of multiple transactions is equivalent to several sequential executions of the same transactions.

metadata.title: Distributed Transactions
metadata.definition: Learn how to manage transactions that span multiple databases or systems, including challenges and solutions for consistency and reliability (See also: PDC-Coordination).

metadata.title: Concurrency Control: 2PL
metadata.definition: Research 2-phase locking (2PL) mechanism to ensure serialization in concurrent environments (See also: OS-Concurrency).

metadata.title: Deadlock Handling Strategies
metadata.definition: Learn methods to detect, prevent, and resolve deadlocks in concurrent database systems.

metadata.title: Quorum Consistency Models
metadata.definition: Explore quorum-based data consistency models, used to ensure reliability and availability in distributed systems.

metadata.title: Recovery & Buffer Manager
metadata.definition: understand the relationship and interaction between the recovery manager and the cache manager in a database management system.

metadata.title: Optimistic Concurrency Control
metadata.definition: Study optimistic concurrency control methods where transactions are assumed to be conflict-free and conflict checking is performed at the commit stage.

metadata.title: Timestamp Concurrency Control
metadata.definition: Learn how to use timestamps to control the execution order of concurrent transactions and ensure serialization.

metadata.title: Write-Ahead Logging
metadata.definition: Learn Write-Ahead logging (WAL) techniques to ensure transaction persistence during database recovery.

metadata.title: ARIES Recovery System
metadata.definition: Study in detail the ARIES recovery system, including the analyze, REDO and UNDO phases, used to recover the database after a crash.

metadata.title: Why NoSQL?
metadata.definition: understand the reasons and use cases when NoSQL systems are preferred over traditional RDBMS (e.g. impedance mismatch between Application [CRUD] and RDBMS).

metadata.title: Key-Value & Document Models
metadata.definition: Research the characteristics and applications of Key-Value and Document data models in NoSQL systems.

metadata.title: NoSQL Storage Systems
metadata.definition: Explore the types of storage systems used in NoSQL environments, including Key-Value systems and Data Lakes.

metadata.title: Sharding & Replication
metadata.definition: Learn data distribution techniques such as Sharding and Replication in NoSQL systems to increase scalability and availability (See also: PDC-Communication).

metadata.title: Graph Databases
metadata.definition: Research graph databases, modeling and querying data as nodes and edges, suitable for data with complex relationships.

metadata.title: NoSQL Consistency Models
metadata.definition: understand the different consistency models in NoSQL, including update and read consistency, Quorum consistency, and the CAP (Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance) theorem (See also: PDC-Communication).

metadata.title: Map-Reduce Models
metadata.definition: Learn big data processing paradigms like Map-Reduce, Multi-stage Map-Reduce, and Incremental Map-Reduce in a NoSQL context (See also: PDC-Communication).

metadata.title: NoSQL Case Studies
metadata.definition: Study real-life cases of cloud storage systems (e.g., S3), graph databases, and analyze situations where NoSQL is not suitable (See also: SPD-Web).

metadata.title: Data Security vs. Privacy
metadata.definition: Clear distinction between data security (protecting data from unauthorized access) and data privacy (managing how personal data is collected, used and shared) (See also: SEC-Foundations).

metadata.title: Database Attack Protection
metadata.definition: Learn methods and techniques to protect data and database systems from threats and attacks, including injection attacks such as SQL injection (See also: SEC-Foundations).

metadata.title: PII Protection
metadata.definition: Master the concept of Personally Identifiable Information (PII) and strategies to protect it from misuse or unauthorized disclosure (See also: SEC-Foundations, SEP-Security, SEP-Privacy).

metadata.title: Data Security & Privacy Ethics
metadata.definition: Discuss ethical issues related to data collection, storage, processing, and sharing, especially in the context of security and privacy (See also: SEC-SEP, SEP-Ethical-Analysis, SEP-Security, SEP-Privacy).

metadata.title: Data Security States
metadata.definition: understand the importance and different methods to protect data in different states: when data is inactive (at rest), while in transit (in transit) and while being processed (during processing) (See also: SEC-Foundations, SEC-Crypto).

metadata.title: Database Auditing & Forensics
metadata.definition: The study of database auditing, including activity logging techniques, and its important role in digital forensics to detect and analyze security breaches (See also: SEC-Forensics).

metadata.title: Data Inference Attacks
metadata.definition: Learn how to infer sensitive information from non-sensitive data and measures to prevent inference attacks, especially in the context of database systems (See also: SEC-Crypto).

metadata.title: Data Privacy Regulations
metadata.definition: Master key laws and regulations related to data security and privacy, such as GDPR, HIPAA, etc., and their impact on data system design and management (See also: SEP-Security, SEP-Privacy, SEC-Foundations, SEC-Governance).

metadata.title: Data Integrity Risks
metadata.definition: analyze common risk factors that can affect data integrity and preventative measures to maintain data accuracy and consistency (See also: SEC-Governance).

metadata.title: Ransomware
metadata.definition: Learn about ransomware attacks and effective strategies to prevent data loss, data destruction, and ensure recovery from such attacks (See also: SEC-Coding, SEC-Forensics).

metadata.title: Data Exploration
metadata.definition: Master data exploration techniques, including data dynamics, representations, descriptive statistics, and visualization methods to better understand data sets.

metadata.title: Data Science Life Cycle
metadata.definition: understand the stages in the data science lifecycle, from business understanding to deployment and user adoption, as a basis for data analytics and machine learning projects (See also: AI-ML).

metadata.title: Data Mining Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms and techniques are used to discover patterns, trends, and insights from large data sets.

metadata.title: Machine Learning Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms allow systems to learn from data, recognize patterns, and make decisions without being explicitly programmed.

metadata.title: Classification Algorithms
metadata.definition: Machine learning algorithms are used to classify data into predefined categories or classes based on their characteristics.

metadata.title: Clustering Algorithms
metadata.definition: Machine learning algorithms are used to group similar data points together into clusters, based on their similarity.

metadata.title: Association Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms are used to discover relationships (association rules) between variables in large data sets.

metadata.title: Regression Algorithms
metadata.definition: Machine learning algorithms are used to predict a continuous variable (dependent variable) based on one or more independent variables.

metadata.title: Data Collection
metadata.definition: The process of collecting, filtering, and cleaning data from various sources to prepare it for processing and analysis.

metadata.title: Data Governance
metadata.definition: A set of policies, standards, roles, and processes to ensure the quality, availability, usability, integrity, and security of data within an organization.

metadata.title: Data Fairness
metadata.definition: Ensure that data collection, use and analysis do not result in discrimination or disadvantage to particular groups of individuals.

metadata.title: Data Bias
metadata.definition: Systematic errors in the data or in the way the data is collected, leading to unfair or inaccurate results or decisions.

metadata.title: Data Visualization Techniques
metadata.definition: Methods and tools for presenting data in graphic or visual form to help users more easily understand and analyze information.

metadata.title: Data Visualization Applications
metadata.definition: How data visualization techniques are used to explore, present, and communicate findings from data analysis.

metadata.title: Entity Resolution
metadata.definition: The process of identifying and linking records that represent the same entity in one or more data sets.

metadata.title: EDA Methods
metadata.definition: Initial techniques for analyzing data sets aim to summarize their main characteristics, often using visual methods.

metadata.title: Distributed DBMS
metadata.definition: Database management systems allow data to be stored and managed on many different physical computers, but still operate as a single logical database.

metadata.title: Distributed Data Storage
metadata.definition: A method of storing data on multiple networked nodes or servers, allowing for scalability, fault tolerance, and efficient data access.

metadata.title: Distributed Query Processing
metadata.definition: Technique for handling queries on data stored across multiple locations in a distributed database system.

metadata.title: Distributed Transaction Model
metadata.definition: The model manages transactions involving multiple data sources or resources on different nodes in a distributed system, ensuring consistency and integrity.

metadata.title: Homogeneous Distributed DB
metadata.definition: Distributed database solutions where all nodes use the same database software and data schema.

metadata.title: Heterogeneous Distributed DB
metadata.definition: Distributed database solutions where nodes can use different database management systems or data schemas.

metadata.title: Client-Server Distributed DB
metadata.definition: Distributed database architecture where clients send requests to servers that manage and store data.

metadata.title: Parallel DBMS
metadata.definition: A database management system uses multiple processors and/or disks at the same time to execute database operations to improve performance.

metadata.title: Parallel DBMS Architecture
metadata.definition: Different architectural models for parallel DBMSs, including shared memory, shared disk, and shared nothing.

metadata.title: Shared-Memory Architecture
metadata.definition: A Parallel DBMS architecture where all processors share a common memory address space.

metadata.title: Shared-Disk Architecture
metadata.definition: A Parallel DBMS architecture where all processors have access to the same set of disks.

metadata.title: Nothing-Shared Architecture
metadata.definition: A Parallel DBMS architecture where each processor has its own memory and disk, not shared directly with other processors.

metadata.title: Speedup & Scale-up
metadata.definition: Parallel system performance measurement concepts: speedup is reducing execution time with fixed data and more resources; Scaling is maintaining execution time as data and resources increase.

metadata.title: MapReduce Model
metadata.definition: A programming model and software framework for processing large data sets using distributed algorithms across a computer cluster.

metadata.title: Data Replication
metadata.definition: The process of creating and maintaining multiple copies of data at different locations to increase availability, fault tolerance, and performance.

metadata.title: Weak Consistency Models
metadata.definition: The models ensure that data will eventually be consistent across all replicas, but allow that different replicas may be temporarily out of sync.

metadata.title: Unstructured Data Vectorization
metadata.definition: The process of converting unstructured data (text, video, audio) into digital representations (vectors) that can be processed by computer algorithms.

metadata.title: Vector Storage
metadata.definition: Systems or techniques designed to store and retrieve vector representations of unstructured data efficiently.

metadata.title: TF-IDF Ngram Vectorization
metadata.definition: A technique that converts text into numeric vectors, using term-frequency index-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) and word groups (ngrams) to capture context.

metadata.title: Word2Vec
metadata.definition: A word embedding technique to create vector representations of words, where words with similar meanings have vector representations close to each other in the vector space.

metadata.title: Array Database
metadata.definition: A type of database designed to efficiently store and manage large multi-dimensional array structured data sets, such as satellite images or sensor data.

metadata.title: Array Data Processing
metadata.definition: Techniques and methods for storing, querying, and manipulating array data types in databases.

metadata.title: Semi-structured Database
metadata.definition: Databases store data that does not follow the fixed structural model of a relational database, but contains tags or delimiters to separate semantic elements. JSON is a common example.

metadata.title: Semi-structured DB Storage
metadata.definition: Methods and systems are used to store semi-structured data efficiently, balancing flexibility and performance.

metadata.title: Nested Data Encoding
metadata.definition: Techniques for representing hierarchical or nested data types (as in JSON) into a format that can be stored and processed efficiently.

metadata.title: Nested Data Compression
metadata.definition: Methods for reducing the storage size of nested data types in semi-structured databases.

metadata.title: Semi-structured DB Indexing
metadata.definition: Indexing techniques to speed up queries on semi-structured data, taking into account their flexible and nested structure.

metadata.title: B-tree Index
metadata.definition: The B-tree index data structure is used for efficient search, insertion, and deletion of data, applied in the context of semi-structured databases.

metadata.title: Skip Index
metadata.definition: A type of index that allows queries to 'jump' over parts of unrelated data, speeding up searches in semi-structured data structures.

metadata.title: Bloom Filter
metadata.definition: A space-saving probabilistic data structure used to check whether an element is a member of a set, which can be applied to speed up queries on semi-structured data.

metadata.title: Inverted Index
metadata.definition: An index structure maps content values ​​to their location in the database, commonly used for full-text search in semi-structured data.

metadata.title: Bitmap Compression
metadata.definition: Technique that compresses bitmap indexes to save storage space and improve query performance, especially useful for data with many repeating values.

metadata.title: Space-filling Curve Indexing
metadata.definition: The indexing technique uses space-filling curves to map multidimensional geographic data into a one-dimensional order, optimizing the storage and querying of semi-structured geographic data.

metadata.title: Semi-structured Query Processing
metadata.definition: Methods and strategies for executing queries in semi-structured databases, supporting both online transaction processing (OLTP) and online analytical processing (OLAP) use cases.

metadata.title: Semi-structured CRUD Trade-offs
metadata.definition: analyze the performance and complexity trade-offs when performing CRUD (create, read, update, delete) operations on semi-structured databases, due to their flexible nature.

metadata.title: Postgres JSON Case Study
metadata.definition: Study how PostgreSQL supports and manages JSON data, including the functionality and performance when working with this semi-structured data type.

metadata.title: MongoDB Case Study
metadata.definition: Study how MongoDB, a document-based NoSQL database, stores and processes semi-structured data (especially BSON, similar to JSON).

metadata.title: Snowflake JSON Case Study
metadata.definition: Study how Snowflake, a cloud-based data warehouse, processes and analyzes JSON data, leveraging its special features for semi-structured data.

metadata.title: Data Scale Issues
metadata.definition: Ethical, social, and technical challenges and implications arise from collecting, storing, and processing extremely large data sets, including privacy and security.

metadata.title: Data Privacy
metadata.definition: Overview of concepts, principles and laws related to protecting personal information from unauthorized access, use or disclosure.

metadata.title: Privacy by Design Compliance
metadata.definition: An approach that integrates privacy protection requirements into the system, product or service design and development process from the beginning.

metadata.title: Data Anonymization
metadata.definition: Techniques and principles for removing or masking personally identifiable information from data, making individuals unidentifiable.

metadata.title: Data Ownership
metadata.definition: Legal rights and responsibilities regarding data, including rights to access, use, modify, and share data.

metadata.title: Data Custodian Role
metadata.definition: Responsibility for technical management and data maintenance, ensuring data is stored securely, accessible and in compliance with policies.

metadata.title: Intended Data Use
metadata.definition: The planned and authorized purposes for which the collected and stored data will be used.

metadata.title: Unintended Data Use
metadata.definition: Uses of data that were not originally intended or authorized may lead to ethical, legal, or social issues.

metadata.title: Data Reliability
metadata.definition: The degree to which data can be trusted to be accurate, complete, consistent, and available when needed.

metadata.title: Data Provenance
metadata.definition: A detailed record of the origin of the data and the sequence of operations that have been applied to it since its creation.

metadata.title: Data Lineage
metadata.definition: The complete history of the data, including where it originated, how it was transformed, moved and used over time.

metadata.title: Metadata Management
metadata.definition: The process of managing information about data (metadata) to help organize, access, and understand data more effectively.

metadata.title: Data Security
metadata.definition: Measures and tools to protect data from unauthorized access, modification, destruction or disclosure.

metadata.title: Collaborative Data Management
metadata.definition: Data stewards and data users must collaborate to ensure accurate data is accessed and used only appropriately.

metadata.title: Responsive Data Management
metadata.definition: The data stored and accessed must always meet the needs/requirements of the organization.

metadata.title: Discrete Mathematics
metadata.definition: Discrete Mathematics requirements.

metadata.title: Set Theory
metadata.definition: Set theory, including basic operations.

metadata.title: Set Union
metadata.definition: Union operation between sets.

metadata.title: Set Intersection
metadata.definition: Intersection operation between sets.

metadata.title: Set Difference
metadata.definition: Subtraction (difference) operation between sets.

metadata.title: Cartesian Product
metadata.definition: Cartesian product operation between sets.

metadata.title: Probability & Statistics
metadata.definition: Probability and Statistics requirements for those specializing in DM-Analytics.

metadata.title: Hash Functions & Tables
metadata.definition: Hash functions, and hash tables, are desired data structures in data management.

metadata.title: Balanced Binary Trees
metadata.definition: Types of balanced binary trees, e.g. AVL, 2-3-4, Red-Black Trees.

metadata.title: AVL Tree
metadata.definition: AVL tree, a type of self-balancing binary search tree.

metadata.title: 2-3-4 Tree
metadata.definition: 2-3-4 plant, a type B plant.

metadata.title: Red-Black Tree
metadata.definition: Red-Black Tree, a self-balancing binary search tree.

metadata.title: B-Trees & B+ Trees
metadata.definition: B and B+ tree data structures, commonly used in database systems.

metadata.title: Database Design & Modeling
metadata.definition: One of the four main perspectives to approach databases, focusing on data design and modeling.

metadata.title: Database Usage
metadata.definition: One of the four main perspectives to approach databases, focusing on database usage.

metadata.title: Database Administration
metadata.definition: One of the four main perspectives to approach databases, focusing on database system administration.

metadata.title: Database Development
metadata.definition: One of four main perspectives for approaching databases, including implementation algorithms.

metadata.title: Database Implementation Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms are used to implement and operate database systems.

metadata.title: DM-SEP
metadata.definition: One topic in the Database Systems course (3 hours).

metadata.title: DM-Data
metadata.definition: A data-related topic in the Database Systems course (1 hour).

metadata.title: DM-Core
metadata.definition: Core Topics in Data Management (3 hours).

metadata.title: DM-Modeling
metadata.definition: Data modeling topics (5 hours).

metadata.title: DM-Relational
metadata.definition: Relational database topics (4 hours).

metadata.title: DM-Querying
metadata.definition: Topic on data query (6 hours).

metadata.title: DM-Processing
metadata.definition: Topics on data processing (5 hours).

metadata.title: DM-Internals
metadata.definition: Topics on the structure and inner workings of database systems (5 hours).

metadata.title: DM-NoSQL
metadata.definition: NoSQL Database Topics (4 hours).

metadata.title: DM-Security
metadata.definition: Topics on data security (3 hours).

metadata.title: Distributed Data Management
metadata.definition: Basic concepts and principles of distributed data management, allocated 2 class hours.

metadata.title: Core Database Concepts (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Basic database concepts are integrated into the CS Core curriculum, especially in the absence of specialized database courses.

metadata.title: Database Access
metadata.definition: Students use databases to retrieve data in introductory programming courses, instead of using file I/O or interactive data entry. This level usually includes being provided with an access code.

metadata.title: File I/O
metadata.definition: File import/export method, mentioned as an alternative to database access in introductory courses.

metadata.title: Interactive Input
metadata.definition: Direct data entry, via an interactive interface, is mentioned as an alternative to database access in introductory courses.

metadata.title: Basic SQL Query
metadata.definition: Students are provided with SQL query code to access the database in introductory courses.

metadata.title: Intermediate SQL Query
metadata.definition: Students write their own SQL queries at the intermediate level.

metadata.title: Database Design
metadata.definition: Practice database design in Software Engineering courses or capstone projects.

metadata.title: Databases Across Curriculum
metadata.definition: An approach that integrates database concepts across the curriculum, from introductory to advanced courses, to integrate database-related CS Core concepts.

metadata.title: Database SEP Topics
metadata.definition: Database-related Software Engineering Practice (SEP) topics are integrated into the curriculum using the 'Databases across the curriculum' approach.

metadata.title: Data Security Role
metadata.definition: Examining the role of data from a security perspective (Security - SEC), could be the content of an in-depth course.

metadata.title: Data Ethics (SEP)
metadata.definition: Examining the role of data from a social, ethical, and professional issues (SEP) perspective could be the content of an in-depth course.

metadata.title: Discrete Math (FPL)
metadata.definition: Discrete mathematical principles underpin the field of Programming Language Foundations.

metadata.title: Logic (FPL)
metadata.definition: Logical principles underpin the field of Programming Language Platforms.

metadata.title: Formal Languages (FPL)
metadata.definition: Formal language principles underpin the field of Programming Language Platforms.

metadata.title: Abstract Computation Models
metadata.definition: understand the basic abstract model of computation that programming languages ​​share.

metadata.title: Program Development Model
metadata.definition: understand the basic model of program development.

metadata.title: PL Abstractions
metadata.definition: Master common abstractions used in programming languages.

metadata.title: Programming Paradigms
metadata.definition: understand different programming paradigms (e.g., object-oriented, functional, imperative).

metadata.title: Programming Concepts
metadata.definition: Presents the basic concepts that make up programming languages.

metadata.title: PL Principles
metadata.definition: Presents the basic principles that govern programming languages.

metadata.title: Formal PL Specification
metadata.definition: Ability to specify programming languages ​​formally and concisely.

metadata.title: Formal Program Behavior
metadata.definition: Formal specification of the behavior of a program.

metadata.title: PL Implementation
metadata.definition: Explain how programming languages ​​are implemented.

metadata.title: Compare Programming Paradigms
metadata.definition: Compare the strengths and weaknesses of different programming models.

metadata.title: PL-OS Interface
metadata.definition: Describe how programming languages ​​communicate with operating systems.

metadata.title: PL-Hardware Interface
metadata.definition: Describe how programming languages ​​communicate with hardware.

metadata.title: Choose PL & Paradigm
metadata.definition: Ability to choose the programming model and language best suited to the specific problem.

metadata.title: Programming Paradigms
metadata.definition: understand different programming paradigms to make informed design choices.

metadata.title: PL Features
metadata.definition: understand the features and structures of programming languages.

metadata.title: PL Structures
metadata.definition: understand the structures and features of programming languages.

metadata.title: Define PL Features
metadata.definition: understand how programming language features are defined.

metadata.title: Compose PL Features
metadata.definition: understand how programming language features are put together.

metadata.title: Software Execution Efficiency
metadata.definition: Knowledge of how to improve software execution efficiency through understanding language features and implementations.

metadata.title: Long-term Software Maintenance
metadata.definition: Knowledge of how to improve long-term software maintainability through understanding language features and implementations.

metadata.title: Language Translation
metadata.definition: Basic knowledge of the programming language translation process.

metadata.title: Program Analysis
metadata.definition: Basic knowledge of program analysis techniques.

metadata.title: Program Runtime Behavior
metadata.definition: Basic knowledge of program behavior during execution.

metadata.title: Memory Management (PL)
metadata.definition: Basic knowledge of memory management in a programming language environment.

metadata.title: Concurrent Process Interaction
metadata.definition: Knowledge of interactions between concurrent processes.

metadata.title: Message Passing (Concurrency)
metadata.definition: Knowledge of message passing mechanisms for communication between concurrent processes.

metadata.title: Shared Memory (Concurrency)
metadata.definition: Knowledge of shared memory mechanisms for communication between concurrent processes.

metadata.title: Synchronization (Concurrency)
metadata.definition: Knowledge of synchronization mechanisms to coordinate concurrent processes.

metadata.title: Programming Language Design
metadata.definition: Requires deeper familiarity with the fundamentals for designing new languages.

metadata.title: OOP
metadata.definition: A programming model based on the concept of 'objects' that can contain data and code. The number of core hours spent on this topic has decreased by 4 hours.

metadata.title: Functional Programming
metadata.definition: A programming model that constructs programs by applying and combining functions, avoiding changing states. The number of core hours spent on this topic has been reduced by 2 hours.
