metadata.title: Event-driven & Reactive PL
metadata.definition: A programming model in which the flow of program execution is determined by events and continuously reacts to changes. The number of core hours spent on this topic has increased by 1 hour.

metadata.title: Parallel & Distributed Computing
metadata.definition: Research how to split and execute tasks simultaneously across multiple processors or computers to increase performance. This unit is renamed from 'Concurrency and Parallelism' and has core hours increased by 3 hours.

metadata.title: Type Systems
metadata.definition: A set of rules that assign a 'type' to programming language constructs to detect errors and increase reliability. The topics 'Basic Type Systems' and 'Type Systems' have been merged into this unit, with the core hours reduced by 1 hour.

metadata.title: Program Abstraction & Representation
metadata.definition: Methods of representing the structure and meaning of a computer program at different levels of abstraction. This unit is renamed from 'Program Representation' and has core hours reduced by 1 hour.

metadata.title: Program Analysis & Tools
metadata.definition: The study of automatically examining a program's source or object code to detect errors, optimize, or understand program behavior. This unit was renamed from 'Static Analysis'.

metadata.title: Runtime Behavior & Systems
metadata.definition: The study of how a program behaves during execution, including memory management, garbage collection, and services provided by the runtime environment. This unit was renamed from 'Runtime Systems'.

metadata.title: Shell Scripting
metadata.definition: Write scripts using a command line interface (shell) to automate system tasks or file management. This is a new unit added to the program with 2 core hours.

metadata.title: System Memory Model
metadata.definition: The study of how operating systems and hardware execute programs, manage and allocate memory, and how programs interact with memory. This is a new unit added to the program with 3 core hours.

metadata.title: Formal Methods
metadata.definition: Software development methods rely on rigorous mathematics to describe, design and verify systems, to ensure correctness and safety. This is a newly added unit of knowledge.

metadata.title: Programming Language Design
metadata.definition: Important principles and factors to consider when designing a new programming language, including syntax, semantics, data types, and execution model. This is a newly added unit of knowledge.

metadata.title: Programming Language Basics
metadata.definition: Basic concepts and principles that underlie understanding and analyzing various programming languages. This is a newly added unit of knowledge.

metadata.title: Society, Ethics, Professionalism
metadata.definition: Social, ethical, and professional aspects related to the field of computer science and software development. This is a newly added unit of knowledge.

metadata.title: Software Development Basics
metadata.definition: Core concepts and skills required for software development, often taught in introductory courses. This is another area of ​​knowledge that FPL can build on or overlap.

metadata.title: Programming Paradigms
metadata.definition: A basic programming style or approach that guides the organization and structure of a program. Modern languages ​​often integrate multiple paradigms.

metadata.title: Imperative Programming
metadata.definition: A programming model focuses on describing the steps (commands) that a program must perform to change its state. Often integrated with other paradigms such as object oriented.

metadata.title: Logic Programming
metadata.definition: A programming model based on formal logic, in which programs are represented as facts and rules, and computation is performed by inference. Often integrated with other paradigms such as object oriented.

metadata.title: Distributed, Concurrent, Parallel Integration
metadata.definition: understand and integrate the concepts of distributed, concurrency, and parallelism with various programming models as a core area in the context of multicore computing, cloud computing, and computer networks.

metadata.title: Event-Driven Development
metadata.definition: Master the software development aspects related to event-driven programming, especially important for real-time and pervasive computing applications.

metadata.title: Reactive Programming Development
metadata.definition: Master the software development aspects related to reactive programming, especially important for real-time and pervasive computing applications.

metadata.title: Parallel Computing Development
metadata.definition: Master the software development aspects related to parallel computing, especially important for real-time and pervasive computing applications.

metadata.title: Distributed Computing Development
metadata.definition: Master the software development aspects related to distributed computing, especially important for real-time and pervasive computing applications.

metadata.title: Formal Program Correctness Proofs
metadata.definition: Use formal methods to prove the correctness of a program, an optional advanced topic.

metadata.title: Formal Program Properties Proofs
metadata.definition: Use formal methods to demonstrate other properties of the program, an optional advanced topic.

metadata.title: OOP (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Overview of object-oriented programming, including core concepts required for all students.

metadata.title: OOP (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Additional aspects of object-oriented programming, recommended for specialized students.

metadata.title: Functional Programming (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of functional programming, required for all students.

metadata.title: Functional Programming (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Advanced topics in functional programming, recommended for majors.

metadata.title: Logic Programming (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Concepts and applications of logic programming, recommendations for specialized students.

metadata.title: Shell Scripting (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Basic knowledge of shell script programming, required for all students.

metadata.title: Event-Reactive Programming (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of event-driven and reactive programming, required for all students.

metadata.title: Event-Reactive Programming (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Advanced topics in event-driven and reactive programming, recommended for majors.

metadata.title: Parallel Distributed Computing (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of parallel and distributed computing, required for all students.

metadata.title: Parallel Distributed Computing (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Advanced topics in parallel and distributed computing, recommended for majors.

metadata.title: Aspect-Oriented Programming (KA Core)
metadata.definition: An introduction to aspect-oriented programming, recommended for majors.

metadata.title: Type Systems (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of type systems in programming languages, required for all students.

metadata.title: Type Systems (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Advanced topics in type systems, recommended for majors.

metadata.title: System Memory Model (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Concepts of how systems execute programs and manage memory, recommended for specialized students.

metadata.title: Language Translation Execution (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Fundamentals of how programming languages ​​are translated and executed, required for all students.

metadata.title: Language Translation Execution (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Advanced topics in language translation and implementation, recommended for majors.

metadata.title: Program Abstraction Representation (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Program abstraction and representation methods, recommendations for specialized students.

metadata.title: Syntax Analysis (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Parsing techniques in compilers and interpreters.

metadata.title: Compiler Semantic Analysis (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Semantic analysis methods are used in compilers.

metadata.title: Program Analysis Tools (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Techniques and tools for analyzing programs to determine properties and behavior.

metadata.title: Code Generation (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Methods for generating machine code from high-level source code.

metadata.title: Runtime Behavior Systems (KA Core)
metadata.definition: understand program behavior during execution and runtime support systems.

metadata.title: Advanced Programming Constructs (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Study advanced programming structures and techniques.

metadata.title: Language Pragmatics (KA Core)
metadata.definition: The study of how programming languages ​​are used and influence their design and use.

metadata.title: Formal Semantics (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Methods for describing the semantics of programming languages ​​formally and accurately.

metadata.title: Formal Methods (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Math-based software development methods to increase reliability and correctness.

metadata.title: Programming Language Design (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Study the principles and philosophies behind the design of programming languages.

metadata.title: Society, Ethics, Professionalism (SEP)
metadata.definition: Social, ethical and professional issues related to the field of programming languages ​​are integrated into Social, Ethical and Professional Knowledge (SEP) classes.

metadata.title: Imperative as OOP Subset
metadata.definition: understand imperative programming not as a separate paradigm but as a subset of object-oriented programming.

metadata.title: OOP Design: State & Behavior
metadata.definition: Object-oriented design techniques, focusing on decomposing the system into objects with state (data) and behavior (methods).

metadata.title: OOP Design: Class Hierarchy
metadata.definition: Object-oriented design technique, focusing on building class hierarchies to model relationships and structures within a system.

metadata.title: Class Definition: Fields
metadata.definition: How to define fields (member variables) in a class to store the state of an object.

metadata.title: Class Definition: Methods
metadata.definition: How to define methods (member functions) in a class to define the object's behavior.

metadata.title: Constructors
metadata.definition: How to define constructors in a class to initialize objects when they are created.

metadata.title: Subclass
metadata.definition: Concept of subclass, a class that inherits from another class for extension or specialization.

metadata.title: Inheritance
metadata.definition: The concept of inheritance, allows subclasses to inherit properties and methods from the superclass, including cases of multiple inheritance.

metadata.title: Multiple Inheritance
metadata.definition: The concept of multiple inheritance, where a class can inherit from multiple parent classes, and related challenges.

metadata.title: Method Overriding
metadata.definition: The concept of method overriding, allows a child class to provide its own implementation of a method already defined in the parent class.

metadata.title: Dynamic Dispatch
metadata.definition: The concept of dynamic dispatching, the mechanism that determines which methods will be called at runtime based on the type of the object.

metadata.title: Exception Handling
metadata.definition: Exception handling techniques for robust program management of errors and unusual situations.

metadata.title: Encapsulation: Privacy
metadata.definition: apply privacy as an object-oriented idiom for encapsulation, controlling access to class members.

metadata.title: Encapsulation: Data Hiding
metadata.definition: apply data hiding as an object-oriented idiom for encapsulation, hiding the internal implementation details of an object.

metadata.title: Encapsulation: Member Visibility
metadata.definition: Controls the visibility of class members (public, private, protected) as part of encapsulation.

metadata.title: Encapsulation: Interfaces
metadata.definition: Use interfaces as an encapsulation idiom, revealing only the method signature without the implementation.

metadata.title: Abstract Base Classes
metadata.definition: Use abstract base classes to define common interfaces that subclasses must implement.

metadata.title: Encapsulation: Traits
metadata.definition: Use traits as an encapsulation mechanism, allowing reuse of behavior across classes without inheritance.

metadata.title: Encapsulation: Mixins
metadata.definition: Use mixins as an encapsulation mechanism, allowing classes to combine functionality from multiple sources.

metadata.title: Dynamic vs Static Properties
metadata.definition: Compare and differentiate dynamic and static properties in programming languages, including how they are defined and behave at compile time and run time.

metadata.title: Composition vs Inheritance
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast object-oriented design paradigms such as composition and inheritance, analyzing the pros and cons of each and when to use each.

metadata.title: Subtyping Polymorphism
metadata.definition: Study the basic concept of subtyping in programming languages.

metadata.title: Subtyping & Implicit Upcasting
metadata.definition: Learn about subtype polymorphism and automatic implicit upcasts in programming languages ​​with type checking.

metadata.title: Liskov Substitution Principle
metadata.definition: understand the principle of behavioral substitution, where a subtype can replace a parent type without changing the correctness of the program (Liskov principle).

metadata.title: Subtyping & Inheritance Relation
metadata.definition: analyze the complex relationship between the concept of subtyping and inheritance in object-oriented design.

metadata.title: Collections, Iterators & Libraries
metadata.definition: Learn about data collection classes (e.g., lists, sets, maps), iterators, and other standard library components in programming languages.

metadata.title: Metaprogramming & Reflection
metadata.definition: The study of metaprogramming, which allows a program to manipulate itself, and reflection, the ability to examine and modify a program's structure and behavior at runtime.

metadata.title: Imperative vs OOP
metadata.definition: List and explain the basic differences between the imperative programming model and the object-oriented programming model.

metadata.title: Class Design, Implement, Test
metadata.definition: The process of designing, implementing, and testing a class to meet specific behavioral requirements.

metadata.title: Class Hierarchy & Code Reuse
metadata.definition: Build a simple class hierarchy using the subclassing mechanism for efficient code reuse across different subclasses.

metadata.title: Dynamic Dispatch & Control Flow
metadata.definition: Predict and verify the flow of control in programs using dynamic dispatch.

metadata.title: Procedural vs Functional vs OOP
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast how computational solutions to a problem differ in procedural, functional, and object-oriented approaches.

metadata.title: Data Definition & Protection
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast mechanisms for defining and protecting data elements in procedural, functional, and object-oriented approaches.

metadata.title: Inheritance vs Composition Costs
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast the benefits and costs/impacts of using inheritance (subclassing) and composition (especially how to build components based on higher-order functions).

metadata.title: OOP Inheritance & Subtyping Relation
metadata.definition: Explain the relationship between object-oriented inheritance (code sharing and overriding) and subtype polymorphism (the idea of ​​a subtype being usable in a context that expects the parent type).

metadata.title: OOP Encapsulation Mechanisms
metadata.definition: Use object-oriented encapsulation mechanisms such as interfaces and private members.

metadata.title: Iterators & Collection Operations
metadata.definition: Define and use iterators and other operations on aggregates, including operations that take functions as arguments, in a variety of programming languages, choosing the most natural expressions for each language.

metadata.title: Efficient Collections & Iterators
metadata.definition: Effectively use collection classes and iterators to solve a problem.

metadata.title: Lambda Expressions & Evaluation
metadata.definition: understand lambda expressions (anonymous functions) and how they are evaluated in functional programming.

metadata.title: Lambda Variable Binding & Scope
metadata.definition: Master the variable binding and scope rules that apply to lambda expressions.

metadata.title: Lambda Parameter Passing
metadata.definition: understand the mechanics of passing parameters when using lambda expressions.

metadata.title: Nested Lambda & Reduction Order
metadata.definition: analyze nested lambda expressions and their reduction order.

metadata.title: Side-Effect Free Programming
metadata.definition: The concept of side-effect free programming, where functions depend only on their inputs and do not cause changes in external state.

metadata.title: Pure Functions & Compositional Reasoning
metadata.definition: Understanding that function calls have no side effects facilitates compositional reasoning.

metadata.title: Immutable Variables & Data Copying
metadata.definition: Study the concept of immutable variables and compare data copying and reduction in functional programming.

metadata.title: Recursion vs Loops vs Map/Reduce
metadata.definition: Compare and apply recursion, loops, and pipelining techniques such as map/reduce to solve problems.

metadata.title: Structured Data Processing (FP)
metadata.definition: Master how to handle complex data structures like trees by defining functions with appropriate cases for each variant or node of data, a fundamental technique in functional programming.

metadata.title: Composite Data Functions
metadata.definition: understand and apply function design principles to complex data, in which large functions are built upon applying smaller functions to each constituent element of the data.

metadata.title: Persistent Data Structures
metadata.definition: Learn about immutable data structures, where every modification creates a new version of the structure without changing the original version, ensuring persistence and easy state management.

metadata.title: Higher-Order Functions
metadata.definition: Master the concept and use of higher-order functions – functions that can take other functions as arguments, return a function, or store functions – to write flexible and abstract code.

metadata.title: Metaprogramming
metadata.definition: Learn about metaprogramming, a programming technique in which a program has the ability to manipulate (analyze, modify, create) other programs or itself during runtime or compilation.

metadata.title: Reflection
metadata.definition: Master the concept of reflection, the ability of a program to inspect, introspect, and modify its own structure and behavior at runtime.

metadata.title: Function Closures
metadata.definition: Understanding function closure, a function is 'encapsulated' along with its lexical reference environment, allowing the function to access variables from an external scope even when that scope is no longer active.

metadata.title: Closure Creation at Runtime
metadata.definition: understand how function closures are created at runtime by 'capturing' the environment from its declared scope.

metadata.title: Closures: Callbacks
metadata.definition: apply function closure in common use cases such as call-backs, where a function is passed as an argument to be executed later by another function.

metadata.title: Closure Idioms: Iterators
metadata.definition: Use function closures as arguments to iterators or collection traversals to customize the behavior of each element.

metadata.title: Closure Idioms: Reusable Code
metadata.definition: Develop reusable code patterns by passing functions (or closures) as arguments, allowing flexibility in behavior without modifying the main structure.

metadata.title: Closure Data Encapsulation
metadata.definition: apply function closure as a mechanism to encapsulate data, where the data is kept private within the closure's environment and can only be accessed and manipulated through that closure function.

metadata.title: Lazy Evaluation
metadata.definition: understand delayed evaluation, an evaluation strategy in which execution of an expression is postponed until its value is actually needed, which optimizes performance and allows processing of an infinite stream of data.

metadata.title: Eager Evaluation
metadata.definition: understand strict evaluation, an evaluation strategy in which expressions are evaluated immediately when they are assigned or passed as arguments.

metadata.title: Graph Reduction Machine
metadata.definition: Learn about graph reducers, an execution model for functional programming languages, especially those that use deferred evaluation, where expressions are represented as graphs and reduced as needed.

metadata.title: Call-by-Need
metadata.definition: Master the concept of call-by-need, an argument passing strategy that combines call-by-name and call-by-value, where the argument is evaluated no more than once as needed and the result is cached.

metadata.title: Lazy Evaluation Implementation
metadata.definition: Learn and implement techniques for implementing deferred evaluation mechanisms in systems or programming languages.

metadata.title: Logic Programming Integration
metadata.definition: Explore how functional programming concepts and techniques can be integrated or interacted with the logic programming model to create hybrid programming languages ​​and systems.

metadata.title: Equational Logic
metadata.definition: Master the concept of equational logic, a system of logic based on solving equations and the principle of substituting equals, commonly used in functional-logic programming and rewriting theory.

metadata.title: Narrowing
metadata.definition: Learn about narrowing, a powerful combination of evaluation and unification used in functional logic programming to find solutions.

metadata.title: Residuation
metadata.definition: understand the concept of residuation, a mechanism in functional-logic programming that allows calculations to be delayed until enough information is available to perform them without looking up.

metadata.title: Semantic Unification
metadata.definition: Understanding semantic unification, an extension of traditional unification, considers the meaning or semantics of expressions in addition to their syntactic structure.

metadata.title: Imperative Integration
metadata.definition: Study how functional programming concepts and techniques can be integrated or interacted with the traditional imperative programming paradigm, creating hybrid programming approaches.

metadata.title: OOP Integration
metadata.definition: Explore how functional programming concepts can be integrated or interacted with the object-oriented programming paradigm, for example in API design or software architecture.

metadata.title: Immutable State Algorithms
metadata.definition: Skills in designing and implementing basic algorithms that comply with the principle of immutability in functional programming, avoiding directly changing the state of variable variables to minimize errors and increase predictability.

metadata.title: Value Equality Algorithms
metadata.definition: Skills in designing and implementing algorithms that focus on value equality rather than reference equality are especially important in functional programming and with immutable data.

metadata.title: Higher-Order Functions
metadata.definition: Skill in writing high-order functions that take other functions as arguments or return other functions as results, taking advantage of the flexibility and code reuse in functional programming.

metadata.title: Paradigm Problem Solving
metadata.definition: analyze and compare how different programming paradigms (procedural, functional, object-oriented) approach, structure, and solve the same computational problem, including the advantages and disadvantages of each.

metadata.title: Data Protection Paradigms
metadata.definition: analyze and compare different methods for defining and protecting data (e.g., encapsulation, immutability, scope) in procedural, functional, and object-oriented programming paradigms.

metadata.title: Lambda SECD Machine
metadata.definition: Able to explain in detail how a simple lambda expression is deployed and executed on an abstract virtual machine such as a SECD machine, illustrating the process of storing and reclaiming the environment.

metadata.title: SECD Machine
metadata.definition: Learn about the architecture and operation of the SECD (Stack, Environment, Control, Dump) machine, a classic abstract virtual machine used to execute lambda expressions and functional programming languages.

metadata.title: VM Environment Management
metadata.definition: understand the technical mechanisms for storing and managing (including revoking) execution environments in the context of virtual machines, especially with regard to closures and lexical scoping.

metadata.title: Closure Scope & Variables
metadata.definition: Ability to properly analyze and understand how variables and lexical scope operate in programs that use function closures, including accessing variables from the outside environment.

metadata.title: Functional Encapsulation
metadata.definition: apply encapsulation mechanisms in functional programming, including closures to protect internal state and modular interfaces to organize and hide implementation details.

metadata.title: Functional Modular Interface
metadata.definition: Master how to design and use modular interfaces to organize and manage code components in a functional programming context, promoting modularity and reusability.

metadata.title: Stateful vs Stateless Execution
metadata.definition: Distinguish and compare the differences between stateful and stateless execution models, especially emphasizing the advantages and disadvantages of each model in functional programming and system architectures.

metadata.title: Stateful Execution
metadata.definition: understand the stateful execution model, where functions or components can maintain and modify internal state between calls, affecting output.

metadata.title: Stateless Execution
metadata.definition: Understanding the stateless execution model, where functions or components do not store any internal state and always return the same output for the same input, makes it easy to test and parallelize.

metadata.title: Iterators Definition & Usage
metadata.definition: Skill in defining and using iterators to efficiently and flexibly traverse data sets, often in a functional programming context.

metadata.title: Aggregate Operations
metadata.definition: Skills in defining and using common operations on data sets such as filter, map, reduce, and other operations.

metadata.title: Higher-Order Aggregate Operations
metadata.definition: apply operations on collections (e.g. map, filter, reduce) that themselves take other functions as arguments, allowing flexible customization of data processing behavior.

metadata.title: Iterator & Aggregate Idioms
metadata.definition: Select and use the most natural and effective idioms in different programming languages ​​for working with iterators and set operations, optimizing readability and performance.

metadata.title: Common Subexpression Graph Reduction
metadata.definition: Ability to illustrate in detail the graph reduction process when executing a lambda expression, especially when common subexpressions are present, to understand how to optimize execution in functional languages.

metadata.title: Lambda Common Subexpressions
metadata.definition: understand the concept and impact of common subexpressions in lambda expressions, and how they can be leveraged to improve performance through techniques such as graph reduction.

metadata.title: Nested Lambda ABC Machine
metadata.definition: Ability to illustrate the execution of a simple nested lambda expression on an abstract machine like the ABC machine, understanding how levels of nesting are handled.

metadata.title: ABC Machine
metadata.definition: Learn about the architecture and operation of the ABC machine, an abstract machine designed to execute functional programming languages, especially in the context of lazy evaluation and general data structures.

metadata.title: Narrowing, Residuation, Semantic Unification Examples
metadata.definition: Ability to give and explain simple examples to illustrate complex concepts such as narrowing, residuation, and semantic unification, clarifying how they work in functional-logic programming.

metadata.title: Concurrency Structures Examples
metadata.definition: Illustrate concurrency constructs with simple programming examples, such as reading and writing to a buffer simultaneously or sequentially.

metadata.title: Universal & Existential Quantifiers
metadata.definition: Compare and distinguish between universal quantifiers and existential quantifiers in predicate logic.

metadata.title: First & Higher-Order Logic
metadata.definition: Distinguish between First Order Predicate Logic, which only quantifies variables, and Higher Order Logic, which can quantify predicates or functions.

metadata.title: Complex Relations with Logic Connectives
metadata.definition: Skills in using logical connections (AND, OR, NOT, IF-THEN) to build complex relationships from basic relationships.

metadata.title: Horn Clauses, Facts, Goals
metadata.definition: understand the definitions and roles of Horn clauses, facts, goals and subgoals in logic programming.

metadata.title: Unification & Algorithm
metadata.definition: The concept of unification and its algorithm, along with the distinction between unification, assertion, and expression evaluation in the context of logic programming.

metadata.title: Relations & Functions Mixing
metadata.definition: How to use a combination of relations and functions in logic programming to represent more complex problems.

metadata.title: Cuts, Backtracking, Nondeterminism
metadata.definition: Concept of cuts to control the search process, backtracking mechanism and non-determinism in logic programs.

metadata.title: Closed & Open World Assumption
metadata.definition: Distinguish between closed-world assumptions (what is not known is false) and open-world assumptions (what is not known may be true or false).

metadata.title: Loop Variable Copy Cost
metadata.definition: analyze the memory overhead incurred by variable copying in iterative programs, especially in the context of logic programming.

metadata.title: Partial Computation & Search Pruning
metadata.definition: Programming techniques and structures allow storing intermediate computational results and pruning unnecessary branches in the search tree to optimize performance.

metadata.title: Functional-Logic Integration
metadata.definition: Explore how to integrate the functional and logic programming paradigms through in-depth concepts such as equational logic, narrowing, residuation, and semantic unification.

metadata.title: Advanced Logic Programming
metadata.definition: Introduces advanced areas of logic programming, including higher-order logic programming, constrained logic programming, and inductive logic programming.

metadata.title: Logic Prog. Integration
metadata.definition: Methods and challenges when integrating logic programming with other popular programming paradigms, such as object-oriented programming.

metadata.title: Advanced Logic Structures
metadata.definition: Learn advanced programming constructs in programming logic such as difference-lists, how to create custom data structures, and aggregation operators.

metadata.title: Error Handling
metadata.definition: Error and exception handling techniques and methods in shell scripts to ensure stable and reliable program operation.

metadata.title: Piping
metadata.definition: Concept and usage of pipes to connect the output of one command to the input of another command in the shell.

metadata.title: System Commands
metadata.definition: Knowledge of basic system commands and their use in shell scripts.

metadata.title: OS Interaction
metadata.definition: How shell scripts interact with and control operating system functions through commands and system calls.

metadata.title: Environment Variables
metadata.definition: Concepts, how to set, access and use environment variables in shell scripting.

metadata.title: File Abstraction & Ops
metadata.definition: How shell scripts handle and manipulate files is through file abstraction concepts and related operators (e.g. read, write, check for existence).

metadata.title: Shell Data Structures
metadata.definition: Use basic data structures such as arrays and lists in shell scripting to organize and manage data.

metadata.title: Regular Expressions
metadata.definition: understand and use regular expressions to search, match, and manipulate text in shell scripts.

metadata.title: Programs & Processes
metadata.definition: Concept of programs and processes in the operating system environment, and how shell scripts manage or interact with them.

metadata.title: Workflow Automation
metadata.definition: Design and automate task sequences or workflows using shell scripts.

metadata.title: Reactive Programming Advantages
metadata.definition: Compare procedural and reactive programming paradigms, emphasizing the advantages of reactive programming in handling and responding to events.

metadata.title: Reactive Components
metadata.definition: understand the components that make up a reactive programming system, including event sources, signals, listeners, dispatchers, event objects, adapters, and event handlers.

metadata.title: Stateless vs. State-Transition
metadata.definition: Distinguish between stateless and state-transition programming models.

metadata.title: Reactive Use Cases
metadata.definition: Identify common and typical applications of event-driven and reactive programming in areas such as graphical user interfaces (GUIs), mobile devices, robotics, and servers.

metadata.title: Event Handlers & Listeners
metadata.definition: Skills in defining and implementing event handlers or listeners in a reactive programming framework.

metadata.title: Event Parameterization
metadata.definition: How to parameterize event dispatchers and the arguments (data) associated with the event to pass information.

metadata.title: External vs. Internal Events
metadata.definition: Distinguish and handle events that arise from outside the system (e.g., user interactions) and events that are generated internally by the program.

metadata.title: MVC Separation
metadata.definition: understand and apply the principle of separation of Model, View, and Controller components in event-driven application design.

metadata.title: Event-Driven State Machines
metadata.definition: Conceptualize event-driven and reactive programs as state transition systems, where events trigger state changes.

metadata.title: MVC Architecture
metadata.definition: Ability to describe an interactive system using a Model-View-Controller (MVC) architecture, clearly distinguishing data model (Model), user interface (View), and control logic (Controller) components.

metadata.title: Safety & Liveness
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of safety and liveness in parallel and distributed computing, ensuring programs execute correctly and can progress.

metadata.title: Race Conditions
metadata.definition: Definition and examples of race conditions in parallel programs, where multiple threads access and change shared data without proper synchronization.

metadata.title: Dependencies & Preconditions
metadata.definition: Understanding of data dependencies and preconditions in parallel tasks, necessary to ensure correctness and order of execution.

metadata.title: Fault Models
metadata.definition: Models to classify and analyze the types of errors that can occur in parallel and distributed systems, e.g. node failures, network failures.

metadata.title: Parallel Termination
metadata.definition: The concept of termination of parallel programs or tasks, ensuring that all components have completed their work and the system has reached its final state.

metadata.title: Parallel Programming Models
metadata.definition: Different methods and frameworks for designing and implementing parallel and distributed programs.

metadata.title: Actor Model
metadata.definition: The parallel programming model is based on Actors, independent computational units that communicate by exchanging messages.

metadata.title: Procedural vs. Reactive
metadata.definition: Compare and differentiate between traditional procedural programming paradigms and reactive programming paradigms in a parallel context.

metadata.title: Synchronous vs. Asynchronous
metadata.definition: understand the differences and applications of synchronous and asynchronous programming models in managing parallel tasks.

metadata.title: Data Parallelism
metadata.definition: Data parallelism technique, where the same operation is applied simultaneously to different elements of a large data set.

metadata.title: Concurrency Properties
metadata.definition: Important properties of parallel systems relate to the ordering and consistency of data.

metadata.title: Order-Based Properties
metadata.definition: Properties related to the execution order of operations in a parallel environment.

metadata.title: Commutativity
metadata.definition: The property of operations that their order of execution does not affect the final result.

metadata.title: Operation Independence
metadata.definition: The property of operations is not dependent on each other and can be performed in parallel without affecting each other.

metadata.title: Consistency Properties
metadata.definition: Attributes that ensure data consistency in a parallel or distributed system.

metadata.title: Atomicity
metadata.definition: The concept of atomicity, ensures that a set of operations is performed completely or not at all.

metadata.title: Consensus
metadata.definition: The concept of consensus in a distributed system, where processes must reach a common agreement on a value or state.

metadata.title: Parallel Execution Control
metadata.definition: Mechanisms and techniques to control the execution flow of parallel tasks.

metadata.title: Async/Await
metadata.definition: The asynchronous programming model uses the `async` and `await` keywords to manage non-blocking operations.

metadata.title: Promises
metadata.definition: Concept of Promises as an object that represents the final result of an asynchronous operation.

metadata.title: Threads
metadata.definition: Thread mechanism to execute different parts of the program simultaneously, serving the purpose of execution control.

metadata.title: Parallel Communication
metadata.definition: Methods and tools for parallel components to communicate and work together.

metadata.title: Mutex
metadata.definition: Mutual exclusion locking mechanism (mutex) to protect shared resources from concurrent access.

metadata.title: Message Passing
metadata.definition: Models communication between processes or threads through message exchange instead of memory sharing.

metadata.title: Shared Memory
metadata.definition: Communication model where processes or threads access and modify the same memory region.

metadata.title: Cobegin-coend
metadata.definition: Language construct for specifying a block of instructions that can be executed in parallel, starting with `cobegin` and ending with `coend`.

metadata.title: Monitor
metadata.definition: A high-level synchronization mechanism allows threads to securely access shared resources through protected methods.

metadata.title: Channels
metadata.definition: The communication mechanism allows threads or goroutines to send and receive data securely.

metadata.title: Threads
metadata.definition: Use a thread as a unit of execution for communication and coordination purposes in a parallel program.

metadata.title: Guards
metadata.definition: Guards are used to control the execution of sections of code based on the state of the system in a concurrent environment.

metadata.title: Futures
metadata.definition: The concept of Futures is an object that represents a value that will be available in the future, usually as a result of an asynchronous calculation.

metadata.title: Data Parallelism Support
metadata.definition: Language features and programming constructs that support data parallelism, including examples such as `forall`, loop unrolling techniques, and paradigms such as Map/Reduce.

metadata.title: Memory Consistency Effects
metadata.definition: Understanding of how memory-consistency models affect programming language semantics and correct code generation in multiprocessor systems.

metadata.title: REST APIs
metadata.definition: Architecture and principles of Representational State Transfer Application Programming Interfaces (REST APIs) for communication between distributed systems.

metadata.title: Parallel & Distributed Computing
metadata.definition: Overview of advanced technologies and approaches in parallel and distributed computing, including cloud computing, high performance computing (HPC), quantum computing, and ubiquitous computing.

metadata.title: Message Passing Overhead
metadata.definition: analyze the performance costs (such as latency, bandwidth) associated with message passing mechanisms in distributed systems.

metadata.title: Concurrency Granularity
metadata.definition: understand the importance of choosing the right granularity for concurrent tasks to optimize performance and exploit resources efficiently.

metadata.title: Concurrency & Other Paradigms
metadata.definition: The relationship and integration between concurrency and other programming paradigms, such as functional programming.

metadata.title: Aspects
metadata.definition: Definition of aspect in aspect-oriented programming (AOP), representing cross-cutting concerns.

metadata.title: Join Points
metadata.definition: Points in a program's execution flow where an aspect can be inserted (e.g., method invocation, field access).

metadata.title: Advice
metadata.definition: Code is executed at a certain junction by an aspect.

metadata.title: Before Advice
metadata.definition: The `advice` code is executed before a join point is made.

metadata.title: After Advice
metadata.definition: The `advice` code is executed after a join point completes, including returning, throwing, or finally.

metadata.title: Around Advice
metadata.definition: The `advice` code wraps and can control the execution of a junction.

metadata.title: Pointcuts
metadata.definition: Expression defining the set of junctions at which an `advice` will be applied.

metadata.title: Pointcut Designators
metadata.definition: Keywords or syntax are used in `pointcut` to specify different types of junction points (e.g. `call`, `execution`).

metadata.title: Weaving (Static & Dynamic)
metadata.definition: The process of integrating aspects into the code base, including static weaving (at compile or load time) and dynamic weaving (at run time).

metadata.title: AOP Alternatives
metadata.definition: Alternative or complementary methods to aspect-oriented programming to handle cross-references, such as using annotations or support tools from the IDE.

metadata.title: Data Type Definition
metadata.definition: The concept of a data type is a set of values ​​along with a set of operations that can be performed on those values.

metadata.title: Primitive Data Types
metadata.definition: Basic data types are built into programming languages, such as integers, floats, and booleans.

metadata.title: Composite Data Types
metadata.definition: Data types are built from other types using set operations, for example: records/structs, unions, arrays, lists, functions, references.

metadata.title: Data Type Binding
metadata.definition: How data types are associated with variables, function arguments, function returns, and fields in data structures.

metadata.title: Type Safety
metadata.definition: The concept of type safety as an important element of program correctness, prevents errors caused by using values ​​inconsistent with the intended type.

metadata.title: Type Errors
metadata.definition: Errors arise when values ​​are used inconsistently with the intended data type, and the role of type safety in preventing them.

metadata.title: Static & Dynamic Typing Pros/Cons
metadata.definition: Learn about the goals and limitations of both static and dynamic typing systems, especially in detecting and eliminating errors as early as possible in software development.

metadata.title: Polymorphism Definition & Benefits
metadata.definition: understand the definition and general advantages of polymorphism in programming languages.

metadata.title: Parametric Polymorphism
metadata.definition: Master the concept of parametric polymorphism, where a function or data type can be written generically to operate on different types without modification.

metadata.title: Subtyping Polymorphism
metadata.definition: understand subtype polymorphism, where an object can be considered to be of its own type or any of its parent types.

metadata.title: Overloading
metadata.definition: Master the concept of overloading, which allows multiple functions or operators to have the same name but differ in type or number of parameters.

metadata.title: Type Coercion
metadata.definition: understand forced conversion, the automatic or implicit process of converting values ​​from one data type to another.

metadata.title: Monomorphic vs. Polymorphic Types
metadata.definition: Distinguish and compare between monomorphic (works with only one specific type) and polymorphic (can work with many types).

metadata.title: Polymorphism Comparison
metadata.definition: analyze and compare the characteristics, advantages and disadvantages of parametric polymorphism, ad-hoc polymorphism (overloading) and subtype polymorphism.

metadata.title: Generic Parameters & Typing
metadata.definition: understand how global parameters work in styling and how they enable flexible and reusable code.

metadata.title: Generic Libraries Usage
metadata.definition: Know how to effectively use generic libraries, such as collection data structures (lists, sets, maps) in languages ​​that support generics.

metadata.title: Prescriptive vs. Descriptive Polymorphism
metadata.definition: understand the difference between prescriptive polymorphism (where types must conform to a specific interface or rule) and descriptive polymorphism (where behavior is inferred from structure).

metadata.title: Polymorphism Implementation Models
metadata.definition: understand different paradigms for implementing polymorphism in programming languages, such as monomorphization or erasure.

metadata.title: Subtyping
metadata.definition: understand the basic concept of subtyping, where one data type can safely be substituted for another.

metadata.title: Structural Type Equivalence
metadata.definition: understand structural equivalence, where two types are considered equivalent if they have the same underlying structure.

metadata.title: Name Type Equivalence
metadata.definition: understand name equivalence, where two types are considered equivalent if they are defined using the same type name.

metadata.title: Static Typing: Early Error Detection
metadata.definition: Explain the benefits of static typing in detecting program errors at the early compilation stage.

metadata.title: Dynamic Typing: Late Error Detection
metadata.definition: Explain the benefit of dynamic typing in allowing errors to occur at runtime or avoiding some errors until execution.

metadata.title: Static Typing: Invariant Enforcement
metadata.definition: Understanding how static typing helps enforce program invariants, improves reliability during code development and maintenance.

metadata.title: Dynamic Typing: Deferred Type Decisions
metadata.definition: Explain the benefit of dynamic styling in allowing style decisions to be deferred, facilitating rapid prototyping.

metadata.title: Dynamic Typing: Flexible Code Patterns
metadata.definition: understand how dynamic typing supports flexible models, allowing the convenient use of heterogeneous collections.

metadata.title: Function Type Rules
metadata.definition: understand the style rules that apply to functions and how they ensure the correctness of function calls.

metadata.title: Product Type Rules
metadata.definition: Master the styling rules that apply to product types (also called records or structures) and how they handle the components of product types.

metadata.title: Sum Type Rules
metadata.definition: Master the styling rules that apply to aggregate types (also called unions or variants) and how they handle different cases.

metadata.title: Static Typing: Code Misuse
metadata.definition: Understanding static typing helps prevent abuse or misuse of code, improving program safety.

metadata.title: Dynamic Typing: Code Reusability
metadata.definition: Explain how dynamic styling can promote more flexible code reuse, especially in scenarios where the type doesn't need to be known completely in advance.

metadata.title: Static Typing: Incomplete Program Detection
metadata.definition: Understanding static typing can help detect parts of programs that are incomplete or style-inconsistent.

metadata.title: Dynamic Typing: Incomplete Program Execution
metadata.definition: Explain how dynamic typing can allow incomplete or incomplete programs to run, useful for iterative development.

metadata.title: Typing & Static Analysis
metadata.definition: analyze the relationship between the type system and other static analysis techniques to ensure program correctness.

metadata.title: Type System Decidability
metadata.definition: Grasp the concept of determinism in relation to type systems, especially the ability to determine the type correctness of a program automatically.

metadata.title: Compositional Type Constructors
metadata.definition: Understanding the fundamentals of type constructors allows building complex types from simpler types.

metadata.title: Product Types
metadata.definition: Master the concept of product types, which represent collections of values ​​of different types (e.g. records, structures).

metadata.title: Sum Types
metadata.definition: Master the concept of aggregate types, which represent a value that can be of one of many different types (e.g. union, variant).

metadata.title: Function Types
metadata.definition: understand function types, describe the input and output types of a function.

metadata.title: Quantified Types
metadata.definition: Master the concept of quantified type, allowing type variables to be introduced and used within a specific scope (e.g. Forall in polymorphism).

metadata.title: Recursive Types
metadata.definition: understand recursive types, types defined by themselves, commonly used for data structures such as linked lists and trees.

metadata.title: Type Checking
metadata.definition: understand type checking, where a system checks the data types of expressions in a program to ensure consistency and safety.

metadata.title: Subtype Polymorphism
metadata.definition: Further understanding subtype polymorphism, a form of polymorphism that allows a function or method to operate on objects of different types as long as they are subtypes of a specified type.

metadata.title: Implicit Upcasting
metadata.definition: understand how implicit casting (safely converting a subtype to its parent type) works in typed languages.

metadata.title: Liskov Substitution Principle
metadata.definition: understand the behavioral substitution principle (e.g., the Liskov substitution principle), where a subtype object can replace a parent object without changing the correctness of the program.

metadata.title: Subtyping & Inheritance
metadata.definition: analyze the close but distinct relationship between subtyping and inheritance in object-oriented programming languages.

metadata.title: Type Safety (Preservation & Progress)
metadata.definition: Understanding the formal definition of type safety, including the concepts of preservation and progress, ensures that the program never encounters type errors.

metadata.title: Type Inference
metadata.definition: understand the concept of type inference, the ability of a compiler or interpreter to automatically determine the type of expressions without the need for an explicit type declaration.

metadata.title: Static Overloading
metadata.definition: understand static overloading, where the choice of function or method to be overloaded is determined at compile time based on parameter type.

metadata.title: Propositions as Types
metadata.definition: Explore the Curry-Howard relationship, where logical statements correspond to types in the type system, and proofs correspond to programs.

metadata.title: Implication as Function Type
metadata.definition: understand how in the Curry-Howard relationship, the logical implication (A => B) is mapped to the functional type (A -> B).

metadata.title: Conjunction as Product Type
metadata.definition: understand how in the Curry-Howard relationship the logical conjunctions (A and B) are mapped to the product type (A x B).

metadata.title: Disjunction as Sum Type
metadata.definition: understand how in the Curry-Howard relationship, the logical selection (A or B) is mapped to the total type (A + B).

metadata.title: Dependent Types
metadata.definition: Learn about dependent types, an advanced concept where data types can depend on data values.

metadata.title: Universal Quant. as Dependent Function
metadata.definition: understand the relationship between universal quantifiers and dependency functions in the context of dependency types.

metadata.title: Existential Quant. as Dependent Product
metadata.definition: understand the relationship between existential quantification and dependency products in the context of dependency types.

metadata.title: Primitive Type Values
metadata.definition: Describes a set of values ​​of a primitive type (e.g., integer, boolean, character) in a programming language.

metadata.title: Composite Type Values
metadata.definition: Describes a collection of values ​​of a complex type (e.g., array, record, class) in a programming language.

metadata.title: Static Type Violations
metadata.definition: Describes the types of operations that are prohibited by the static type system at compile time, such as passing an argument of the wrong type to a function.

metadata.title: Type System Error Detection
metadata.definition: Give specific examples of program errors that a type system is capable of detecting (e.g., trying to add a string to an integer).

metadata.title: Static Checked Properties
metadata.definition: Defines program properties that are checked at compile time (static checking) in various programming languages.

metadata.title: Dynamic Checked Properties
metadata.definition: Defines program properties that are checked at run time (dynamic testing) in a variety of programming languages.

metadata.title: Type Check False Positive
metadata.definition: Describe a program example that does not pass type checking in a particular language but will still run without errors (an example of a type system false positive).

metadata.title: Type Errors: Debugging & Coding
metadata.definition: apply knowledge of types and the ability to interpret type error messages to write code accurately and debug programs effectively.

metadata.title: Type Rules: Valid Operations
metadata.definition: Explain how style rules in a programming language define the set of valid operations that can be performed on a particular data type.

metadata.title: Complex Type Rules
metadata.definition: List and explain the specific type rules that govern how a given complex type (e.g., array, structure, class) is used.

metadata.title: Undecidability & Conservative Approximation
metadata.definition: Explain why nondeterminism in determining program properties requires type systems to conservatively approximate program behavior.

metadata.title: Generic Types Definition & Use
metadata.definition: Ability to define and use program elements (functions, classes, methods) that apply generic styles to achieve flexibility.

metadata.title: Generics for Collections
metadata.definition: Make effective use of generic types when working with collections (e.g. List<T>, Map<K, V>) to ensure type safety and reusability.

metadata.title: Generics, Subtyping, Overloading Comparison
metadata.definition: Discuss and clearly distinguish the differences between the concepts of generics (parametric polymorphism), subtyping (subtype polymorphism) and overloading (overloading).

metadata.title: Static Typing Benefits
metadata.definition: Explain the various benefits of static typing during the software development, maintenance, and debugging phases.

metadata.title: Static Typing Limitations
metadata.definition: Explain how the limitations of static typing, including potential rigidity and the need for explicit type declarations, affect writing, maintenance, and debugging.

metadata.title: Formal Type System Definition
metadata.definition: Be able to define a formal and compositional type system, including rules for each language construct.

metadata.title: Basic Type Constructors: Values
metadata.definition: For basic type constructors (e.g., product, sum, function), clearly identify the sets of values ​​they can describe.

metadata.title: Basic Type Constructors: Invariants
metadata.definition: For basic type constructors, specify the invariants they enforce to ensure program correctness.

metadata.title: Sound Type System Invariants
metadata.definition: Describes precisely the invariants that a sound type system ensures are preserved during program execution.

metadata.title: Type Safety Proof (Preservation & Progress)
metadata.definition: Be able to prove type safety for a simple language using preservation and progress theorems.

metadata.title: Unification-based Type Inference
metadata.definition: It is possible to implement a type inference algorithm based on unification for a simple programming language.

metadata.title: Static Overloading & Dynamic Behavior
metadata.definition: Explain how static overloading and related resolution algorithms affect a program's dynamic behavior at runtime.

metadata.title: Function Call Translation
metadata.definition: Explain how to translate function and procedure calls, including parameter passing mechanisms, so that they can be executed on an abstract machine.

metadata.title: Function Return Translation
metadata.definition: Learn how to interpret and handle returns from function or procedure calls, including restoring state and releasing resources.

metadata.title: Parameter Passing Mechanisms
metadata.definition: Study different parameter passing mechanisms (e.g., pass by value, pass by reference) and how they are implemented on an abstract machine during language translation.

metadata.title: High-Level Data Structures
metadata.definition: Learn low-level memory allocation and data access for high-level data structures such as basic data types, n-dimensional arrays, vectors, records, and objects.

metadata.title: Stack Memory Deallocation
metadata.definition: understand how memory for local variables on the stack is automatically released when a function or procedure terminates and returns.

metadata.title: Manual Heap Memory Management
metadata.definition: Study manual memory management techniques, including how to allocate, free, and reuse memory on the heap.

metadata.title: Garbage Collection Reachability
metadata.definition: Learn about garbage collection as an automatic memory management technique that focuses on the concept of reachability to identify objects that need to be freed.

metadata.title: Green Computing
metadata.definition: Introduction to green computing and the principles related to minimizing the environmental impact of information technology.

metadata.title: Language Core Abstractions
metadata.definition: Explain how core language constructs such as data abstraction and control abstraction are implemented in a system.

metadata.title: Memory Organization
metadata.definition: Explain how programming language implementations typically organize memory into global data, program code, heap, and stack sections.

metadata.title: Recursion Memory Mapping
metadata.definition: Describe how features such as recursion and memory management are mapped into the memory organization model of a programming language.

metadata.title: Memory Leak
metadata.definition: Explains the causes of memory leaks and the methods programmers can use to avoid or fix them.

metadata.title: Dangling Pointer
metadata.definition: Explains the causes of hanging pointer problems and the methods programmers can use to avoid or fix them.

metadata.title: JIT Execution Model
metadata.definition: Learn about the Just-In-Time (JIT) execution model and how it works in language translation and execution.

metadata.title: Compiler Execution Model
metadata.definition: Learn about the compiler's execution model, including the stages of compilation and machine code generation.

metadata.title: Interpreter Execution Model
metadata.definition: Learn about the interpreter's execution model, where source code is read and executed line by line.

metadata.title: Intermediate Code
metadata.definition: Research the role and usage of intermediate code in the language translation process to increase portability and optimization.

metadata.title: Bytecode
metadata.definition: Learn about bytecode as a common form of intermediate code, used by virtual machines like the JVM.

metadata.title: JIT Pros & Cons
metadata.definition: analyze the limitations and benefits of the Just-In-Time (JIT) execution model compared to compilers and interpreters.

metadata.title: Compiler Pros & Cons
metadata.definition: analyze the limitations and benefits of compilers in converting source code to machine code.

metadata.title: Interpreter Pros & Cons
metadata.definition: analyze the limitations and benefits of interpreters in executing source code.

metadata.title: Cross Compiler
metadata.definition: Learn about cross compilers, tools that translate source code for a target platform different from the one on which it is running.

metadata.title: Transpiler
metadata.definition: Learn about transpiler, a tool that translates source code from one programming language to another programming language of equivalent level of abstraction.

metadata.title: BNF Grammar Representation
metadata.definition: Learn how to use BNF to describe the syntax of context-free grammars, which are fundamental to language design and parsing.

metadata.title: EBNF Grammar Representation
metadata.definition: Learn how to use EBNF to describe the syntax of a context-free grammar, which provides a more extensible and readable syntax than BNF.

metadata.title: Parse Tree Generation
metadata.definition: Learn how to build a parse tree for simple statements such as arithmetic expressions or if-then-else statements to represent their syntactic structure.

metadata.title: Native Code Execution
metadata.definition: Learn about program execution as the processor's native machine code, delivering peak performance.

metadata.title: Virtual Machine Execution
metadata.definition: Learn about program execution in a virtual machine environment, which provides portability and a layer of abstraction from hardware.

metadata.title: Language Translation Process
metadata.definition: Study the entire language translation process, from parsing to execution, including the main stages.

metadata.title: Lexical Analysis
metadata.definition: Learn about the lexical analysis stage in the language translation process, turning character strings into tokens.

metadata.title: Parsing
metadata.definition: Learn about the grammar analysis stage to build a syntax tree structure (parse tree or abstract syntax tree) from tokens.

metadata.title: Optional Type Checking
metadata.definition: Learn about the type checking phase of the language translation process, which can be required or optional depending on the language, to detect type errors.

metadata.title: Code Generation
metadata.definition: Learn about the stage of translating source code to target code (machine code or intermediate code) in the compilation process.

metadata.title: Code Optimization
metadata.definition: Learn about code optimization techniques to improve the performance, size, or energy consumption of the generated program.

metadata.title: Linking
metadata.definition: Learn about the process of linking compiled code modules and libraries to create a complete executable program.

metadata.title: Loading
metadata.definition: Learn about the process of loading a linked program into memory to prepare it for execution.

metadata.title: Execution
metadata.definition: Learn about program execution after it has been translated, linked, and loaded into memory.

metadata.title: Object Runtime Representation
metadata.definition: Study how objects are represented at runtime, including the structure of method tables to manage polymorphism and dynamic method invocation.

metadata.title: Closure Runtime Representation
metadata.definition: Study how functions can be passed as parameters or returned from other functions, especially the concept of closure, and how they can be represented at runtime to preserve their definition environment.

metadata.title: Secure Compiler Development
metadata.definition: Learn the principles and techniques for developing secure compilers to prevent security vulnerabilities in the generated code and ensure the integrity of the compilation process.

metadata.title: Syntax, Parsing, Semantics
metadata.definition: The ability to clearly distinguish between aspects of syntax (the formal structure of the language) and parsing (the process of checking syntax) and semantics (the meaning of language structures) and evaluation (the process of executing a program).

metadata.title: BNF/EBNF Syntax Definition
metadata.definition: Use Backus-Naur Grammar (BNF) and Extended Backus-Naur Grammar (EBNF) to specify the syntax of simple programming constructs such as `if-then-else` conditional statements, data type declarations, and looping constructs in popular programming languages ​​such as C++ or Python.

metadata.title: Parse Tree Illustration
metadata.definition: Illustrates how to construct and interpret a parse tree for a simple arithmetic statement or expression.

metadata.title: Syntax Diagram to BNF/EBNF
metadata.definition: Illustrates the process of converting syntax diagrams into BNF or EBNF rules for simple constructs such as `if-then-else`, type declarations, and looping structures.

metadata.title: Parsing Ambiguity & Precedence
metadata.definition: Illustrate ambiguity in parsing using examples such as nested `if-then-else` statements or arithmetic expressions, and show how this ambiguity can be resolved by applying precedence order.

metadata.title: Garbage Collection Pros & Cons
metadata.definition: Discuss the benefits and limitations of garbage collection, including the concept of reachability of objects in memory.

metadata.title: BNF & Regular Expressions
metadata.definition: Concept of Backus-Naur Grammar (BNF) to describe language syntax and Regular Expressions to describe character patterns.

metadata.title: Program Processing Programs
metadata.definition: Types of programs that receive input from other programs, such as interpreters, compilers, type-checkers, and documentation generators.

metadata.title: Language Components
metadata.definition: Defines the basic components of a programming language, including alphabets, delimiters, sentences, syntax, and semantics.

metadata.title: Syntax vs Semantics
metadata.definition: Clearly distinguish between syntax – how to write code correctly – and semantics – the meaning of the code.

metadata.title: Program
metadata.definition: understand that a program is a set of meaningful, unambiguous statements, written according to the rules of a language.

metadata.title: Constants
metadata.definition: Concept of constants in programming.

metadata.title: Variables
metadata.definition: Concept of variables in programming.

metadata.title: Declarations
metadata.definition: Concept of declaration in programming, including nested declarations.

metadata.title: Statements
metadata.definition: Concept of command in programming.

metadata.title: Expressions
metadata.definition: Concept of expressions in programming.

metadata.title: Assignment
metadata.definition: Concept of value assignment to variables.

metadata.title: Selection Statements
metadata.definition: Concept of selection structure or conditional statement.

metadata.title: Definite Iteration
metadata.definition: The concept of a definite iteration structure, such as a `for` loop.

metadata.title: Indefinite Iteration
metadata.definition: The concept of an indefinite iteration structure, such as a `while` loop.

metadata.title: Iterators
metadata.definition: Concept of iterators to traverse data structures.

metadata.title: Functions
metadata.definition: Concept of function in programming.

metadata.title: Procedures
metadata.definition: The concept of procedure in programming.

metadata.title: Modules
metadata.definition: Concept of modules to organize and reuse code.

metadata.title: Exception Handling
metadata.definition: Concept of exception handling mechanism in programming.

metadata.title: Mutable vs Immutable
metadata.definition: Compare mutable and immutable variables, discuss the advantages and disadvantages of reusing existing memory locations versus copying and keeping old values; storing intermediate calculations vs. recalculating.

metadata.title: Variable Scopes
metadata.definition: Types of variables in programming: static variables, local variables, non-local variables and global variables; needs and problems that arise when using non-local and global variables.

metadata.title: Scope Rules
metadata.definition: Scope rules of variables, including static scoping and dynamic scoping; visibility of variables and the concept of side-effects.

metadata.title: Side Effects
metadata.definition: Side-effects can occur due to the use of non-local variables, global variables and aliased variables.

metadata.title: L-values and R-values
metadata.definition: Concept of L-values ​​(representing assignable memory locations) and R-values ​​(representing the value of an expression); how to map mutable variable names to L-values ​​and immutable variable names to R-values.

metadata.title: Environment vs Store
metadata.definition: Distinguish between environment (environment - maps variable names to memory addresses or values) and memory (store - maps memory addresses to values), along with their properties.

metadata.title: Data/Control Abstraction
metadata.definition: Concepts of data abstraction and control abstraction in language design.

metadata.title: Inter-Unit Communication
metadata.definition: Mechanisms for exchanging information between program units such as procedures, functions and modules, including non-local variables, global variables, parameter-passing and import-export mechanisms between modules.

metadata.title: Source Code Representation
metadata.definition: Data structures are used to represent source code for execution, translation, or transport purposes.

metadata.title: Low-Level Instructions
metadata.definition: Low-level forms of command representation such as virtual machine commands, assembly language, and binary representation.

metadata.title: Lambda Calculus
metadata.definition: Concept of Lambda calculus, a formal system for studying functions and their applications.

metadata.title: Variable Binding
metadata.definition: The concept of variable binding in formal systems and programming languages.

metadata.title: Variable Renaming
metadata.definition: The concept of variable renaming, often used to avoid name conflicts.

metadata.title: PL Semantics
metadata.definition: Types of programming language semantics: operational semantics, axiomatic semantics, denotational semantics, and behavioral semantics.

metadata.title: Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)
metadata.definition: Definition and usage of abstract syntax trees (ASTs) to represent the grammatical structure of code.

metadata.title: Abstract vs Concrete Syntax
metadata.definition: Contrast abstract syntax – which focuses on the semantic structure – and concrete syntax – which focuses on the precise textual representation of the language.

metadata.title: Regular vs Context-Free Grammars
metadata.definition: Compare and distinguish between regular grammars and context-free grammars, two basic types of grammar in formal language theory.

metadata.title: Lexical Analysis & Parsing
metadata.definition: The concept of lexical analysis/scanning and parsing is based on given language specifications.

metadata.title: Lexical Analysis with Regex
metadata.definition: Lexical analysis or scanning uses regular expressions to identify tokens.

metadata.title: Tokens
metadata.definition: Concept of tokens (lexical symbols) and their role in the parsing process.

metadata.title: Parsing Strategies
metadata.definition: Parsing strategies include top-down (e.g., recursive descent, LL) and bottom-up (e.g., LR, GLR) methods.

metadata.title: Lookahead Tables
metadata.definition: The concept of lookahead tables and how they are applied in the parsing process.

metadata.title: Chomsky Hierarchy
metadata.definition: The Chomsky Hierarchy classifies formal languages ​​based on their representational capabilities.

metadata.title: Derivations & Ambiguity
metadata.definition: The concepts of left-most derivation and right-most derivation arise in grammar, and ambiguity may arise.

metadata.title: Grammar Transformation
metadata.definition: Grammar transformation techniques to remove ambiguity or make the grammar more suitable for specific parsing strategies.

metadata.title: Parser Error Recovery
metadata.definition: Error recovery mechanisms are used in the parser to handle syntax errors and continue analysis.

metadata.title: Scanner/Parser Generation
metadata.definition: Method for automatically generating scanners and parsers from the declarative specifications of the language.

metadata.title: Operator Associativity
metadata.definition: The concept of associativity of operators in syntax definitions, helps resolve ambiguities in expressions.

metadata.title: High-Level IR Manipulation
metadata.definition: How to define, traversing, and modifying high-level program representations, typically ASTs or other intermediate representations, during semantic analysis.

metadata.title: Scope & Binding Resolution
metadata.definition: Techniques for resolving the scope resolution of identifiers and binding resolution of names to corresponding objects in the program.

metadata.title: Static Semantics
metadata.definition: Concept of static semantics, the rules of the language can be checked at compile time.

metadata.title: Type Checking
metadata.definition: Type checking process to ensure consistency of data types in the program.

metadata.title: Declare Before Use
metadata.definition: The rule requires variables or functions to be defined or declared before being used in a program.

metadata.title: Extended Static Checking
metadata.definition: Frameworks and tools enable annotations to be added to source code to support extended static checks, beyond basic syntax and type checks, to enhance software reliability.

metadata.title: L-values and R-values
metadata.definition: The concept of L-values ​​is expressions that have a memory address (assignable) and R-values ​​are expressions that only have a value (non-assignable) in the context of a programming language.

metadata.title: Call Semantics
metadata.definition: The rules and manner by which a function (or procedure) is called, including how arguments are passed and return values ​​are processed, as well as how the state of the program changes during the function call.

metadata.title: Parameter Passing
metadata.definition: Different methods for passing arguments to functions, including pass by value (copy by value), pass by reference (pass address), pass by result-value (copy in and out), pass by name (text replacement), and pass by need (lazy evaluation), along with their variations and comparisons.

metadata.title: Attribute Grammars
metadata.definition: Declarative specification techniques such as attribute grammars, and their applications in limited context-based grammar processing, allow the definition of attributes associated with nodes in the syntax tree and their systematic computation.

metadata.title: AST
metadata.definition: The tree data structure represents the abstract syntactic structure of source code, used in compilers and program analyzers.

metadata.title: Context-Sensitive Analysis
metadata.definition: Source-level static analysis techniques that consider the code's execution context, such as type checking or identifier resolution, to determine their binding locations.

metadata.title: Type Checker
metadata.definition: The tool or component of the compiler is responsible for checking the correctness of using data types in the program according to the rules of the language.

metadata.title: Identifier Resolution
metadata.definition: The process of determining which variable or function is referenced by a particular identifier in the source code, and the locations in the program where an identifier is declared and associated with a value or object.

metadata.title: Semantic Analysis (AG)
metadata.definition: The way attribute grammar is used to describe and perform semantic analysis, checking the validity and meaning of a program goes beyond syntax.

metadata.title: Basic Block
metadata.definition: A basic block is a sequence of instructions in program code such that if one instruction is executed then all other instructions in the sequence will also be executed, used as the basic unit in many program analysis.

metadata.title: CFG
metadata.definition: A control flow graph (CFG) is a graph that represents all possible paths a program can traverse during execution, with nodes being the basic blocks and edges representing the transfer of control between them.

metadata.title: Def-Use Chain
metadata.definition: A definition-use chain is a data structure or analysis in which each definition of a variable is associated with all the places that variable can be used after that definition.

metadata.title: SSA
metadata.definition: Static single assignment (SSA) is an intermediate representation of program code in which each variable is assigned a value only once, simplifying data flow analysis.

metadata.title: Undecidability in Analysis
metadata.definition: Concept of problems that cannot be solved algorithmically (e.g., stopping problems) and the limitations they impose on the ability to perform accurate and complete program analyses.

metadata.title: Flow-Insensitive Analysis
