metadata.definition: A type of program analysis that does not consider the order of execution of instructions, is often faster but less accurate, e.g. type checking.

metadata.title: Scalable Pointer Alias Analysis
metadata.definition: Techniques that analyze the relationship between pointers and determine when two different expressions may refer to the same memory location (alias), designed to work efficiently on large programs.

metadata.title: Flow-Sensitive Analysis
metadata.definition: A type of program analysis that considers the execution order of instructions and program state at different points in the control flow, for example, forward and backward data flow analysis.

metadata.title: Forward Dataflow Analysis
metadata.definition: A data flow analysis technique that gathers information about a program by going from the beginning to the end of the control flow.

metadata.title: Backward Dataflow Analysis
metadata.definition: A data flow analysis technique that gathers information about a program by going back from the end to the beginning of the control flow.

metadata.title: Path-Sensitive Analysis
metadata.definition: A type of program analysis that examines specific execution paths through code, allowing the detection of errors or properties that appear only on certain paths, e.g., software model checking and software verification.

metadata.title: Software Model Checking
metadata.definition: An automatic verification technique that explores all possible states of a program to verify specified properties.

metadata.title: Software Verification
metadata.definition: The process of ensuring that software meets given requirements or specifications, often through formal or semi-formal methods.

metadata.title: Analysis Tools & Frameworks
metadata.definition: Software and libraries that support the construction of program analysis tools, including lexer/parser generators, graph processing libraries, and analysis development environments.

metadata.title: Static Analysis for Optimization
metadata.definition: Static analysis is used to gather information about a program without executing it, which is then used to make more effective code optimization decisions.

metadata.title: Data Dependence Analysis
metadata.definition: analyze dependencies between read and write data operations to identify parts of the program that can be safely and efficiently executed in parallel.

metadata.title: Analysis for Verification & Debugging
metadata.definition: How program analysis techniques are used to partially test software for correctness or automatically detect potential errors.

metadata.title: Automatic Parallelization Analysis
metadata.definition: Source code analysis techniques to automatically identify and convert parts of a program into a parallel form that can run on multiple processors.

metadata.title: Concurrency Bug Detection
metadata.definition: Program analysis methods to identify errors related to concurrency, such as race conditions or deadlocks.

metadata.title: Data Flow Graph
metadata.definition: A diagram that describes how data moves and is transformed by mathematical operations in a program.

metadata.title: Approximation in Analysis
metadata.definition: The notion that for a non-trivial program analysis to be sound and stopable, it must usually accept a certain level of approximation, sometimes omitting some details for the sake of feasibility.

metadata.title: Soundness
metadata.definition: The property of a program analyzer that ensures that it never misses any errors or unexpected properties (e.g., if it says there are no errors, there really are no errors).

metadata.title: Termination
metadata.definition: The property of a program analysis that ensures that it will always finish in a finite amount of time, never run indefinitely.

metadata.title: Aliasing Impact on Analysis
metadata.definition: Situation where two or more different expressions in a program refer to the same memory location, causing difficulty and limiting the possibility of reliable program analysis.

metadata.title: Alias Analysis
metadata.definition: Program analysis technique to identify pairs of expressions that can be pseudonyms for each other, helping to improve the accuracy of other analyses.

metadata.title: Analysis for Optimization
metadata.definition: Using the results of program analysis to transform code, aiming to improve the performance or other characteristics of a program without changing its semantics.

metadata.title: Analysis for Partial Verification
metadata.definition: Using the results of program analysis to verify that a program satisfies certain properties or requirements, even if the entire program cannot be verified.

metadata.title: Instruction Set
metadata.definition: The set of all instructions that a processor can understand and execute, is the goal of code generation.

metadata.title: Control Flow (Code Gen)
metadata.definition: How control structures (e.g., if, loop) in source code are converted into jump and conditional statements in machine code or assembly language.

metadata.title: Memory Management (Code Gen)
metadata.definition: Techniques and strategies that compilers use to allocate and free memory for variables, data structures, and other program elements during code generation.

metadata.title: Procedure Call & Dispatch
metadata.definition: How procedure (or function) calls are compiled and how methods (in object-oriented programming) are dispatched to their correct implementation at run time.

metadata.title: Separate Compilation
metadata.definition: The technique of compiling different parts of a program independently, then linking them together to form the final program.

metadata.title: Linking
metadata.definition: The process of combining separate compilation-generated object files and necessary libraries into a single executable program.

metadata.title: Instruction Selection
metadata.definition: The stage in code generation where operations in the program's intermediate representation are mapped to specific instructions of the target instruction set.

metadata.title: Instruction Scheduling
metadata.definition: The stage in the code generation process where the execution order of instructions is optimized to improve performance, often by exploiting the processor's pipeline architecture.

metadata.title: Register Allocation
metadata.definition: The process of assigning program variables to processor registers to optimize data access and minimize main memory usage.

metadata.title: Code Optimization as Analysis
metadata.definition: Realize that code optimization techniques in compilers often rely on program analytics to gather information and make decisions that improve performance.

metadata.title: AI Code Generation
metadata.definition: The use of generative artificial intelligence models to automatically generate program code based on high-level descriptions or requirements.

metadata.title: Compiler Phases
metadata.definition: Overview of the stages required to automatically convert source code into assembly or other low-level languages, including lexical, syntactic, semantic analysis, intermediate code generation, optimization, and final code generation.

metadata.title: Low-Level Function Call
metadata.definition: Explains in detail the low-level code required to make function or method calls in modern languages, including setting up stack frames, passing parameters, saving state, and restoring state.

metadata.title: Calling Convention
metadata.definition: The reason why separate compilation requires standardized function calling conventions so that independently compiled modules can interact properly.

metadata.title: Separate Compilation Limits Optimization
metadata.definition: Discussion of separate compilation limits the compiler's ability to optimize because the full impact of function calls outside the current module cannot be known in advance.

metadata.title: Naive Code Optimization
metadata.definition: Optimization opportunities arise from direct or simple translation, and methods for achieving optimization after the initial translation is performed.

metadata.title: Peephole Optimization
metadata.definition: A technique that locally optimizes code by looking at a small 'window' of instructions and replacing inefficient sequences of instructions with more efficient sequences of instructions.

metadata.title: Stack & Heap Allocation
metadata.definition: How processes use stack and heap data structures to allocate and deallocate activation records and dynamic memory.

metadata.title: Activation Record
metadata.definition: A data structure created on the stack for each function call, containing information such as parameters, local variables, return addresses, and frame pointers.

metadata.title: Frame Pointer & Return Address
metadata.definition: Mechanism by which the runtime system uses the frame pointer and return address stored in the activation record to restore the execution state of the calling function after the called function completes.

metadata.title: Method Dispatch (OOP)
metadata.definition: The way methods in object-oriented programming languages ​​are looked up and dispatched to their correct implementation at run time, often using hash tables or similar data structures.

metadata.title: Object & AR Data Layout
metadata.definition: How the data of objects (data fields, vtable pointers) and activation records (local variables, parameters, return addresses) are arranged in memory.

metadata.title: Heap Object Allocation
metadata.definition: The process of allocating memory for objects on the heap at runtime, typically performed by the language's runtime environment or operating system.

metadata.title: Virtual Method Implementation
metadata.definition: Techniques for implementing virtual concepts in object-oriented programming, allowing polymorphism and dynamic binding, including how virtual methods are called.

metadata.title: Vtable
metadata.definition: Data structures are used in object-oriented programming to implement polymorphism through virtual methods, allowing the runtime system to find the right method to call based on the actual type of the object.

metadata.title: OOP Runtime Behavior
metadata.definition: How concepts like inheritance, polymorphism, and encapsulation affect how object-oriented programs operate and manage resources at runtime.

metadata.title: Parameter Passing Memory
metadata.definition: How memory is allocated and used when information is exchanged between functions or procedures through various parameter passing mechanisms.

metadata.title: Non-Local Variable Allocation
metadata.definition: Memory allocation and access methods for non-local variables (i.e. variables declared in enclosing scopes but not the current scope), typically use static binding to keep track of nested environments.

metadata.title: Dynamic Memory Management
metadata.definition: Techniques for allocating and freeing memory during program runtime.

metadata.title: Malloc/Free
metadata.definition: Standard library functions to allocate (malloc) and free (free) memory dynamically as required by the program.

metadata.title: Mark-Sweep GC
metadata.definition: A two-phase garbage collection algorithm: the mark phase identifies all accessible objects, and the sweep phase reclaims memory from unmarked objects.

metadata.title: Copying GC
metadata.definition: A garbage collection algorithm divides heap memory into two regions and moves live objects from the currently used region to the remaining region.

metadata.title: Reference Counting GC
metadata.definition: A garbage collection algorithm keeps track of the number of references to each object and releases memory when the reference count reaches zero.

metadata.title: Memory Arenas
metadata.definition: A memory management technique in which related objects are allocated from a single large memory region, increasing allocation efficiency and freeing the entire region at once.

metadata.title: JIT Compilation
metadata.definition: A method of compiling code during a program's runtime, often used in virtual machines to convert bytecode to native machine code to improve performance.

metadata.title: Dynamic Recompilation
metadata.definition: A technique of recompiling parts of a program at runtime, often to apply new optimizations based on the program's actual behavior or to adapt to a changing environment.

metadata.title: OS Program Initialization
metadata.definition: The interaction points between the program and the operating system during program initialization, including code loading, stack and heap setup, and initial transfer of control.

metadata.title: Language Interoperability
metadata.definition: Challenges and techniques that enable components written in different programming languages ​​to communicate and operate together, including mechanisms for parameter passing and data representation.

metadata.title: Interop Parameter Passing
metadata.definition: Methods for passing arguments between functions written in different programming languages, often involve standardized calling conventions and data formats.

metadata.title: Interop Data Representation
metadata.definition: How data types and data structures are represented in memory to allow different languages ​​to share and understand data.

metadata.title: Endianness
metadata.definition: Two different byte arrangements in memory for multi-byte values, affecting data compatibility between systems.

metadata.title: Complex Data Type Layout
metadata.definition: How complex data types such as arrays, structures, or objects are arranged and stored in memory.

metadata.title: VM Class Loading
metadata.definition: The process of loading classes or modules into a virtual machine's memory when they are required, often involving code verification and dynamic linking.

metadata.title: VM Threads
metadata.definition: How virtual machines manage and support the concurrent execution of multiple threads within a program.

metadata.title: VM Security Checks
metadata.definition: Security mechanisms are implemented in virtual machines to limit access and prevent malicious behavior, ensuring program and system safety.

metadata.title: Sandboxing
metadata.definition: A security technique in which a program or part of a program is run in a restricted environment, isolated from critical system resources to prevent potential negative effects.

metadata.title: Automatic Memory Management
metadata.definition: Discuss the benefits and drawbacks of automatic memory management, including mechanisms such as garbage collection.

metadata.title: Runtime Metadata
metadata.definition: Explain the use of metadata in object representation and run-time activation records, such as class pointers, array lengths, return addresses, and frame pointers.

metadata.title: Static Memory Allocation
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast memory allocation methods for data elements: static allocation.

metadata.title: Stack Memory Allocation
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast memory allocation methods for data elements: stack-based allocation.

metadata.title: Heap Memory Allocation
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast memory allocation methods for data elements: heap-based allocation.

metadata.title: Garbage Collection Necessity
metadata.definition: Explain why some data elements cannot be automatically released at the end of a procedure/method call and require a garbage collection mechanism.

metadata.title: JIT Pros/Cons
metadata.definition: Discuss the advantages, disadvantages, and difficulties of Just-in-time (JIT) compilation and dynamic recompilation.

metadata.title: Dynamic Recompilation Pros/Cons
metadata.definition: Discuss the advantages, disadvantages, and difficulties of dynamic recompilation.

metadata.title: Mobile Code Sandboxing
metadata.definition: Discusses the use of sandboxing (isolated environments) in mobile code to enhance security.

metadata.title: Runtime System Services
metadata.definition: Identify the services provided by the runtime systems of modern programming languages.

metadata.title: Encapsulation Mechanisms
metadata.definition: understand and use encapsulation mechanisms in programming to manage access and protect data.

metadata.title: Lazy Evaluation
metadata.definition: understand the concept of deferred evaluation, where an expression is evaluated only when its value is actually needed.

metadata.title: Infinite Streams
metadata.definition: Working with infinite data streams, often combined with deferred evaluation.

metadata.title: Lazy vs Eager Evaluation
metadata.definition: Compare and contrast two expression evaluation strategies: lazy evaluation and eager evaluation.

metadata.title: Eager Evaluation
metadata.definition: understand the concept of immediate evaluation, where an expression is evaluated immediately.

metadata.title: Unification
metadata.definition: Compare expression merging, validation, and evaluation mechanisms, especially in logic programming languages.

metadata.title: Assertion Evaluation
metadata.definition: Compare assertion evaluation and expression evaluation mechanisms, especially in the context of programming languages.

metadata.title: Expression Evaluation
metadata.definition: understand expression evaluation methods and rules in different programming languages.

metadata.title: Exception Handling
metadata.definition: understand and use exception handling as a control abstraction mechanism to manage errors and unusual situations.

metadata.title: Continuations
metadata.definition: Learn about continuations as a powerful control abstraction mechanism that enables non-local control of the flow of execution.

metadata.title: Monads
metadata.definition: Learn about monads as a control abstraction and code organization mechanism, especially in functional programming.

metadata.title: Multiple Inheritance
metadata.definition: understand the concept of multiple inheritance in object-oriented programming, its advantages and disadvantages.

metadata.title: Mixins
metadata.definition: Learn about mixins as a way to reuse code and add functionality to classes without traditional multiple inheritance.

metadata.title: Traits
metadata.definition: Learn about traits as a mechanism for grouping methods that can be reused in multiple classes.

metadata.title: Multimethods
metadata.definition: Learn about multimethods (or generic functions) where the choice of method depends on the type of multiple arguments.

metadata.title: Macros
metadata.definition: Use macros as a form of metaprogramming to generate code automatically during compilation or runtime.

metadata.title: Generative Programming
metadata.definition: understand generative programming, a programming method that automatically generates source code, components, or software systems based on specific descriptions or requirements.

metadata.title: Model-Based Development
metadata.definition: Learn about model-based development (MBD), where models are used as the primary means to design, deploy, and test systems.

metadata.title: Regex Pattern Matching
metadata.definition: Perform string manipulation using pattern matching, specifically through regular expressions to search, replace, and parse text.

metadata.title: Regular Expressions
metadata.definition: Use regular expressions to describe and match patterns in strings.

metadata.title: Dynamic Code Evaluation (`eval`)
metadata.definition: understand and use the ability to dynamically evaluate code at runtime, typically via the 'eval' function, and its advantages and associated security risks.

metadata.title: Language Assertions
metadata.definition: Learn about how programming languages ​​support checking assertions to ensure program correctness.

metadata.title: Language Invariants
metadata.definition: Learn about how programming languages ​​support checking invariants of objects or data structures.

metadata.title: Language Pre-conditions
metadata.definition: Learn about how programming languages ​​support checking pre-conditions of functions or methods.

metadata.title: Language Post-conditions
metadata.definition: Learn about how programming languages ​​support checking post-conditions of functions or methods.

metadata.title: Domain-Specific Language (DSL)
metadata.definition: understand the concepts and applications of domain-specific languages, designed for a specific application domain.

metadata.title: Database Languages (DSL)
metadata.definition: Learn about database languages ​​like SQL, which are examples of domain-specific languages.

metadata.title: Data Science Languages (DSL)
metadata.definition: Learn about languages ​​used in data science (like Python with Pandas, R libraries) as examples of domain-specific languages.

metadata.title: Embedded Computing Languages (DSL)
metadata.definition: Learn about languages ​​used in embedded computing (like C, Rust) as examples of domain-specific languages.

metadata.title: Synchronous Languages (DSL)
metadata.definition: Learn about synchronous languages ​​(e.g. Esterel, Luster) used for programming real-time and reactive systems.

metadata.title: Hardware Interface Languages (DSL)
metadata.definition: Learn about languages ​​used to communicate with hardware (e.g. VHDL, Verilog) as examples of domain-specific languages.

metadata.title: High-Performance Parallel Computing
metadata.definition: Study the paradigms and languages ​​used for massively parallel high-performance computing, such as CUDA, OpenMP, MPI.

metadata.title: Technology Influence on PL Design
metadata.definition: Discuss how technological needs drive the development and evolution of programming languages.

metadata.title: Software Requirements on PL Design
metadata.definition: Discuss how software requirements shape the development and evolution of programming languages.

metadata.title: Problem Domains & PL Models
metadata.definition: understand the relationships between different problem domains and the appropriate programming models to solve them.

metadata.title: Good PL Design Criteria
metadata.definition: analyze the criteria for evaluating a good programming language design, including principles such as orthogonality.

metadata.title: PL Design: Orthogonality
metadata.definition: Learn about language design principles like orthogonality, where language features can be used independently and combined consistently.

metadata.title: PL Design: Good Defaults
metadata.definition: Discuss the role of well-chosen defaults in language design and how they affect the programmer's experience.

metadata.title: Control Structure Definition
metadata.definition: understand the principles and techniques for defining control structures in a programming language.

metadata.title: Loop Structure Definition
metadata.definition: understand the principles and techniques for defining repeating constructs in a programming language.

metadata.title: Large Software Modularity
metadata.definition: Discuss the importance and principles of massive software modularization to improve structure and maintainability.

metadata.title: Order of Evaluation
metadata.definition: understand the rules for the order of evaluation of expressions and arguments in various programming languages.

metadata.title: Operator Precedence
metadata.definition: understand the precedence of operators in expressions and how they affect the evaluation results.

metadata.title: Operator Associativity
metadata.definition: understand the associativity of operators (left to right or right to left) and how they determine the order of evaluation when there are multiple operators with the same precedence.

metadata.title: External Calls
metadata.definition: Discusses the need to allow external calls and system libraries, as well as the consequences for language implementations.

metadata.title: System Libraries
metadata.definition: Discuss the role and integration of system libraries into programming languages.

metadata.title: User-Defined Control Abstractions
metadata.definition: Illustrates the use of deferred evaluation to create user-defined control abstractions.

metadata.title: Syntax vs. Semantics
metadata.definition: Distinguish and compare syntax (form of the language) and semantics (meaning of the language) in the context of programming languages.

metadata.title: Language Syntax
metadata.definition: understand how a programming language is described and parsed.

metadata.title: Language Semantics
metadata.definition: understand the importance of semantic definitions to clarify the meaning of linguistic structures.

metadata.title: Axiomatic Semantics
metadata.definition: Learn about axiomatic semantics as a method for describing the meaning of a program through preconditions and postconditions.

metadata.title: Operational Semantics
metadata.definition: Learning about semantics works as a method to describe the meaning of a program by identifying its computational steps.

metadata.title: Denotational Semantics
metadata.definition: Learn about model semantics as a method for describing the meaning of a program by mapping it to abstract mathematical objects.

metadata.title: Type-Based Semantics
metadata.definition: Learn about type-based semantics as a method for analyzing and ensuring program correctness through the type system.

metadata.title: Axiomatic Semantics: Assignment
metadata.definition: apply axiomatic semantics to analyze abstract structures such as assignments using preconditions, postconditions, and invariants.

metadata.title: Axiomatic Semantics: Selection
metadata.definition: apply axiomatic semantics to analyze abstract structures such as options (if-then-else) using preconditions, postconditions, and invariants.

metadata.title: Axiomatic Semantics: Iteration
metadata.definition: apply axiomatic semantics to analyze abstract structures such as iterations (loops) using preconditions, postconditions, and loop invariants.

metadata.title: Preconditions (Axiomatic Semantics)
metadata.definition: Use preconditions to specify a state that must be true before a piece of code is executed in axiomatic semantics.

metadata.title: Postconditions (Axiomatic Semantics)
metadata.definition: Use postconditions to specify the state that must be true after a piece of code is executed in axiomatic semantics.

metadata.title: Loop Invariant
metadata.definition: Using loop invariants to prove the correctness of iterative constructs in axiomatic semantics.

metadata.title: Operational Semantics: Assignment
metadata.definition: analyze the operational semantics of abstract constructs such as assignment, environment usage, and memory.

metadata.title: Operational Semantics: Expressions
metadata.definition: Operational semantic analysis of expression evaluation, environment and memory usage.

metadata.title: Operational Semantics: Selection
metadata.definition: analyze the operational semantics of abstract constructs such as selection, environment usage, and memory.

metadata.title: Operational Semantics: Iteration
metadata.definition: analyze the operational semantics of abstract constructs such as iteration, environment and memory usage.

metadata.title: Operational Semantics: Environment
metadata.definition: understand the role of the environment in operational semantics for tracking variable bindings.

metadata.title: Operational Semantics: Store
metadata.definition: understand the role of memory (store) in operational semantics for monitoring memory status.

metadata.title: Symbolic Execution
metadata.definition: Learn about symbolic execution as a program analysis technique that allows program execution with symbolic rather than concrete input values.

metadata.title: Constraint Checkers
metadata.definition: Learn about constraint checking tools used to verify constraints imposed on variables or program state.

metadata.title: Lambda Calculus
metadata.definition: Study Lambda Calculus as a formal system for expressing computation based on functional abstraction and application.

metadata.title: Language Semantics Induction Proof
metadata.definition: Use induction to prove the properties of all programs in a language, based on the definition of its formal semantics.

metadata.title: Formal Type System Definition
metadata.definition: Research formal definitions and proofs for the type system, ensuring program safety.

metadata.title: Type System Proofs
metadata.definition: Build proofs of the correctness of the type system, such as type consistency.

metadata.title: Propositions as Types
metadata.definition: Learn about the relationship between logical statements and types in advanced type systems.

metadata.title: Implication as Function Type
metadata.definition: understand how logical reasoning can be represented as functions in the context of 'propositions as types'.

metadata.title: Conjunction as Product Type
metadata.definition: understand how logical conjunctions can be represented as product types in the context of 'propositions as types'.

metadata.title: Disjunction as Sum Type
metadata.definition: understand how logical selections can be represented as sum types in the context of 'clauses as types'.

metadata.title: Dependent Types
metadata.definition: Learn about dependent types, a type system in which types can depend on values.

metadata.title: Universal Quantifier as Dependent Function
metadata.definition: understand how universal quantifiers can be represented as dependent functions in a dependent type system.

metadata.title: Existential Quantifier as Dependent Product
metadata.definition: understand how existential quantifiers can be represented as dependent products in a dependent type system.

metadata.title: Parametricity
metadata.definition: Learn about parametricity as a property of the polymorphic type system, which implies behavioral properties of generic functions.

metadata.title: Inductive Proofs for Typed Languages
metadata.definition: The ability to use mathematical induction to prove the properties of all programs in a language that are precisely typed according to a formally defined type system.

metadata.title: Parametricity for Code Behavior
metadata.definition: The ability to use parametricity to infer or establish the behavior of code based solely on information about its type, independent of the specific implementation.

metadata.title: Formal Specification Languages
metadata.definition: The study of languages ​​and methods used to describe the behavior of software systems in a precise, unambiguous, and verifiable manner.

metadata.title: Theorem Provers, Proof Assistants
metadata.definition: Software tools (such as theorem provers, proof assistants) and formal logic platforms are used to support the construction and verification of mathematical and logical proofs.

metadata.title: Constraint Checkers
metadata.definition: Tools are used to automatically check whether a system complies with defined constraints or rules.

metadata.title: Dependent Types
metadata.definition: The concept of data types that depend on values ​​rather than just types, allows the representation of complex specifications (e.g., universal quantifiers as dependent functions, existential quantifiers as dependent products).

metadata.title: Proof Discharge Verified Software
metadata.definition: Engineering specifies software requirements and uses automated or semi-automated tools to complete proof discharges of the correctness of fully verified software systems, using preconditions/postconditions, refinement types, etc.

metadata.title: Formal Modeling and Refinement
metadata.definition: The process of creating formal (mathematical) models of software systems and then manually refining or implementing them to meet design requirements.

metadata.title: Symbolic Testing, Fuzzing
metadata.definition: Automated software testing techniques include symbolic testing to explore execution paths and fuzzing to find errors by providing invalid or unexpected input.

metadata.title: Model Checking
metadata.definition: A technique for verifying the correctness of a hardware or software system design by automatically checking whether an abstract model of the system satisfies certain specifications.

metadata.title: Effective Formal Methods Application
metadata.definition: The ability to recognize the situations and contexts in which formal methods can be applied most effectively, as well as how to structure the development process to maximize their value.

metadata.title: Formal Modeling for Architecture
metadata.definition: Skills in applying formal modeling techniques to design, analyze and verify the correctness of software system architectures.

metadata.title: Proof-Assisted Programming
metadata.definition: Skills in using programming languages ​​that integrate proof assistant tools to build software components that are completely formally specified and verified.

metadata.title: Verification in Programming Languages
metadata.definition: Skill in leveraging verifiers and specification support available in programming languages ​​to formally test and validate desired system properties.

metadata.title: Symbolic Validation Integration
metadata.definition: Skill in incorporating symbolic validation tools into daily software development processes to improve code quality and reliability.

metadata.title: Formal Methods Effectiveness
metadata.definition: Ability to analyze and discuss optimal cases and ways to apply formal methods in the software development process, evaluating their benefits and limitations.

metadata.title: Programming Language Design Principles
metadata.definition: Basic principles guide the design of programming languages ​​that are efficient, easy to use, and highly applicable.

metadata.title: Language Design: Simplicity
metadata.definition: Principle of designing a programming language so that its syntax, semantics, and features are easy to learn, use, and understand.

metadata.title: Language Design: Security
metadata.definition: Programming language design principles to minimize potential security vulnerabilities and prevent unsafe behavior.

metadata.title: Language Design: Fast Translation
metadata.definition: Principle of designing programming languages ​​to be compiled or interpreted quickly, optimizing development and response time.

metadata.title: Language Design: Efficient Object Code
metadata.definition: Programming language design principles to create object code that runs efficiently in terms of time and resources, optimizing application performance.

metadata.title: Language Design: Orthogonality
metadata.definition: Programming language design principle in which independent features can be freely combined without causing unwanted side effects, increasing flexibility and reducing complexity.

metadata.title: Language Design: Readability
metadata.definition: Principles of programming language design so that the source code is easy to understand, read, and maintain by humans.

metadata.title: Language Design: Completeness
metadata.definition: Programming language design principles that provide enough functionality and expressiveness to solve a wide range of problems or tasks.

metadata.title: Language Design: Implementation Strategy
metadata.definition: The methods and techniques considered when designing a language, influence how the compiler, interpreter, or runtime environment is built for that language.

metadata.title: Domain-Specific Language Design
metadata.definition: Ability to design a specific programming language (Domain-Specific Language - DSL) according to the requirements of a specific application area or type of problem.

metadata.title: Language Interoperability
metadata.definition: The ability of different programming languages ​​to work together, exchange data, and call each other's functions or methods.

metadata.title: Language Portability
metadata.definition: The ability of a programming language and programs written in that language to run on different hardware platforms and operating systems without significant modification.

metadata.title: Formal Language Description
metadata.definition: The use of precise mathematical methods to define the syntax and semantics of a programming language, often using tools such as formal grammar and domain theory.

metadata.title: Green Computing
metadata.definition: Principles for designing and using computer systems, software, and programming languages ​​in a way that saves energy and minimizes environmental impact.

metadata.title: PL Design Evaluation
metadata.definition: The ability to understand the elements that make up a good programming language design and apply that knowledge to analyze and evaluate the pros and cons of an actual programming language.

metadata.title: English-centric PL Impact
metadata.definition: Discusses the effects, both positive and negative, of predominantly English-based programming languages ​​on the global developer community and inclusivity.

metadata.title: Programming Accessibility
metadata.definition: Methods and considerations for making programming languages, tools, and development environments more accessible to people with disabilities, including assistive technology support.

metadata.title: PL Human Factors
metadata.definition: Study of how programming language features affect user experience, productivity, comfort, and programmer perception.

metadata.title: Syntax Accessibility
metadata.definition: The influence of the syntactic structure of a programming language on its ease of use and accessibility for different user groups, including those with special needs.

metadata.title: PL Culturalization
metadata.definition: How programming languages ​​and applications can support culturally different formats and conventions (e.g. currency, decimal numbers, dates), ensuring globalization.

metadata.title: Neurodiversity in Programming
metadata.definition: Discuss how programming languages ​​and development environments can be designed to accommodate people with neurological differences, encouraging inclusion in the industry.

metadata.title: Offensive PL Terms
metadata.definition: Study the origins and historical meanings of terms like “class,” “master,” and “slave” in the context of programming languages, and discuss their social and ethical implications.

metadata.title: Multilingual App Support (UTF)
metadata.definition: Methods to make applications more accessible to users globally through support for multiple languages, often using Unicode (UTF) character encoding.

metadata.title: Inclusive PL Design
metadata.definition: The ability to consciously design programming languages ​​so that they are friendly, accessible, and free of potentially offensive terms or constructs promotes an inclusive programming environment.

metadata.title: PL Professionalism
metadata.definition: Attitude and skills that demonstrate the highest standards when using programming languages ​​and formal methods to build systems that are secure and fit for purpose.

metadata.title: Programming Rigour
metadata.definition: Careful attention to detail is necessary when using programming languages ​​and applying formal methods to avoid errors and ensure correctness.

metadata.title: PL Creativity & Responsibility
metadata.definition: Ability to demonstrate innovative approaches in solving programming problems and constructing formal proofs, while taking responsibility for one's choices and results.

metadata.title: Proactive Programming
metadata.definition: It is the programmer's responsibility to anticipate all forms of user input and system behavior, then design solutions that proactively address each case.

metadata.title: Programming Persistence
metadata.definition: Ability to demonstrate perseverance and persistence in finding solutions to complex programming problems, even when the correct approach is not always obvious and requires process refinement.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: Boolean Algebra
metadata.definition: Concepts and rules of Boolean algebra, the foundation for digital logic, electronic circuit design, and programming.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: Proof Techniques
metadata.definition: Various methods and techniques for proving mathematical statements, including direct, indirect, induction, and contradiction proofs.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: Digital Logic
metadata.definition: Basic principles of digital logic, used in the design of computer circuits and digital systems.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: Set Operations
metadata.definition: Concepts of sets, elements and basic operations on sets such as union, intersection, difference, complement.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: Functions & Relations
metadata.definition: Concepts of mapping, functions, types of functions (unijective, complete, bijective) and types of relationships between sets.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: State & Invariants
metadata.definition: The concepts of a system's state and invariants are always true throughout the system's operation.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: Graphs & Relations
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of graphs, vertices, edges, types of graphs (directed, undirected) and how to represent relationships graphically.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: Trees
metadata.definition: Tree data structure, types of trees (binary trees, search trees) and their properties in discrete mathematics.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: Counting
metadata.definition: Counting techniques and principles in discrete mathematics, including permutations, combinations, and compensation principles.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: Recurrence Relations
metadata.definition: Equations define a series of numbers in terms of previous terms in the series, used for algorithmic analysis and problem solving.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: Finite State Machines
metadata.definition: A mathematical model of computation used to design sequential reaction systems, including states and state transitions.

metadata.title: Discrete Math: Regular Grammars
metadata.definition: A type of formal grammar used to describe formal languages, often involving finite state machines and regular expressions.

metadata.title: Logic: Propositional Logic
metadata.definition: Study of propositions and basic logical operations such as negation, union, selection, entailment, equivalence, along with truth tables.

metadata.title: Logic: First-Order Logic
metadata.definition: A logical system represents statements about objects, their properties, and the relationships between them, including universal and existential quantifiers.

metadata.title: Logic: Inductive Reasoning
metadata.definition: Method of logical deduction from specific observations or cases to reach a general conclusion, often used in mathematics and computer science.

metadata.title: Logic: Deductive Reasoning
metadata.definition: The method of logical deduction from one or more general premises believed to be true to reach a specific logical conclusion, ensuring correctness.

metadata.title: Logic: Abductive Reasoning
metadata.definition: Logical reasoning method for finding the simplest and most feasible explanation for a set of observations, commonly used in diagnostics and artificial intelligence.

metadata.title: OOP
metadata.definition: Principles and techniques of object-oriented programming, including concepts such as classes, objects, inheritance, polymorphism, and encapsulation.

metadata.title: Functional Programming
metadata.definition: Programming principles and models based on mathematical functions, including the concepts of pure functions, higher-order functions, immutability, and recursion.

metadata.title: Logic Programming
metadata.definition: Programming method based on formal logic, in which programs are represented as sets of facts and rules, and program execution is a process of inference.

metadata.title: Shell Scripting
metadata.definition: Write scripts to automate tasks and manage systems using shell commands and control structures.

metadata.title: Event-Driven Programming
metadata.definition: The programming model focuses on handling events and reacting to them asynchronously, including the concepts of data flow and events.

metadata.title: Parallel & Distributed Computing
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of program execution on multiple processors or computers, including synchronization, communication, and resource management.

metadata.title: Type Systems (Intro)
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of type systems in programming languages, including type checking, type safety, and basic data types.

metadata.title: System & Memory Model
metadata.definition: How programs are executed on the system and how memory is managed, including stack, heap, pointers, and automatic memory management.

metadata.title: Language Translation & Execution (Intro)
metadata.definition: The basic stages of translating a programming language into machine or intermediate code, and executing the program.

metadata.title: Abstraction & Program Representation
metadata.definition: Techniques for creating abstractions in programs and ways of representing programs at different levels.

metadata.title: Social, Ethical & Professional Issues
metadata.definition: Ethical issues, social responsibility, and professional implications of programming language development and use.

metadata.title: Type Systems (Advanced)
metadata.definition: In-depth study of the design, analysis, and implementation of complex type systems, including type theories, type inference, and advanced type systems.

metadata.title: Language Translation & Execution (Advanced)
metadata.definition: Advanced techniques in language translation, including code optimization, code generation, and runtime architectures.

metadata.title: Parsing
metadata.definition: Methods and algorithms for analyzing the syntactic structure of source code, including lexical analysis, parsing and creating abstract syntax trees (AST).

metadata.title: Semantic Analysis (Compiler)
metadata.definition: Techniques for checking the meaning and validity of a program after parsing, including type checking, symbol table management, and intermediate code generation.

metadata.title: Program Analysis
metadata.definition: Methods for automatically analyzing program behavior and properties, including static analysis, dynamic analysis, and code analysis tools.

metadata.title: Code Generation
metadata.definition: Study techniques and methods for translating high-level source code into executable machine or intermediate code.

metadata.title: Run-time Systems
metadata.definition: Learn about the components and mechanisms that support program execution at runtime, including memory management, garbage collection, and scheduling.

metadata.title: Advanced Programming Constructs
metadata.definition: Explore complex and powerful programming language constructs, such as metaprogramming, aspect-oriented programming, or advanced concurrency mechanisms.

metadata.title: Language Pragmatics
metadata.definition: The study of practical and contextual factors that influence the design, use, and effectiveness of programming languages, including technical, economic, and psychological considerations.

metadata.title: Formal Semantics
metadata.definition: Learn to define the semantics of programming languages ​​precisely and without ambiguity using mathematical and logical tools.

metadata.title: Formal Development Methodologies
metadata.definition: apply formal techniques to design, analyze, and verify software systems to ensure correctness and reliability.

metadata.title: Boolean Algebra
metadata.definition: Study of mathematical operations and logic rules used in digital circuit design and set theory.

metadata.title: Proof Techniques
metadata.definition: Methods to prove the correctness of mathematical propositions, including direct proof, contradiction, and induction.

metadata.title: Digital Logic
metadata.definition: The fundamentals of electronic circuits are based on the binary system, the foundation for computer design.

metadata.title: Sets
metadata.definition: Concept of sets and their basic properties.

metadata.title: Set Operations
metadata.definition: Union, intersection, difference, complement and other operations on sets.

metadata.title: Mapping
metadata.definition: The concept of correspondence between elements of two sets.

metadata.title: Functions
metadata.definition: Definition and properties of functions in discrete mathematics.

metadata.title: Relations
metadata.definition: Study of relationships between elements in sets, including equivalence relationships and ordering relationships.

metadata.title: State
metadata.definition: The concept of the state of a system or an object over time.

metadata.title: Invariants
metadata.definition: Properties of a system or program that do not change throughout its operation.

metadata.title: Graphs
metadata.definition: Research on graph structure, related properties and algorithms.

metadata.title: Trees (Discrete Math)
metadata.definition: Tree structures in discrete mathematics, including binary search trees and spanning trees.

metadata.title: Counting
metadata.definition: Counting techniques in combination and probability, including permutations, combinations, and combinations.

metadata.title: Recurrence Relations
metadata.definition: Equations define a series of numbers based on previous values, often used in algorithm analysis.

metadata.title: Finite State Machine
metadata.definition: Mathematical model for systems that can be in one of a finite number of states.

metadata.title: Regular Grammar
metadata.definition: A type of formal grammar used to define formal languages, often used in formal language theory.

metadata.title: Propositional Logic
metadata.definition: Basic logic is the study of propositions and how they are connected by logical operators.

metadata.title: Negation (Logic)
metadata.definition: Logical operators return true if the original statement is false and vice versa.

metadata.title: Conjunction (Logic)
metadata.definition: Logical operators return true if all the component clauses are true (AND).

metadata.title: Disjunction (Logic)
metadata.definition: Logical operators return true if at least one component clause is true (OR).

metadata.title: Implication (Logic)
metadata.definition: Logical operators express an 'if... then...' relationship between two clauses.

metadata.title: Biconditional (Logic)
metadata.definition: Logical operators express a 'if and only if' relationship between two clauses.

metadata.title: First-Order Logic
metadata.definition: The logic system extends propositional logic by adding predicates, functions, and quantifiers, allowing the representation of more complex sentences.

metadata.title: Logical Reasoning
metadata.definition: Deductive methods for reaching conclusions from given premises.

metadata.title: Induction (Logic)
metadata.definition: Method of inference from specific cases to a general law.

metadata.title: Deduction (Logic)
metadata.definition: Method of inference from general rules to specific conclusions.

metadata.title: Abduction (Logic)
metadata.definition: Deductive method for finding the most likely explanation for a set of observations.

metadata.title: Type Declaration
metadata.definition: How to define new data types or declare types for variables in programming languages.

metadata.title: Primitive Data Types
metadata.definition: Primitive data types such as integers, real numbers, characters, booleans.

metadata.title: Records
metadata.definition: The data structure allows data fields of different types to be grouped under a single name.

metadata.title: Indexed Data Elements
metadata.definition: Data structures whose elements are accessed via an index, such as arrays and vectors.

metadata.title: Arrays
metadata.definition: Linear data structures store elements of the same data type in consecutive memory locations and are accessed by index.

metadata.title: Vectors
metadata.definition: Dynamic arrays can change size during program execution.

metadata.title: Class Declaration
metadata.definition: How to define a class, including its properties and methods, in object-oriented programming.

metadata.title: Subclass Declaration
metadata.definition: How to define a subclass that inherits from a superclass, in object-oriented programming.

metadata.title: Variable Types
metadata.definition: Classify variables based on the type of data they store.

metadata.title: Variable Scope Rules
metadata.definition: The rules define the area in which a variable can be accessed in the program.

metadata.title: Selection Constructs
metadata.definition: Control structures allow a program to execute different blocks of statements based on a condition, e.g. if-else, switch.

metadata.title: Iteration Constructs
metadata.definition: Control structures allow a program to repeat a block of instructions multiple times, for example: for, while, do-while.

metadata.title: Function Call
metadata.definition: Mechanism for calling and executing a function in a program.

metadata.title: Procedure Call
metadata.definition: Mechanism to call and execute a procedure (function that does not return a value) in a program.

metadata.title: Methods (Programming)
metadata.definition: Functions or procedures associated with an object or class in object-oriented programming.

metadata.title: Object Creation
metadata.definition: The process of creating an instance of a class in object-oriented programming.

metadata.title: Abstract Data Type (ADT)
metadata.definition: Defines a data type through its behavior without revealing its internal implementation.

metadata.title: Sequences
metadata.definition: The data structure stores elements in a linear order.

metadata.title: String
metadata.definition: A sequence of characters, often used to represent text.

metadata.title: Stack
metadata.definition: The LIFO (Last In First Out) data structure allows adding and removing elements from one end.

metadata.title: Queue
metadata.definition: The FIFO (First In First Out) data structure allows elements to be added at the end and deleted from the beginning.

metadata.title: Tree
metadata.definition: The hierarchical data structure consists of nodes and edges, with a root node and child branches.

metadata.title: Dictionary
metadata.definition: The data structure stores key-value pairs, allowing quick access to values ​​via keys.

metadata.title: Pointer-based DS
metadata.definition: Data structures use pointers to link elements, allowing for more flexible organization of data in memory.

metadata.title: Linked List
metadata.definition: Linear data structure in which elements do not need to be stored consecutively in memory, but are linked by pointers.

metadata.title: Shared Memory
metadata.definition: Memory regions can be accessed and modified by multiple processes or threads, which are the basis for communication and synchronization.

metadata.title: Hashing
metadata.definition: Technique that transforms a key into an index in an array for quick access to data.

metadata.title: Hash Table
metadata.definition: The data structure uses a hash function to map keys to values, allowing searches, insertions, and deletions with constant average time.

metadata.title: Digital Circuit Design
metadata.definition: Principles and methods of designing electronic circuits that operate with digital signals.

metadata.title: Clocks
metadata.definition: Component that generates signals that synchronize activities in a computer system.

metadata.title: Bus
metadata.definition: A system of communication paths used to transmit data between computer components.

metadata.title: Register
metadata.definition: Small, high-speed memory cells inside the CPU are used to temporarily store data during processing.

metadata.title: Cache Memory
metadata.definition: Small, high-speed memory is used to store frequently accessed data to reduce main memory access time.

metadata.title: RAM
metadata.definition: Random access memory is the computer's main memory used to store running programs and data.

metadata.title: Secondary Memory
metadata.definition: Long-term and non-volatile data storage devices, such as hard drives, SSDs.

metadata.title: CPU
metadata.definition: The central processing unit, which is the 'brain' of the computer, performs most of the calculations and controls.

metadata.title: GPU
metadata.definition: Graphics processor, specialized for image and graphics processing, as well as parallel computing tasks.

metadata.title: Interrupt
metadata.definition: Signal sent to the CPU to pause the current job and handle an emergency event.

metadata.title: Threads
metadata.definition: The smallest unit of execution in a process, allowing a process to perform multiple tasks simultaneously.

metadata.title: Interrupt-driven Programming
metadata.definition: Programming method in which tasks are triggered and processed when an interrupt event occurs.

metadata.title: Thread-based Programming
metadata.definition: Programming method that uses multiple threads to execute different parts of a program simultaneously.

metadata.title: OS Scheduling
metadata.definition: The operating system function to manage and distribute CPU resources to processes or threads.

metadata.title: Scheduling Priority
metadata.definition: Technique of assigning priorities to processes or threads so that the operating system decides the order of execution.

metadata.title: Memory Fragmentation
metadata.definition: The state of memory being divided into many small, non-consecutive blocks, leading to wasted space even though the total capacity is free.

metadata.title: Latency
metadata.definition: The delay between the request for an activity and the start or completion of that activity.

metadata.title: Networking Basics
metadata.definition: Core unit of knowledge on the fundamentals of networking and communications, including the importance of networking, Internet architecture, switching techniques, layering, network components, and queuing concepts. This is a CS Core unit with 2.5 class hours.

metadata.title: Network Importance
metadata.definition: understand the central role networks play in modern computing systems and their contributions to everyday life, as well as the transformation they bring.

metadata.title: Networking Challenges
metadata.definition: understand current and future challenges in designing, deploying, managing, and securing large-scale and complex network systems.

metadata.title: Internet Organization
metadata.definition: Describes the overall structure and organization of the Internet, including its major components and their relationships.

metadata.title: Internet Users
metadata.definition: understand the role of end users in the Internet ecosystem and how they interact with network services and resources.

metadata.title: ISP
metadata.definition: Learn about the functions, roles and types of Internet Service Providers (ISPs) in providing network connectivity.

metadata.title: Autonomous System (AS)
metadata.definition: Concept and role of Autonomous Systems (AS) as independent administrative units participating in the global routing structure of the Internet.

metadata.title: Content Providers
metadata.definition: understand the role of content providers in creating, storing and distributing information and services on the Internet.

metadata.title: CDN
metadata.definition: Concepts, benefits, and basic operations of a Content Delivery Network (CDN) in increasing the speed and efficiency of web content delivery.

metadata.title: Switching Techniques
metadata.definition: Overview of the basic methods for transferring data over a network, including circuit switching and packet switching.

metadata.title: Circuit Switching
metadata.definition: Principle and application of circuit switching technique, where a dedicated path is permanently established for a communication session.

metadata.title: Packet Switching
metadata.definition: Principles and applications of packet switching technology, where data is divided into small packets and transmitted independently over the network.

metadata.title: Network Layers
metadata.definition: understand the network's layered architecture (for example, TCP/IP or OSI model) and the specific roles and functions of each layer.

metadata.title: Application Layer
metadata.definition: Functions and protocols of the application layer, where software applications interact directly with the network to provide services to users.

metadata.title: Transport Layer
metadata.definition: Transport layer functions and protocols, responsible for reliable or unreliable data transfer between processes on different hosts.

metadata.title: Network Layer
metadata.definition: Network layer functions and protocols, responsible for routing packets across the network from source to final destination.

metadata.title: Datalink Layer
metadata.definition: Functions and protocols of the data link layer, responsible for transmitting data frames between devices on the same local network (single-hop).

metadata.title: Physical Layer
metadata.definition: The function of the physical layer, responsible for transmitting raw data bits over a physical transmission medium (e.g., cable, radio waves).

metadata.title: Layering Principles
metadata.definition: understand the fundamental principles behind layered architecture in networks, including the benefits of abstraction and separation of functions.

metadata.title: Network Encapsulation
metadata.definition: Data encapsulation principle, where data from a higher layer is encapsulated with the current layer's header (and footer) when transmitted to lower layers.

metadata.title: Internet Hourglass Model
metadata.definition: Describes the hourglass model of the Internet protocol suite, highlighting the IP layer as the common core, supporting many technologies on the lower layer and many applications on the upper layer.

metadata.title: Network Components
metadata.definition: Identify and differentiate the basic types of devices and components that make up a computer network.

metadata.title: Router
metadata.definition: The function and operating principle of a router is to connect subnets and forward packets between them.

metadata.title: Switches
metadata.definition: The function and operating principle of a switch in connecting devices on the same local area network (LAN) effectively.

metadata.title: Hubs
metadata.definition: The function and limitations of a concentrator are as a basic networking device, operating at the physical layer.

metadata.title: Access Points (APs)
metadata.definition: The function of a wireless access point is to allow wireless devices to connect to a wired network.

metadata.title: Hosts
metadata.definition: The role of terminal devices such as computers, servers, smartphones, etc., in computer networks.

metadata.title: Network Queueing
metadata.definition: understand the basic concepts of queuing in networks and how they affect network performance.

metadata.title: Queueing & Latency
metadata.definition: analyze how wait times in the queues of network devices (e.g., routers) contribute to the overall latency of data transmission.

metadata.title: Queueing & Congestion
metadata.definition: understand how overqueuing and buffer overflow lead to network congestion and performance degradation.

metadata.title: Queueing & QoS
metadata.definition: Explore how priority and queue management policies can affect the level of service (QoS) provided to different types of network traffic.

metadata.title: Network Applications
metadata.definition: Core unit of knowledge about network applications, how they work, and the impact of network structures and protocols on the behavior of distributed applications. This is a CS Core unit with 3.5 hours of study.

metadata.title: Reliability Support
metadata.definition: Core unit of knowledge on the mechanisms and principles that ensure reliability in network communications, including error control, flow control, and congestion control. This is a KA Core unit with 5.75 hours of study.

metadata.title: Routing & Forwarding
metadata.definition: Core unit of knowledge on the principles and techniques of routing (determining paths) and forwarding (moving packets) in networks. This is a KA Core unit with 4 hours of study.

metadata.title: Single-Hop Communication
metadata.definition: Core unit of knowledge on the fundamentals of direct communication between two devices within a single network link. This is a KA Core unit with 3 class hours.

metadata.title: Mobility Support
metadata.definition: Core unit of knowledge on the concepts and technologies that support mobility in networks, including device-to-device communication and multi-hop wireless networks. This is a KA Core unit with 4 hours of study.

metadata.title: Network Security
metadata.definition: Core unit of knowledge on security aspects of computer networks, including threats, countermeasures and access control. This is a KA Core unit with 2.25 hours of study.

metadata.title: Emerging Topics
metadata.definition: Core units of knowledge on cutting-edge and evolving topics in networking and communications, such as network virtualization, quantum networks, and middleboxes. This is a KA Core unit with 4 hours of study.

metadata.title: Proprietary Networks
metadata.definition: The existence and role of large networks owned and operated by specific companies or organizations, often used for distributed computing, storage, and private content distribution.

metadata.title: Distributed Computing
metadata.definition: The concept of distributed computing, where tasks are broken down and performed across multiple computers in a network to achieve a common goal.

metadata.title: Network Storage
metadata.definition: Data storage solutions and technologies are accessed and managed over the network, allowing resources and data to be shared.

metadata.title: Content Delivery
metadata.definition: The methods and systems used to deliver content (e.g., videos, web pages, data) to end users efficiently and quickly.

metadata.title: Satellite Networks
metadata.definition: The technology and applications of the network use satellites to provide connectivity, especially to areas that are remote or difficult to reach through traditional infrastructure.

metadata.title: D2D Communication
metadata.definition: Principles and applications of direct communication between devices without the need for an access point or central server, commonly found in IoT.

metadata.title: IoT
metadata.definition: The concept of a network of physical devices, vehicles, appliances, and other objects embedded with sensors, software, and other technologies to connect and exchange data.

metadata.title: Network Naming
metadata.definition: Systems and methods used to name and identify resources or devices in a network, allowing them to be easily addressed and accessed.

metadata.title: Network Addressing
metadata.definition: Protocols and techniques used to assign and manage addresses (e.g., IP addresses, MAC addresses) to network devices, allowing routing and forwarding of data.

metadata.title: Network Reliability
metadata.definition: Principles and mechanisms that ensure that data is transmitted over a network accurately, completely, and in order, despite errors or interruptions.

metadata.title: Error Control
metadata.definition: Techniques are used to detect and correct errors that occur during data transmission over the network, ensuring data integrity.

metadata.title: Flow Control
metadata.definition: Mechanisms regulate the data transfer rate between sender and receiver to prevent the sender from overwhelming the receiver with too much data, avoiding packet loss.

metadata.title: Congestion Control
metadata.definition: Techniques to prevent and resolve network congestion, where data traffic exceeds the processing capacity of network links or nodes, to maintain stable performance.

metadata.title: Domain Hierarchy
metadata.definition: The hierarchical structure of the domain name system (Domain Name System - DNS) and how it organizes the management and resolution of domain names into IP addresses.

metadata.title: Routing
metadata.definition: The process of determining the best path for data packets from source to destination across a network linking different networks, using routing protocols.

metadata.title: Packet Forwarding
metadata.definition: The act of moving a data packet from an input port of a router or switch to an appropriate output port, based on routing information.

metadata.title: Modulation
metadata.definition: The process of transforming one or more properties of a carrier wave (for example, amplitude, frequency, phase) according to an information signal to transmit data over a transmission channel.

metadata.title: Network Encoding
metadata.definition: The process of converting data into a signal form suitable for transmission over a physical communication channel, including transmission encoding schemes.

metadata.title: Network Framing
metadata.definition: The process of packaging data bits into frames at the data link layer, including adding control and address bits for transmission over a specific physical link.

metadata.title: Network Access Control
metadata.definition: Mechanisms and policies to restrict access to network resources (e.g. servers, data, services) to authorized users or devices.

metadata.title: Network Security
metadata.definition: Overview of principles, technologies, and practices for protecting computer networks and data from threats, attacks, and unauthorized access.

metadata.title: Security Threats
metadata.definition: Identify and classify common types of threats to cybersecurity, e.g., denial of service (DoS) attacks, malware, intrusions, phishing.

metadata.title: Security Countermeasures
metadata.definition: Strategies, tools, and techniques used to minimize risk and protect networks from threats (e.g., firewalls, encryption, VPNs, intrusion detection/prevention systems).

metadata.title: Multi-hop Wireless
metadata.definition: The concept of a wireless network where data is transmitted through multiple intermediate nodes (multi-hop) before reaching the final destination, typically in ad-hoc or sensor networks.

metadata.title: Network Virtualization
metadata.definition: The principle and technology enable the creation of independent and isolated logical networks on the same physical network infrastructure, providing flexibility and efficiency.

metadata.title: Quantum Networking
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of quantum networks, using quantum mechanical principles for secure communication (e.g., quantum key distribution), and developing new applications in computing.

metadata.title: Middleboxes
metadata.definition: Devices or network functions that perform additional packet processing services beyond basic routing or forwarding, for example, firewalls, network address translators (NATs), load balancers.

metadata.title: SDN
metadata.definition: The concept of SDN, where the network control plane is decoupled from the data plane, enables flexible network configuration and management through centralized software.

metadata.title: Naming & Addressing Schemes
metadata.definition: Describes the principles and techniques used to name and address network resources, including systems such as DNS and Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs).

metadata.title: DNS
metadata.definition: understand the function, structure, and operation of the Domain Name System (DNS) in translating domain names into IP addresses.

metadata.title: URIs
metadata.definition: Learn about the concept, syntax, and purpose of Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) in identifying resources on a network.

metadata.title: Distributed Application Models
metadata.definition: Describes the basic architectural models for distributed applications, including how they interact and distribute work across multiple systems.

metadata.title: Client-Server Model
metadata.definition: understand the client/server architecture, in which the client requests a service from the server and the server provides that service.

metadata.title: P2P Model
metadata.definition: Learn about the P2P model, where nodes in the network can act as both clients and servers.

metadata.title: Cloud Computing Model
metadata.definition: The concept of cloud computing, services and architecture related to the provision of computing resources over a network.

metadata.title: Edge Computing
metadata.definition: understand edge computing, where data is processed closer to its source rather than sent to a cloud data center.

metadata.title: Fog Computing
metadata.definition: The concept of fog computing, an intermediate layer between edge and cloud computing, extends cloud services closer to the edge of the network.

metadata.title: Network App Requirements
metadata.definition: analyze the various requirements that network applications place on the network, including quality of service (QoS) factors.

metadata.title: Latency
metadata.definition: Impact of network latency on performance and user experience of applications.

metadata.title: Bandwidth
metadata.definition: The importance of network bandwidth for the data transfer ability of applications.

metadata.title: Fault Tolerance
metadata.definition: The degree to which applications can operate acceptably in the presence of packet loss in the network.

metadata.title: Application Layer Protocols
metadata.definition: Overview of the roles and functions of protocols operating at the application layer in network architecture.

metadata.title: HTTP
metadata.definition: Details about the HTTP protocol, how it works in exchanging data on the World Wide Web.

metadata.title: TCP, UDP, Socket API Interaction
metadata.definition: understand how network applications use transport layer protocols (TCP, UDP) and application programming interfaces (Socket APIs) to send and receive data.

metadata.title: TCP
metadata.definition: TCP's role as a reliable, connection-oriented transport protocol.

metadata.title: UDP
metadata.definition: UDP's role as an unreliable, connection-oriented transport protocol.

metadata.title: Socket API
metadata.definition: How to use Socket APIs for network programming, creating applications that communicate over the network.

metadata.title: Unreliable Delivery
metadata.definition: The concept of transmitting data without mechanisms to ensure arrival, order, or non-duplication, is commonly found in protocols such as UDP.

metadata.title: Network Reliability Principles
metadata.definition: The fundamentals for achieving reliability in network communications, including ensuring data is not lost, is not duplicated, and arrives in the correct order.

metadata.title: Error Control
metadata.definition: Techniques used to detect and correct errors during data transmission over a network.

metadata.title: Data Retransmission
metadata.definition: Mechanism to retransmit lost or corrupted data packets to ensure reliability.

metadata.title: Error Correction
metadata.definition: Data encryption methods so that the original data can be restored even if errors occur during transmission.

metadata.title: Flow Control
metadata.definition: Techniques that regulate the rate at which data is sent between two devices to prevent the recipient from being overloaded.

metadata.title: Stop and Wait Flow Control
metadata.definition: A simple flow control method in which the sender waits for acknowledgment from the receiver after each data packet.

metadata.title: Window-Based Flow Control
metadata.definition: The flow control method allows multiple data packets to be sent at the same time before receiving an acknowledgment, using the sliding window concept.

metadata.title: Congestion Control
metadata.definition: Strategies are used to prevent and handle congestion in the network to maintain performance.

metadata.title: Implicit Congestion Notification
metadata.definition: Detect congestion through indirect signs such as packet loss or increased latency.

metadata.title: ECN
metadata.definition: The mechanism allows routers to directly notify the sender of congestion without dropping the packet.

metadata.title: TCP Performance Issues
metadata.definition: Study the challenges and ways to optimize TCP protocol performance in different network environments.

metadata.title: TCP Tahoe
metadata.definition: One of the first versions of the TCP congestion control algorithm, including slow start, congestion avoidance, and fast recovery phases.

metadata.title: TCP Reno
metadata.definition: Upgraded version of TCP Tahoe, improving fast recovery after small packet loss.

metadata.title: TCP Vegas
metadata.definition: The TCP congestion control algorithm uses queuing delay to detect congestion early, instead of waiting for packet loss.

metadata.title: TCP CUBIC
metadata.definition: Modern TCP congestion control algorithm, designed to operate efficiently on high bandwidth and high latency networks.

metadata.title: Routing Models & Hierarchy
metadata.definition: Overview of the methods and hierarchies used to route packets in computer networks.

metadata.title: Intra-Domain Routing
metadata.definition: Routing protocols and techniques are used within a single Autonomous System (AS) domain.

metadata.title: Inter-Domain Routing
metadata.definition: Routing protocols and techniques are used to exchange routing information between different autonomous domains.

metadata.title: Centralized Routing
metadata.definition: Routing method in which a single central entity is responsible for calculating and distributing routes.

metadata.title: Decentralized Routing
metadata.definition: Routing method in which each router calculates its own routes based on local information and information exchanged with neighboring routers.

metadata.title: Source Routing
metadata.definition: A routing technique in which the sender specifies all or part of the path that the packet will take.

metadata.title: Virtual Circuit
metadata.definition: The concept of a pre-established logical path through the network for a data flow, ensuring some level of quality of service.

metadata.title: QoS Routing
metadata.definition: Routing is based on quality of service requirements such as bandwidth, latency, and packet loss.

metadata.title: Network Forwarding Methods
metadata.definition: The techniques and mechanisms that routers use to forward packets from the input port to the appropriate output port.

metadata.title: Forwarding Table
metadata.definition: The data structure that the router uses to store destination and output port information for packets.

metadata.title: Forwarding Match Algorithms
metadata.definition: Algorithms are used to look up the packet's destination address in the forwarding table and determine the appropriate output port.

metadata.title: IP Scalability Issues
metadata.definition: Research into Internet Protocol (IP) and scalability challenges as the Internet evolves, along with applicable solutions.

metadata.title: NAT
metadata.definition: The mechanism allows multiple devices in a private network to share a single public IP address, helping to solve the problem of IPv4 address exhaustion.

metadata.title: CIDR
metadata.definition: A more flexible method of IP address allocation and route aggregation to improve routing efficiency and reduce routing table size.

metadata.title: BGP
metadata.definition: The primary inter-domain routing protocol used on the Internet to exchange routing information between autonomous domains.

metadata.title: IP Versions
