metadata.definition: Compare and differentiate between versions of the Internet Protocol, mainly IPv4 and IPv6, in terms of addressing structure, features, and extensibility.

metadata.title: IPv4
metadata.definition: Details about the structure, packet format, and working mechanism of IPv4, the most popular version of IP.

metadata.title: IPv6
metadata.definition: Details of the structure, packet format and operating mechanism of IPv6, designed to replace IPv4 and solve the problem of address exhaustion.

metadata.title: Modulation Intro
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of modulation, the process of transforming information signals for transmission through physical media.

metadata.title: Media Bandwidth
metadata.definition: The concept of bandwidth is the maximum capacity of a channel to transmit data on a communication environment.

metadata.title: Transmission Media
metadata.definition: Different types of physical media are used to transmit network signals, for example copper cables, fiber optic cables, radio waves.

metadata.title: Data Encoding
metadata.definition: Methods of converting data into electrical or optical signals for transmission over a network.

metadata.title: Framing
metadata.definition: The process of dividing a data bit stream into separate frames for transmission over a physical channel, including adding a frame header and trailer.

metadata.title: MAC
metadata.definition: Protocols and rules govern how devices share the same communication medium to avoid conflicts.

metadata.title: Random Access MAC
metadata.definition: Media access methods allow devices to transfer data at any time, handling collisions if they occur (e.g. CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA).

metadata.title: Scheduled Access MAC
metadata.definition: Media access methods in which devices are authorized to transmit data according to a specific schedule, avoiding conflicts.

metadata.title: Ethernet
metadata.definition: Popular wired LAN standard, including different versions, frame structures, and operating mechanisms.

metadata.title: WiFi
metadata.definition: Wireless LAN standard (IEEE 802.11), including different operating modes, security, and versions.

metadata.title: Network Switching
metadata.definition: Operating mechanism of switching devices (switches) to forward data frames in the local network.

metadata.title: STP
metadata.definition: The protocol is used to prevent loops in an Ethernet switched network by creating a single spanning tree.

metadata.title: VLAN
metadata.definition: Concept of dividing a physical network into multiple logical networks (VLANs) to enhance security, performance, and management.

metadata.title: LAN Topologies
metadata.definition: Different physical and logical layouts of local area networks, affect performance and reliability.

metadata.title: Data Center Network
metadata.definition: The special architecture and requirements of the networks used in data centers to connect servers and storage devices.

metadata.title: Campus Network
metadata.definition: Network structure and management deployed over a limited geographic area such as a university campus or enterprise.

metadata.title: Network Security
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of cybersecurity, including types of threats, vulnerabilities, and common countermeasures.

metadata.title: Network Threats & Attacks
metadata.definition: analyze unique types of attacks and threats to network systems, how they operate, and their impact.

metadata.title: DoS Attack
metadata.definition: Attacks aim to overload systems or network services, making them unable to provide services to legitimate users.

metadata.title: Spoofing Attack
metadata.definition: Attacks in which an attacker impersonates a legitimate entity for fraud or unauthorized access.

metadata.title: Sniffing Attack
metadata.definition: Technique for gathering information by intercepting and analyzing network traffic passing through a point in the network.

metadata.title: Traffic Redirection Attack
metadata.definition: Attacks aim to redirect network traffic to an unwanted destination, often to intercept or modify data.

metadata.title: MITM Attack
metadata.definition: A type of attack in which an attacker intercepts and can modify communication between two parties without either party knowing.

metadata.title: Message Integrity Attack
metadata.definition: Attacks aim to modify or corrupt data during transmission to change the content or invalidate the message.

metadata.title: Routing Attack
metadata.definition: Attacks aim to manipulate routing information in the network to redirect traffic or cause congestion.

metadata.title: Ransomware
metadata.definition: The malware spreads through the network, encrypting data and demanding a ransom for decryption.

metadata.title: Traffic Analysis Attack
metadata.definition: Technique that monitors and analyzes network traffic patterns to deduce sensitive information without decrypting the content.

metadata.title: Network Security Countermeasures
metadata.definition: Collection of techniques, tools, and policies used to protect networks from threats and attacks.

metadata.title: Network Cryptography
metadata.definition: Application of cryptography to protect confidentiality, integrity and authentication in network communications.

metadata.title: SSL
metadata.definition: The security protocol was once used to establish secure communication channels over networks, a predecessor to TLS.

metadata.title: TLS
metadata.definition: Cryptographic protocols are used to provide communication security over computer networks, protecting the integrity and confidentiality of data.

metadata.title: Symmetric Cryptography
metadata.definition: Cryptographic algorithms use the same key for both encryption and decryption.

metadata.title: Asymmetric Cryptography
metadata.definition: Cryptographic algorithms use a pair of keys (public key and private key) for encryption and decryption.

metadata.title: Secure Network Architecture
metadata.definition: Architectural designs and models are used to build and deploy highly secure networks.

metadata.title: Secure Channel
metadata.definition: Communication channels are protected by encryption and other measures to ensure data security and integrity.

metadata.title: Secure Routing Protocol
metadata.definition: Routing protocols are designed with security mechanisms to protect against routing attacks.

metadata.title: DNSSEC
metadata.definition: Security measures are applied to DNS to protect the integrity and authenticity of DNS records.

metadata.title: VPN
metadata.definition: Technology that allows a secure connection to be made over a public network (such as the Internet) to access private network resources.

metadata.title: DMZ
metadata.definition: A physical or logical network segment that contains externally exposed services, designed to enhance the security of the internal network.

metadata.title: ZTNA
metadata.definition: A network security model based on the 'never trust, always verify' principle, requiring strict authentication and authorization for every access request.

metadata.title: Advanced Network Security
metadata.definition: Advanced cyber security concepts, often related to protection in highly distributed and complex environments.

metadata.title: Anonymous Communication Protocol
metadata.definition: Protocols are designed to protect the identities of users or parties participating in network communications.

metadata.title: Network Isolation
metadata.definition: Technique that separates parts of the network to limit the spread of attacks or unauthorized access.

metadata.title: Network Monitoring
metadata.definition: The process of monitoring and analyzing network traffic, performance, and events to detect unusual activity or threats.

metadata.title: IDS
metadata.definition: Systems monitor network and system activity to detect signs of attacks or policy violations.

metadata.title: Firewall
metadata.definition: Devices or software that control the flow of data into and out of a network based on defined security rules.

metadata.title: Anti-Spoofing Protection
metadata.definition: Techniques and measures to prevent attacks that spoof IP, MAC addresses, or other identifying information.

metadata.title: DoS Protection
metadata.definition: Measures and systems designed to detect, mitigate and prevent denial of service attacks.

metadata.title: Honeypots
metadata.definition: Systems or networks designed to attract and monitor attacker activity, gathering information about attack techniques.

metadata.title: Network Forensics
metadata.definition: Techniques and tools used to identify the origin of attacks or malicious traffic in a network.

metadata.title: BGPsec
metadata.definition: Security extensions to the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) to authenticate routing information and prevent routing attacks.

metadata.title: RPKI
metadata.definition: A public key-based system for authenticating ownership information of Internet resources (IP addresses and AS numbers), to enhance routing security.

metadata.title: Network Countermeasures
metadata.definition: Describes specific network-based countermeasures deployed to combat security threats.

metadata.title: Network Security Case Studies
metadata.definition: analyze different aspects of cyber security through real-life case studies.

metadata.title: Mobile Communication Principles
metadata.definition: The fundamentals of mobile communication, including technologies such as 4G and 5G.

metadata.title: Mobile Communication Registration
metadata.definition: Describe aspects of the registration process in mobile communication.

metadata.title: Wireless LAN Principles (802.11)
metadata.definition: The fundamentals of wireless local area networks, primarily focusing on the 802.11 (Wi-Fi) standard, including how to support mobile users.

metadata.title: Device-to-Device (D2D) Communication
metadata.definition: Principles of direct communication between devices, such as communication in IoT.

metadata.title: D2D Communication Applications
metadata.definition: Describe practical applications of direct communication between devices.

metadata.title: Multi-hop Wireless Networks
metadata.definition: The principles and architecture of wireless networks where data is transmitted over multiple hops, including ad hoc networks, opportunistic networks, and delay-tolerant networks.

metadata.title: Multi-hop Network Applications
metadata.definition: Describe practical applications of multihop wireless networks, such as ad hoc networks.

metadata.title: Middleboxes
metadata.definition: Intermediate network devices perform additional functions beyond basic routing, including advances in the use of AI, intent-based networking, filtering, deep packet inspection, load balancing, NAT, and CDN.

metadata.title: AI in Middleboxes
metadata.definition: Advances in the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in intermediate network devices.

metadata.title: Intent-Based Networking (IBN)
metadata.definition: The concept and principles of intent-based networking enable network management through business objectives rather than specific device configurations.

metadata.title: Packet Filtering
metadata.definition: Packet filtering is performed by intermediate network devices for traffic control or security.

metadata.title: Deep Packet Inspection (DPI)
metadata.definition: Technique that examines the detailed content of network packets to perform security, traffic management, or analysis functions.

metadata.title: Load Balancing
metadata.definition: The function of distributing network traffic among multiple servers or resources to optimize usage and avoid overload, performed by intermediate network devices.

metadata.title: Network Address Translation (NAT)
metadata.definition: The technique of mapping private IP addresses to public IP addresses, and vice versa, is used to preserve IP addresses and provide a basic layer of security.

metadata.title: Content Delivery Network (CDN)
metadata.definition: The server system distributes web and multimedia content to end users based on geographical location, to increase access speed and reduce load on the origin server.

metadata.title: Network Virtualization
metadata.definition: Concepts and principles of network virtualization, including technologies such as SDN and data center networks.

metadata.title: Software-Defined Networking (SDN)
metadata.definition: The network architecture separates the control plane from the data plane, allowing flexible network management and configuration through software.

metadata.title: Data Center Networking
metadata.definition: Network architecture and technology specifically designed for data centers to support high traffic and virtualized applications.

metadata.title: Quantum Networks
metadata.definition: An introduction to the field of quantum networks, including concepts such as quantum teleportation, quantum security, and the quantum Internet.

metadata.title: Quantum Teleportation
metadata.definition: The concept of quantum teleportation in the context of quantum networks.

metadata.title: Quantum Network Security
metadata.definition: Security issues and solutions related to quantum networks.

metadata.title: Quantum Internet
metadata.definition: The concept and potential of an Internet based on quantum principles.

metadata.title: Satellite Communication
metadata.definition: Principles and applications of satellite communication.

metadata.title: Millimeter Wave (mmWave) Communication
metadata.definition: Wireless communication technology uses the millimeter wave band, often used in 5G.

metadata.title: Visible Light Communication (VLC)
metadata.definition: Communication technology that uses visible light to transmit data wirelessly.

metadata.title: Probability (Networking Math)
metadata.definition: Basic probability concepts and techniques essential for the field of Networking and Communications.

metadata.title: Statistics (Networking Math)
metadata.definition: Basic statistical concepts and techniques essential for the field of Networking and Communications.

metadata.title: Discrete Math (Networking Math)
metadata.definition: Basic discrete mathematics concepts and techniques essential for the field of Networking and Communications.

metadata.title: Linear Algebra (Networking Math)
metadata.definition: Basic linear algebra concepts and techniques essential for the field of Networking and Communications.

metadata.title: Queueing Theory Basics
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of queuing theory, used to analyze network performance.

metadata.title: Networking Basics (Introductory)
metadata.definition: Foundational concepts and fundamentals of computer networking for an introductory course.

metadata.title: Network Applications (Introductory)
metadata.definition: The types of applications that operate on networks and how they interact with network protocols for an introductory course.

metadata.title: Network Reliability (Introductory)
metadata.definition: Mechanisms and principles for ensuring reliability in network communications for an introductory course.

metadata.title: Routing & Forwarding (Introductory)
metadata.definition: Principles, algorithms, and protocols used to route and forward packets in networks for an introductory course.

metadata.title: Single-hop Communication (Introductory)
metadata.definition: Principles and mechanisms of direct, multi-hop device-to-device communication for an introductory course.

metadata.title: Network Mobility (Introductory)
metadata.definition: Issues and solutions related to supporting users and mobile devices in networks for introductory courses.

metadata.title: Network Security (Introductory)
metadata.definition: Principles, techniques, and mechanisms for protecting networks from threats and attacks for an introductory course.

metadata.title: Networking SEP Context
metadata.definition: Social, ethical and professional issues related to the field of Networking and Communications.

metadata.title: Emerging Networking Topics (Introductory)
metadata.definition: Emerging technologies and trends in the field of computer networking for an introductory course.

metadata.title: Networking Basics (Advanced)
metadata.definition: Foundational concepts and fundamentals of computer networks at an advanced level.

metadata.title: Network Applications (Advanced)
metadata.definition: The types of applications that operate on the network and how they interact with network protocols at an advanced level.

metadata.title: Network Reliability (Advanced)
metadata.definition: Mechanisms and principles to ensure reliability in network communications at an advanced level.

metadata.title: Routing & Forwarding (Advanced)
metadata.definition: The principles, algorithms, and protocols used to route and forward packets in networks at an advanced level.

metadata.title: Single-hop Communication (Advanced)
metadata.definition: The principles and mechanisms of direct communication between devices without requiring multiple hops at an advanced level.

metadata.title: Network Mobility (Advanced)
metadata.definition: Issues and solutions related to supporting users and mobile devices in the network at an advanced level.

metadata.title: Network Security (Advanced)
metadata.definition: Principles, techniques, and mechanisms to protect networks from advanced threats and attacks.

metadata.title: Privacy (SEP)
metadata.definition: Issues related to privacy in the context of technology and networks, from a social, ethical and professional perspective (as part of the total 2 hours of SEP topics in the advanced course).

metadata.title: Security (SEP)
metadata.definition: Security aspects from a social, ethical and professional perspective, in relation to technology and networks (as part of the total 2 hours of SEP topics in the advanced course).

metadata.title: Sustainability (SEP)
metadata.definition: Sustainability issues related to technology and networks, from a social, ethical and professional perspective (as part of the total 2 hours of SEP topics in the advanced course).

metadata.title: Emerging Networking Topics (Advanced)
metadata.definition: Emerging technologies and trends in the field of computer networking at an advanced level.

metadata.title: Software & Systems Development
metadata.definition: Foundational knowledge of how to develop software, computer systems (including operating systems) and applications, is the minimum requirement for all Computer Science graduates according to CS Core standards of CS2023.

metadata.title: Beyond Professional Ethics
metadata.definition: understand and act on broader responsibilities beyond those in the professional code of ethics, including global competencies, culture, and an awareness of the importance and impact of local values ​​and practices.

metadata.title: Global & Cultural Competence
metadata.definition: Ability to understand, interact and work effectively in multicultural and global environments, with an awareness of differences in values ​​and practices.

metadata.title: Local Values Impact
metadata.definition: understand the importance and impact of local values, priorities and practices around the world on work and professional responsibilities.

metadata.title: Maximize Computing Benefits
metadata.definition: Strive to ensure that computer technology provides maximum benefit to society at large.

metadata.title: Prevent Computing Harm
metadata.definition: Act to protect individuals from negative or harmful effects that may arise from the use or development of computer technology.

metadata.title: Professional Dispositions
metadata.definition: A set of essential attitudes, values ​​and personal characteristics that help a professional not only succeed at work but also thrive in the long term.

metadata.title: CS Adaptability
metadata.definition: Ability to continuously adjust and learn to adapt to the constant evolution of computer science.

metadata.title: CS Collaboration
metadata.definition: Skills to work effectively with others on group projects, as most real-world applications are team efforts.

metadata.title: CS Creativity
metadata.definition: Ability to think creatively to develop new solutions and apply existing solutions to new contexts.

metadata.title: Solution Diligence
metadata.definition: Care and attention to detail ensure the correctness and completeness of solutions.

metadata.title: Computational Persistence
metadata.definition: The ability to persevere through difficulties and challenges in solving computational problems, which is an iterative process.

metadata.title: Proactive Problem Solving
metadata.definition: Ability to proactively anticipate and resolve potential issues related to usability, security, ethics, etc., before they arise.

metadata.title: Solution Lifecycle Responsibility
metadata.definition: Demonstrate responsibility in all aspects of a technology solution, including the design, implementation and maintenance phases.

metadata.title: CS Lifelong Learning
metadata.definition: Ability to self-learn, self-direct self-development and commitment to lifelong learning to adapt to the rapid development of computer science.

metadata.title: CS Education Diversity
metadata.definition: Computer Science education has been facing a long-standing challenge of diversity in participation. The industry benefits from the active participation of all classes and all demographic groups, regardless of demographic identity. CS2023 recommends that programs strive to convey the message that Computer Science belongs to everyone and promote active participation by all populations. The CS2023 guidelines include a practice paper on accessibility in computer science education.

metadata.title: CS Professional Skills
metadata.definition: Employers are always looking for professional qualities (often called soft skills) such as perseverance, self-direction and adaptability in graduates. CS2023 emphasizes the need to clarify this, which has always been implicit, so that students are aware of the importance of these qualities for future career success and develop them during their studies. In CS2023, the most relevant professional qualities have been identified in each knowledge area.

metadata.title: CS Faculty Resource Pressure
metadata.definition: At many educational institutions, explosive growth in student numbers has put significant pressure on faculty resources, as reflected in class sizes and course loads. Managing faculty workloads is critical to ensuring the vitality of faculty, both in terms of the quality of their teaching and their professional development.

metadata.title: CS Faculty Recruitment & Retention
metadata.definition: Recruiting and retaining faculty is a significant challenge, especially given the high demand for graduates with advanced degrees in Computer Science. A prominent trend over the past decade is the formation of a team of lecturers dedicated to teaching. Educational institutions must find a balance between meeting teaching needs and supporting professional development for lecturers to ensure they keep their knowledge updated and maintain their enthusiasm.

metadata.title: CS Curriculum Evolution
metadata.definition: Computer Science is a rapidly evolving industry, bringing both new opportunities and associated challenges. Updating courses and curricula to keep up with the times requires significant resources from computer science educators and should be recognized and supported. CS2023 has highlighted emerging technologies and significantly expanded the rapidly growing sectors to meet this challenge.

metadata.title: Quantum Computing
metadata.definition: Quantum computing is highlighted by CS2023 as an emerging technology that Computer Science curricula need to consider. A hands-on article on quantum computing education has been included in the CS2023 guide.

metadata.title: Machine Learning
metadata.definition: Machine learning is a rapidly growing field in Computer Science and has been significantly expanded in the CS2023 curriculum guidelines, reflecting its growing importance in the industry.

metadata.title: Generative AI in CS Education
metadata.definition: Discusses the potential of generative AI to revolutionize computer science education, including impact on course content, pedagogy, and assessment techniques. This is a general principle that applies to the design and teaching of courses in all fields, including Operating Systems.

metadata.title: Generative AI Education Challenges
metadata.definition: Exploiting generative AI to serve the goals of formal education is one of the most important challenges facing the community over the next few years. This also applies to how AI is integrated and used in teaching and learning topics related to Operating Systems.

metadata.title: Generative AI Impact on CS KAs
metadata.definition: CS2023 includes a chapter that lists well-founded speculations about the implications of generative AI for various fields of knowledge. This includes predictions about how generative AI could influence the content and methods of teaching in the field of Operating Systems.

metadata.title: Generative AI in Intro Programming
metadata.definition: CS2023 includes a curriculum practice article on the implications of generative AI for introductory programming. Introductory programming is fundamental to many aspects of computer science, including understanding and developing Operating System components.

metadata.title: CS Math & Theory Foundation
metadata.definition: Emphasize that theoretical and mathematical foundations are core to what makes computer science a science and are essential for long-term career success. For Operating Systems, this includes understanding algorithms, data structures, and underlying theoretical models.

metadata.title: CS Theory vs. Tools Balance
metadata.definition: Discuss the challenge of finding the right balance between the goals of providing a solid theoretical/mathematical foundation and equipping students with tool/technology skills for immediate employability. This is a challenge common to all areas of knowledge, including Operating Systems, where both theory (e.g., process management) and practice (e.g., using debugging tools) are important.

metadata.title: Growing CS Math Demand
metadata.definition: Recognizes the growing need for mathematics in computer science (e.g., in machine learning) and the frequent inadequate mathematical preparation of students entering programs. This is an important consideration for curriculum design, including for Operating Systems courses that involve optimization or performance analysis.

metadata.title: CS2023 KA Math Requirements
metadata.definition: CS2023 has separately identified mathematics requirements for each knowledge area, including Operating Systems, to provide flexibility in the curriculum to accommodate varying levels of student preparation.

metadata.title: Flexible CS Math Requirements
metadata.definition: CS2023 provides flexibility so that students with limited mathematics proficiency can better navigate the curriculum. Instructors may require a prerequisite mathematics course or teach required mathematics as part of a computer science course, applicable to subjects with specific mathematics requirements such as Operating Systems.

metadata.title: Integrate Socio-Ethical Issues
metadata.definition: Emphasize that a computer solution is not just technical but must also incorporate social, ethical, and professional considerations. This is a fundamental principle that applies to the design and implementation of systems, including Operating Systems, where design decisions can have far-reaching impacts.

metadata.title: Integrating Ethics in Technical CS
metadata.definition: Identify the challenge of integrating social, ethical, and professional issues into the technical coverage of the curriculum so that they become inevitable. This is the responsibility of every educator, which applies to the teaching of technical subjects such as Operating Systems, where issues of privacy, security, and equity may arise.

metadata.definition: Values, beliefs, and attitudes can change, helping to shape desirable workplace behaviors (e.g., persistence, self-direction). They are essential factors for success at work and are sought after by employers.

metadata.title: Persistence
metadata.definition: A professional quality that demonstrates perseverance, not giving up in the face of difficulties, is considered essential at the introductory level of study.

metadata.title: Self-Direction
metadata.definition: A professional quality that demonstrates the ability to self-manage studies and work, and independently solve problems, is expected at advanced levels of study.

metadata.title: Good Communication
metadata.definition: A professional quality refers to the willingness and intention to apply communication skills to complete tasks.

metadata.title: Collaboration
metadata.definition: A professional quality that refers to the willingness and intention to apply collaborative skills to complete tasks, especially needed for group projects.

metadata.title: Meticulousness
metadata.definition: A professional quality that demonstrates care and attention to detail, required for fields requiring a mathematical background.

metadata.title: Curriculum Competency Model
metadata.definition: Curriculum patterns in which the knowledge, skills, and professional qualities needed to perform a task are grouped together.

metadata.title: CS Core
metadata.definition: Topics every computer science graduate is required to know. Every computer science curriculum is expected to cover all of these topics.

metadata.title: KA Core
metadata.definition: Topics are recommended for further study in a specific Knowledge Area, providing further specialization beyond CS Core topics.

metadata.title: Non-core Topics
metadata.definition: Topics are classified as electives, not in the CS Core or KA Core categories, allowing students to choose by interest or major.

metadata.title: GIT
metadata.definition: Knowledge area of ​​Graphics and Interactive Techniques (GIT) in the CS2023 program.

metadata.title: IAS (CS2013)
metadata.definition: The Information Assurance and Security (IAS) knowledge area in the CS2013 program, was renamed Security (SEC) in CS2023.

metadata.title: SEC (CS2023)
metadata.definition: The Security (SEC) knowledge area in the CS2023 program, is the new name of Information Assurance and Security (IAS) from CS2013.

metadata.title: IM (CS2013)
metadata.definition: The Information Management (IM) knowledge area in the CS2013 program, was renamed Data Management (DM) in CS2023.

metadata.title: DM (CS2023)
metadata.definition: The Data Management (DM) knowledge area in the CS2023 program is the new name of Information Management (IM) from CS2013.

metadata.title: IS (CS2013)
metadata.definition: The knowledge field of Intelligent Systems (IS) in the CS2013 program, was renamed Artificial Intelligence (AI) in CS2023.

metadata.title: AI (CS2023)
metadata.definition: The field of knowledge of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the CS2023 program, is the new name of Intelligent Systems (IS) from CS2013.

metadata.title: PBD (CS2013)
metadata.definition: The Platform Based Development (PBD) knowledge area in the CS2013 program, was renamed to Specialized Platform Development (SPD) in CS2023.

metadata.title: SPD (CS2023)
metadata.definition: The Specialized Platform Development (SPD) knowledge area in the CS2023 program, is the new name for Platform-based Development (PBD) from CS2013.

metadata.title: PL (CS2013)
metadata.definition: The Programming Languages ​​(PL) knowledge area in the CS2013 program, was renamed Programming Languages ​​Foundation (FPL) in CS2023.

metadata.title: FPL (CS2023)
metadata.definition: The knowledge area of ​​Foundations of Programming Languages ​​(FPL) in the CS2023 program is the new name of Programming Language (PL) from CS2013.

metadata.title: SP (CS2013)
metadata.definition: The knowledge area Social Issues and Professional Practice (SP) in the CS2013 program, was renamed Society, Ethics and Professional Practice (SEP) in CS2023.

metadata.title: SEP (CS2023)
metadata.definition: The knowledge area of ​​Society, Ethics, and the Profession (SEP) in the CS2023 program is the new name of Social Issues and Professional Practice (SP) from CS2013.

metadata.title: Computational Science (Deprecated)
metadata.definition: The Computational Science (CN) knowledge area from CS2013 has been removed from the CS2023 curriculum because there is very little computer science content that does not overlap with other knowledge areas. In CS2013, it is allocated 1 core hour for modeling and simulation.

metadata.title: Modeling & Simulation
metadata.definition: A core topic is allocated 1 hour of study in the Computational Science (CN) area of ​​CS2013.

metadata.title: Modeling Application
metadata.definition: Modeling applications are considered a cross-cutting topic in computer science.

metadata.title: Modeling Research
metadata.definition: Modeling research as it stands is seen as more relevant in the CS+X (Computer Science combined with other fields) space, rather than as a core area of ​​knowledge.

metadata.title: CS + X
metadata.definition: The concept of the CS+X space, where the principles of computer science are applied or studied in conjunction with other fields.

metadata.title: CS Math
metadata.definition: The role of the mathematical component in computer science has been expanded in CS2023, reflecting its increase in importance.

metadata.title: Discrete Structures (CS2013)
metadata.definition: One of the main mathematical components in the CS2013 curriculum, now part of the Mathematical and Statistical Foundations (MSF) in CS2023.

metadata.title: Probability (MSF)
metadata.definition: New mathematics component added to the Mathematical and Statistical Foundations (MSF) area in CS2023.

metadata.title: Statistics (MSF)
metadata.definition: New mathematics component added to the Mathematical and Statistical Foundations (MSF) area in CS2023.

metadata.title: Linear Algebra (MSF)
metadata.definition: New mathematics component added to the Mathematical and Statistical Foundations (MSF) area in CS2023.

metadata.title: MSF (CS2023)
metadata.definition: The Mathematical and Statistical Foundations (MSF) knowledge area in CS2023, expands from CS2013's Discrete Structures to include probability, statistics, and linear algebra.

metadata.title: SEP
metadata.definition: One of the key Knowledge Areas (KAs) in the CS2023 syllabus, focusing on ethical issues, social responsibility, and professional aspects of the computer science profession.

metadata.title: HCI
metadata.definition: One of the Knowledge Areas (KAs) listed in the CS2023 syllabus is the study of the design and use of computer systems that interact well with humans.

metadata.title: MSF
metadata.definition: One of the Knowledge Areas (KAs) listed in the CS2023 syllabus, covering the foundational and in-depth knowledge of mathematics and statistics required for other areas of computer science.

metadata.title: Systems Fundamentals (SF)
metadata.definition: One of the Knowledge Areas (KAs) listed in the CS2023 syllabus, focusing on the fundamental principles and concepts of how computer systems are structured and operate.

metadata.title: Specialized Platform Development (SPD)
metadata.definition: One of the Knowledge Areas (KAs) listed in the CS2023 syllabus, involves the development of applications and solutions on specialized technology platforms.

metadata.title: KA Definition (CS2023)
metadata.definition: In the CS2023 syllabus, a Knowledge Area is expanded to include Learning Units and Career Trends. Formula: Knowledge Area = {Knowledge Units} + {Career Trends}.

metadata.title: Knowledge Unit
metadata.definition: Specific knowledge blocks make up a Knowledge Area in the CS2023 curriculum.

metadata.title: Professional Trends
metadata.definition: These are values, beliefs and attitudes that can be changed, helping to form consistent and desirable behaviors in the work environment. They are sought after by employers and essential to career success.

metadata.title: Persistence Trend
metadata.definition: A desirable career trend, demonstrating perseverance and persistence in work. Especially considered an essential element at the introductory level for students.

metadata.title: Self-Direction Trend
metadata.definition: A desirable career trend, demonstrating the ability to self-manage and orient work independently. Expected at advanced levels of study and research.

metadata.title: Communication Trend
metadata.definition: A desirable career trend, which refers to the willingness and intention to apply effective communication skills to complete tasks.

metadata.title: Collaboration Trend
metadata.definition: A desirable career orientation, which refers to the willingness and intention to work together to complete tasks, especially important in group projects.

metadata.title: Competency Model
metadata.definition: Curriculum patterns in which the knowledge, skills, and career dispositions needed to perform a task are grouped together.

metadata.title: Meticulousness Trend
metadata.definition: A desirable career trend, demonstrating care and attention to detail, especially needed when working with mathematical foundations.

metadata.title: CS Core Topics
metadata.definition: Required topics that every computer science graduate must master. Every computer science curriculum is expected to cover all core CS topics.

metadata.title: KA Core Topics
metadata.definition: Recommended topics for more in-depth study in a specific Area of ​​Knowledge. They complement the core CS topics.

metadata.title: Non-Core Topics
metadata.definition: Optional or elective topics in the CS2023 curriculum, not in the CS Core or KA Core categories.

metadata.title: MSF
metadata.definition: The foundational knowledge area of ​​mathematics and statistics is the mainstay of modern computer science education. MSF inherits the 'Discrete Structures' area of ​​ACM CS2013 and covers mathematical and statistical topics essential to growing fields such as artificial intelligence, machine learning, data science and quantum computing.

metadata.title: Discrete Structures
metadata.definition: The mathematics literacy area, covered in the ACM CS2013 report, was the predecessor to the current MSF area. Although still an important part, the range of mathematics required for modern computer science has expanded beyond just discrete structures.

metadata.title: Continuous Math
metadata.definition: The field of mathematics underpins many recent burgeoning computer science fields such as artificial intelligence, machine learning, data science, and quantum computing. It is emphasized that it is necessary along with discrete structures.

metadata.title: Probability
metadata.definition: An important area of ​​mathematics, proposed to be concentrated in modern computer science programs. It is rated 98% for importance for careers in industry and graduate study, especially essential for AI, machine learning, robotics, data science and quantum computing.

metadata.title: Statistics
metadata.definition: An important field of statistics, it is proposed to be concentrated in modern computer science programs. It is rated 98% for importance for careers in industry and graduate study, especially essential for AI, machine learning, robotics, data science and quantum computing.

metadata.title: Linear Algebra
metadata.definition: An important area of ​​mathematics, proposed to be concentrated in modern computer science programs. It is rated 89% in importance for careers in industry and graduate study, with particular importance for AI, machine learning, robotics, data science and quantum computing.

metadata.title: Discrete Math (CS Core)
metadata.definition: The fundamentals of discrete mathematics, considered a core requirement for all Computer Science (CS) majors. Total 29 hours of study.

metadata.title: Discrete Math (KA Core)
metadata.definition: More in-depth knowledge of discrete mathematics complements CS Core to form a standard 40-hour course. Total 11 class hours.

metadata.title: Probability (CS Core)
metadata.definition: The basics of probability reflect a strong consensus in the academic community about its importance. Total 11 class hours.

metadata.title: Probability (KA Core)
metadata.definition: More in-depth knowledge of probability complements CS Core to form a standard 40-hour course. Total 29 hours of study.

metadata.title: Statistics Basics (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Introduces basic definitions in statistics, including becoming familiar with terms such as mean and standard deviation. Total 10 hours of study.

metadata.title: Statistics (KA Core)
metadata.definition: More in-depth knowledge of statistics complements CS Core to create a standard 40-hour course. Total 30 hours of study.

metadata.title: Linear Algebra Basics (CS Core)
metadata.definition: Introduces basic definitions in linear algebra, including becoming familiar with terms such as vectors. Total 5 class hours.

metadata.title: Linear Algebra (KA Core)
metadata.definition: More in-depth knowledge of linear algebra complements CS Core to form a standard 40-hour course. Total 35 hours of study.

metadata.title: Calculus I (KA Core)
metadata.definition: Standard Calculus I course, corresponding to the requirements of most academic programs. Total 40 hours of study.

metadata.title: Calculus II
metadata.definition: The Calculus II course, which is an additional option (40 hours) for programs seeking to strengthen calculus requirements, is not required.

metadata.title: Calculus-based Probability
metadata.definition: The probability course requires calculus knowledge, for programs that want a more rigorous and in-depth approach.

metadata.title: Calculus-based Statistics
metadata.definition: The statistics course series requires calculus knowledge, for programs that want a more rigorous and in-depth approach.

metadata.title: Non-Calculus Probability
metadata.definition: Probability versions do not require calculus knowledge, an option for programs.

metadata.title: Non-Calculus Statistics
metadata.definition: Statistics course versions do not require calculus knowledge, an option for programs.

metadata.title: Applied Linear Algebra (Non-Calculus)
metadata.definition: An application-focused linear algebra course, with no calculus prerequisite, is one way to take the KA Core section.

metadata.title: Advanced Linear Algebra
metadata.definition: An advanced linear algebra course, which may require calculus or deeper knowledge, is one way to take the KA Core or go beyond.

metadata.title: Set Theory, Relations, Functions
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of sets, relations, functions, and the calculation of sets, including operations, sum/product rules, the inclusion-exclusion principle, and distinguishing between finite, countable, and uncountable sets.

metadata.title: Recursive Definitions
metadata.definition: apply recursive definitions to sequences and structures (e.g., Fibonacci numbers, linked lists, parse trees, fractals), solve basic recursive relationships, and prove by induction the recursive definitions. Contact recursive/iterative code, describe and prove closed form for recursive relationships.

metadata.title: Proof Techniques
metadata.definition: Basic proof techniques include direct proof, proof by contradiction, and proof by induction (mathematical and structural), how to correctly identify and apply them, and choosing the appropriate technique for each problem.

metadata.title: Permutations, Combinations, Counting
metadata.definition: Basic concepts and techniques in counting, including permutations, combinations, and applications of the pigeonhole principle.

metadata.title: Modular Arithmetic
metadata.definition: Principles and operations in modulo arithmetic.

metadata.title: Logic Fundamentals
metadata.definition: Basic concepts of logic, including truth tables, joins (operators), rules of inference, formulas, normal forms, and simple predicate logic.

metadata.title: Graph Theory Basics
metadata.definition: Basic definitions related to graph theory.

metadata.title: Order Notation
metadata.definition: Introduction to order notation (Big O, Big Omega, Big Theta) used to describe algorithm performance.

metadata.title: Mean (Statistics)
metadata.definition: Basic concept of mean value in statistics, a term that students should be familiar with in CS Core.

metadata.title: Standard Deviation (Statistics)
metadata.definition: Basic concept of standard deviation in statistics, a term students should be familiar with in CS Core.

metadata.title: Vectors (Linear Algebra)
metadata.definition: The basics of vectors in linear algebra, a term students should be familiar with in CS Core.

metadata.title: Structural Induction
metadata.definition: The concept of structural induction and its relationship to recursion and recursively defined structures.

metadata.title: Weak vs. Strong Induction
metadata.definition: Explain the relationship between weak induction and strong induction.

metadata.title: Weak Induction Applications
metadata.definition: Give an example of how to use weak induction appropriately.

metadata.title: Strong Induction Applications
metadata.definition: Give an example of how to use strong induction appropriately.

metadata.title: Counting Methods
metadata.definition: apply counting reasoning methods.

metadata.title: Sum Rule (Counting)
metadata.definition: apply addition rules in counting problems.

metadata.title: Product Rule (Counting)
metadata.definition: apply the multiplication rule in counting problems.

metadata.title: Inclusion-Exclusion Principle
metadata.definition: apply the inclusion-exclusion principle.

metadata.title: Arithmetic Progression (Counting)
metadata.definition: apply arithmetic progressions in counting problems.

metadata.title: Geometric Progression (Counting)
metadata.definition: apply exponential progression in counting problems.

metadata.title: Pigeonhole Principle
metadata.definition: apply the pigeonhole principle in the context of a formal proof.

metadata.title: Permutation Calculation
metadata.definition: Perform permutation calculations of a set.

metadata.title: Combination Calculation
metadata.definition: Perform combinatorial calculations of a set.

metadata.title: Permutation/Combination Interpretation
metadata.definition: Interpret the meaning of permutation and combination in the context of a specific application.

metadata.title: Mapping Real-world to Counting
metadata.definition: Mapping real-world applications to appropriate formal counting methods.

metadata.title: Counting with Constraints
metadata.definition: Determine the number of ways to arrange people around the table, subject to seating arrangement constraints.

metadata.title: Counting Card Hands
metadata.definition: Determines the number of ways to get certain decks of cards (e.g. full flood).

metadata.title: Modular Arithmetic Operations
metadata.definition: Perform calculations involving modulo arithmetic.

metadata.title: Greatest Common Divisor (GCD)
metadata.definition: Explain the concept of greatest common divisor (GCD).

metadata.title: Euclidean Algorithm
metadata.definition: apply Euclid's algorithm to calculate the greatest common divisor (GCD).

metadata.title: Natural Language to Propositional Logic
metadata.definition: Converts logic statements from ordinary language to propositional logic expressions.

metadata.title: Natural Language to Predicate Logic
metadata.definition: Converts logic statements from ordinary language to predicate logic expressions.

metadata.title: Formal Methods (Propositional Logic)
metadata.definition: apply formal methods of symbolic propositional logic.

metadata.title: Formal Methods (Predicate Logic)
metadata.definition: apply formal methods of symbolic predicate logic.

metadata.title: Logic Formula Validity
metadata.definition: Calculate the validity of formulas in propositional and predicate logic.

metadata.title: Logic Normal Forms
metadata.definition: Calculate normal forms of logical expressions.

metadata.title: Negating Logic Statements
metadata.definition: Negation of a logical statement.

metadata.title: Inference Rules (Propositional Logic)
metadata.definition: Use rules of inference to construct proofs in propositional logic.

metadata.title: Inference Rules (Predicate Logic)
metadata.definition: Use inference rules to construct proofs in predicate logic.

metadata.title: Modeling with Symbolic Logic
metadata.definition: Describe how symbolic logic can be used to model real-life situations or applications.

metadata.title: Symbolic Logic in Software Analysis
metadata.definition: Describe applications of symbolic logic in software analysis, such as proving the correctness of a program.

metadata.title: Symbolic Logic in Database Queries
metadata.definition: Describe the application of symbolic logic in database queries.

metadata.title: Symbolic Logic in Algorithms
metadata.definition: Describe the application of symbolic logic in algorithms.

metadata.title: Formal Logic Proofs for Real Problems
metadata.definition: apply formal logic proofs to real-world problems, such as predicting software behavior.

metadata.title: Informal Logic for Real Problems
metadata.definition: apply informal but rigorous logical reasoning to real-world problems, such as solving puzzles.

metadata.title: Predicting Software Behavior (Logic)
metadata.definition: Use logic to predict software behavior.

metadata.title: Logic Puzzles
metadata.definition: Use logic to solve puzzles.

metadata.title: Propositional Logic Advantages
metadata.definition: Describe the advantages of propositional logic.

metadata.title: Propositional Logic Limitations
metadata.definition: Describe the limitations of propositional logic.

metadata.title: Predicate Logic Advantages
metadata.definition: Describe the advantages of predicate logic.

metadata.title: Predicate Logic Limitations
metadata.definition: Describe the limitations of predicate logic.

metadata.title: Prop. Logic Proof Validity
metadata.definition: Explain what it means for a proof in propositional logic to be valid.

metadata.title: Pred. Logic Proof Validity
metadata.definition: Explain what it means for a proof in predicate logic to be valid.

metadata.title: Graph Theory Basics
metadata.definition: Illustrate with examples the basic terms of graph theory.

metadata.title: Graph Properties
metadata.definition: Illustrate with examples some properties of graph types.

metadata.title: Special Graph Cases
metadata.definition: Illustrate with examples special cases of various types of graphs, including trees.

metadata.title: Pre-order Traversal
metadata.definition: Presenting methods for traversing trees in pre-order.

metadata.title: Post-order Traversal
metadata.definition: Presenting methods for traversing trees in post-order.

metadata.title: In-order Traversal
metadata.definition: Presenting methods for traversing trees in in-order.

metadata.title: BFS
metadata.definition: Presenting the breadth-first search (BFS) method for graphs.

metadata.title: DFS
metadata.definition: Presenting the depth-first search (DFS) method for graphs.

metadata.title: Graph Problem Modeling
metadata.definition: Model a variety of real-world computer science problems using appropriate graphs.

metadata.title: Tree Problem Modeling
metadata.definition: Model a variety of real-world computer science problems using suitable trees.

metadata.title: Network Topology Representation
metadata.definition: Use graphs or trees to represent network topology.

metadata.title: File System Tree
metadata.definition: Use trees to represent the organization of a hierarchical file system.

metadata.title: Social Network Graph
metadata.definition: Use graphs to represent social networks.

metadata.title: Graph & Tree Data Structures
metadata.definition: Show how concepts from graphs and trees appear in data structures.

metadata.title: Graph & Tree Algorithms
metadata.definition: Show how concepts from graphs and trees appear in the algorithm.

metadata.title: Graph & Tree Proof Techniques
metadata.definition: Show how concepts from graphs and trees appear in proof techniques.

metadata.title: Structural Induction
metadata.definition: understand structural induction as a proof technique involving graphs and trees.

metadata.title: Graph & Tree Counting
metadata.definition: Show how concepts from graphs and trees appear in counting problems.

metadata.title: Sample Space
metadata.definition: Definition of sample space in probability theory, the set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment.

metadata.title: Event
metadata.definition: Define an event as a subset of the sample space.

metadata.title: Probability
metadata.definition: Define probability and axioms of probability.

metadata.title: Conditional Probability
metadata.definition: Define and calculate the probability of one event occurring given that another event has occurred.

metadata.title: Bayes' Rule
metadata.definition: Definition and application of Bayes' rule to update the probability of an event based on new information.

metadata.title: Probabilistic Process Formalization
metadata.definition: The ability to convert a verbal description of a probabilistic process into formal concepts such as the sample space, the probability of outcomes, and the events involved.

metadata.title: Simple Event Probability
metadata.definition: Skills in calculating probabilities for basic events, using probability definitions and formulas.

metadata.title: Event Independence
metadata.definition: The ability to determine whether two events are independent or not.

metadata.title: Conditional Probability & Bayes' Rule
metadata.definition: Skills in calculating conditional probabilities and using Bayes' rule to solve probability problems, along with the ability to explain the principles of this rule.

metadata.title: Discrete Random Variable
metadata.definition: Define and understand discrete random variables.

metadata.title: Indicator Random Variable
metadata.definition: Definition and understanding of indicator random variables.

metadata.title: Random Variable Definition
metadata.definition: Ability to define random variables and indicator random variables.

metadata.title: Random Variable Independence
metadata.definition: The skill of determining whether two random variables are independent of each other or not.

metadata.title: Discrete Uniform Distribution
metadata.definition: understand and recognize uniform discrete distributions.

metadata.title: Bernoulli Distribution
metadata.definition: understand and recognize the Bernoulli distribution.

metadata.title: Binomial Distribution
metadata.definition: understand and recognize the binomial distribution.

metadata.title: Geometric Distribution
metadata.definition: understand and recognize geometric distributions.

metadata.title: Common Discrete Distributions
metadata.definition: Ability to recognize and differentiate common discrete distributions such as uniform, Bernoulli, binomial, and geometric.

metadata.title: Continuous Random Variable
metadata.definition: Define and understand continuous random variables.

metadata.title: Continuous Uniform Distribution
metadata.definition: understand and recognize uniform continuous distribution.

metadata.title: Normal Distribution
metadata.definition: understand and recognize normal distribution (Gaussian distribution).

metadata.title: Exponential Distribution
metadata.definition: understand and recognize exponential distributions.

metadata.title: Common Continuous Distributions
metadata.definition: Ability to identify and differentiate common continuous distributions such as uniform, normal, and exponential.

metadata.title: Cumulative Distribution Function
metadata.definition: Define and understand the cumulative density function (CDF) for a continuous random variable.

metadata.title: CDF Probability Calculation
metadata.definition: Skills in using the cumulative density function to calculate probabilities for continuous random variables.

metadata.title: Expected Value
metadata.definition: Defines the expectation (mean value) of a random variable.

metadata.title: Variance
metadata.definition: Define the variance of a random variable.

metadata.title: Expectation & Variance
metadata.definition: Ability to clearly define the concepts of expectation and variance of random variables.

metadata.title: Calculate Exp. & Variance
metadata.definition: Skill in calculating expected value and variance for common discrete and continuous random variables.

metadata.title: Law of Large Numbers
metadata.definition: understand the Law of Large Numbers, which describes the behavior of the sample mean as the number of samples increases.

metadata.title: Central Limit Theorem
metadata.definition: understand the Central Limit Theorem, which describes that the distribution of the sum (or mean) of independent and homogeneous random variables tends to be normally distributed as the number of variables increases.

metadata.title: LLN & CLT Relation
metadata.definition: Ability to explain the importance and application of the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem in probability calculations and statistical analysis.

metadata.title: Joint Distribution
metadata.definition: Define and understand the simultaneous distribution of multiple random variables.

metadata.title: Marginal Distribution
metadata.definition: Define and understand the marginal distribution, as derived from the concurrent distribution.

metadata.title: Conditional Distribution
metadata.definition: Define and understand the conditional distribution of a random variable given the value of another random variable.

metadata.title: Distribution Types Comparison
metadata.definition: Ability to distinguish and explain relationships between simultaneous, marginal, and conditional distributions.

metadata.title: Calculate Discrete Distributions
metadata.definition: Skill in calculating marginal and conditional distributions from a complete distribution for discrete random variables.

metadata.title: Calculate Continuous Distributions
metadata.definition: Skill in calculating marginal and conditional distributions from a complete distribution for continuous random variables.

metadata.title: Conditional Expectation
metadata.definition: Define and understand the conditional expectation of a random variable.

metadata.title: Calculate Discrete Cond. Exp.
metadata.definition: Skill in calculating conditional expectations for discrete random variables.

metadata.title: Calculate Continuous Cond. Exp.
metadata.definition: Skill in calculating conditional expectations for continuous random variables.

metadata.title: Probability: Text Prediction
metadata.definition: Ability to describe how to apply probabilistic models to real-life situations, such as in text prediction systems.

metadata.title: Probability: Hash Tables
metadata.definition: Ability to describe how to apply probabilistic models to real-life situations, such as in hash table performance analysis.

metadata.title: Probability: Quantum Computing
metadata.definition: Ability to describe how to apply probabilistic models to real-life situations, such as in quantum computing.

metadata.title: Probabilistic Algorithms
metadata.definition: Skills in applying probabilistic processes and models to design or analyze stochastic algorithms.

metadata.title: Probability: Security Apps
metadata.definition: Skills in applying probabilistic processes and models in security applications.

metadata.title: Probability vs. Statistics
metadata.definition: understand the fundamental differences in goals, methods, and approaches between probability theory and statistics.

metadata.title: Population (Statistics)
metadata.definition: Basic definition of the complete set of objects or events of interest in statistics.

metadata.title: Sample (Statistics)
metadata.definition: Basic definition of a subset of a population selected for statistical analysis.

metadata.title: Measures of Central Tendency
metadata.definition: The concept of values ​​representing the center of a data set. Includes the ability to recognize, describe and calculate averages, medians and quantiles to locate data.

metadata.title: Variance & Interquartile Range
metadata.definition: Concept of a measure of dispersion of a data set. Includes the ability to identify, describe and calculate variances and interquartile ranges to determine data dispersion.

metadata.title: Frequency Table
metadata.definition: Ability to create and interpret frequency tables to summarize the distribution of data.

metadata.title: Data Visualization
metadata.definition: Ability to display data graphically and interpret various types of graphs, especially histograms.

metadata.title: Univariate Data
metadata.definition: The concept of data having only one variable or one attribute.

metadata.title: Point Estimation
metadata.definition: The concept of using sample data to calculate a single value (point) to estimate a population parameter. Includes the ability to formulate maximum likelihood estimation in the linear-Gaussian setting as a least squares problem and calculate maximum likelihood estimates.

metadata.title: Confidence Interval
metadata.definition: The concept of an estimated range of values ​​for a population parameter, along with a degree of confidence that the interval contains the true parameter. Includes the ability to calculate confidence intervals as a measure of uncertainty.

metadata.title: Maximum A Posteriori (MAP)
metadata.definition: Ability to calculate maximum posterior estimates and establish relationships with the regularized least squares method.

metadata.title: Sampling
metadata.definition: Concepts and techniques of selecting a subset from a population for analysis.

metadata.title: Sampling Bias
metadata.definition: The concept of systematic bias in the sampling process, leading to inaccurate estimates.

metadata.title: Sample Sufficiency
metadata.definition: The concept of evaluating whether the size and quality of a sample is sufficient to draw reliable conclusions about a population.

metadata.title: Bayesian vs. Frequentist
metadata.definition: Differences and comparisons between two main approaches in inferential statistics: Bayesian statistics and frequentist statistics.

metadata.title: Multivariate Data
metadata.definition: The concept of data having multiple variables or attributes for each observation.

metadata.title: Multivariate Estimation
metadata.definition: Parameter estimation for multivariate data. Includes the ability to formulate the multivariate maximum likelihood estimation problem as a least squares problem and to interpret the geometric properties of maximum likelihood estimation.

metadata.title: Multivariate Correlation
metadata.definition: Concept of statistical relationships between multiple variables. Includes the ability to formalize and understand the concept of data correlation (e.g., in 2D).

metadata.title: Multivariate Regression
metadata.definition: Regression techniques for multivariate data. Includes the ability to infer and calculate the maximum likelihood solution for linear regression, infer and calculate the maximum posterior estimate for linear regression, and perform both types of estimation in the context of a polynomial regression problem.

metadata.title: Data Transformation
metadata.definition: Techniques that transform data to improve model performance or make data more consistent with assumptions.

metadata.title: Dimensionality Reduction
metadata.definition: Techniques for reducing the number of random variables are considered by obtaining a smaller set of key variables. Includes the ability to apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to data dimensionality reduction problems.

metadata.title: Data Smoothing
metadata.definition: Techniques that reduce noise or fluctuations in data to highlight trends and patterns.

metadata.title: Statistical Models & Algorithms
metadata.definition: Knowledge of statistical models and related algorithms for data analysis and prediction.

metadata.title: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
metadata.definition: Data dimensionality reduction technique. Includes the ability to formulate and reason about PCA as a least squares problem, interpret PCA geometry, and describe when PCA works well (relating to correlated data).

metadata.title: Compression-Reconstruction Trade-off
metadata.definition: Concept of trade-off between data size reduction (compression) and the ability to recover the original data from the compressed version.

metadata.title: Linear Regression: Curve Fitting
metadata.definition: Ability to apply linear regression to fit curves to data. Includes geometric interpretation of linear regression solution (maximum likelihood).

metadata.title: Overfitting
metadata.definition: Concept of the phenomenon of models overlearning training data, leading to poor performance on new data.

metadata.title: Cross-validation
metadata.definition: Ability to discuss and apply cross-validation techniques in the context of overfitting and model selection (e.g., degrees of polynomials in a regression context).

metadata.title: Hypothesis Testing
metadata.definition: Concepts and methods for testing statistical hypotheses about populations based on sample data.

metadata.title: Vector Definition & Representation
metadata.definition: Describe the algebraic and geometric representations of vectors in Rn.

metadata.title: Vector Operations
metadata.definition: Vector operations include vector addition, vector multiplication by a scalar, and dot product.

metadata.title: Vector Geometric Interpretation
metadata.definition: understand the geometric meaning of vectors in Rn.

metadata.title: Angle Between Vectors
metadata.definition: Ability to calculate angle between two vectors in Rn.

metadata.title: Vector Properties in Rn

metadata.title: Matrix Definition
metadata.definition: Basic definition of matrices.

metadata.title: Basic Matrix Operations
metadata.definition: Basic matrix operations such as matrix addition, matrix multiplication with a scalar.

metadata.title: Meaning of Ax=b
metadata.definition: understand the matrix equation Ax=b as a system of linear equations and how it is represented.

metadata.title: Advanced Matrix Operations

metadata.title: Matrix-Vector Equation
metadata.definition: understand and work with equations involving matrices and vectors.

metadata.title: Matrix Geometric Interpretation
metadata.definition: Interpret matrices and their operations in geometric space.

metadata.title: Geometric Transformations by Matrix
metadata.definition: Relate various matrix transformations (e.g., rotation, scale, translation) to geometric illustrations.

metadata.title: Homogeneous Linear Systems
metadata.definition: Ability to relate a matrix to a system of homogeneous linear equations.

metadata.title: Linear Systems

metadata.title: Elementary Row Operations
metadata.definition: Ability to perform basic row operations on matrices.

metadata.title: Augmented Matrix
metadata.definition: Ability to relate extended matrices to a system of linear equations.

metadata.title: Gaussian Elimination
metadata.definition: Ability to perform Gauss elimination to solve systems of linear equations.

metadata.title: Linear Independence
metadata.definition: The concept of vector sets cannot be represented as a linear combination of other vectors in the same set.

metadata.title: Span

metadata.title: Vector Space Basis
metadata.definition: The concept of a set of linearly independent vectors forming a subspace.

metadata.title: Vector Subspace
metadata.definition: Define and understand the properties of a subspace in a vector space.

metadata.title: Orthogonality
metadata.definition: The concept of vectors or subspaces being perpendicular to each other.

metadata.title: Projection (Linear Algebra)
metadata.definition: Concept of projecting a vector onto a subspace or another vector.

metadata.title: Least Squares (Linear Algebra)
metadata.definition: Method to find approximate solutions for inconsistent linear equations by minimizing the sum of squares of the residuals.

metadata.title: Orthogonal Basis
metadata.definition: Concept of a basis whose vectors are all orthogonal to each other.

metadata.title: Polynomial Linear Combination
metadata.definition: Concept of creating a new polynomial by taking a weighted sum of other polynomials.

metadata.title: Bezier Curve
metadata.definition: The concept of parametric curves is widely used in computer graphics and computer-aided design.

metadata.title: Eigenvector
metadata.definition: The concept of vectors only scales (scales) by a constant when a linear transformation is applied.

metadata.title: Eigenvalue
metadata.definition: The concept of scalar values ​​represents the scaling factor to which the eigenvectors are scaled.

metadata.title: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
metadata.definition: understand PCA as an important application of linear algebra to data dimensionality reduction.

metadata.title: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)
metadata.definition: The concept of a strong matrix decomposition has many applications in computer science.

metadata.title: PageRank Algorithm
metadata.definition: understand the PageRank algorithm and how it uses linear algebra to rank web pages.

metadata.title: Linear Algebra in Computer Graphics
metadata.definition: Explore applications of linear algebra in computer graphics, such as geometric transformations and projections.

metadata.title: Subspace Examples
metadata.definition: List examples of subspaces of a vector space.

metadata.title: Subspace & Vector Space Properties
metadata.definition: Recognize and use the basic properties of subspaces and vector spaces.

metadata.title: Identifying Subspaces
metadata.definition: Determines whether specific subsets of a vector space are subspaces or not.

metadata.title: Basis Existence in Abstract Spaces
metadata.definition: Discuss the existence of a basis for an abstract vector space.

metadata.title: Vector Coordinates (Given Basis)
metadata.definition: Describes the coordinates of a vector relative to a given basis.

metadata.title: Basis & Dimension (Finite Spaces)
metadata.definition: Determine the basis and dimensions of a finite dimensional space.

metadata.title: Spanning Sets for Vectors in Rn
metadata.definition: Discuss the generating systems (spanning sets) for vectors in Rn.

metadata.title: Linear Independence for Vectors in Rn
metadata.definition: Discuss linear independence for vectors in Rn.

metadata.title: Vector Space Dimension Definition
metadata.definition: Defines the number of dimensions of a vector space.

metadata.title: Gram-Schmidt Orthonormalization
metadata.definition: Explain the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization process.

metadata.title: Orthogonal Projection Definition
metadata.definition: Define orthogonal projections.

metadata.title: Orthogonal Complement Definition
metadata.definition: Define orthogonal complements.

metadata.title: Orthogonal Projection Calculation
metadata.definition: Computes the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace, with a basis for that subspace.

metadata.title: Projection & Least Squares Relation
metadata.definition: Explain the relationship between orthogonal projections and least square approximations.

metadata.title: Polynomials as General Vectors
metadata.definition: Define polynomials as general vectors.

metadata.title: Polynomial Basis Linear Combination
metadata.definition: Explain linear combinations of basic polynomials.

metadata.title: Orthogonality for Polynomials
metadata.definition: Describe orthogonality for polynomials.

metadata.title: Bernstein Polynomials
metadata.definition: Distinguish between fundamental polynomials and Bernstein polynomials.

metadata.title: Bernstein & Bezier Curves
metadata.definition: applying Bernstein polynomials to Bezier curves.

metadata.title: Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors
metadata.definition: Find the eigenvalues ​​and eigenvectors of a matrix.

metadata.title: Geometric Eigenvalues/vectors
metadata.definition: Define eigenvalues ​​and eigenvectors from a geometric perspective.

metadata.title: Characteristic Poly for Eigen
metadata.definition: Use characteristic polynomials to calculate eigenvalues ​​and eigenvectors.

metadata.title: Eigenspace Diagonalization
metadata.definition: Use matrix eigenspaces, when possible, to diagonalize a matrix.

metadata.title: Matrix Diagonalization
metadata.definition: Perform diagonalization of matrices.

metadata.title: Eigenvalues Significance
metadata.definition: Explain the meaning of eigenvalues ​​and eigenvectors.

metadata.title: Characteristic Polynomial
metadata.definition: Find the characteristic polynomial of a matrix.

metadata.title: Eigenvector Linear Transform
metadata.definition: Use eigenvectors to represent a linear transformation of a particular basis.

metadata.title: PCA Geometry
metadata.definition: Explain the geometric properties of Principal Component Analysis (PCA).

metadata.title: PCA Dimension Reduction
metadata.definition: Relating Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to data dimensionality reduction.

metadata.title: PCA & Least Squares
metadata.definition: Relate Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to solving least-squares problems.

metadata.title: PCA & Eigenproblems
metadata.definition: Relate Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to solving eigenvector problems.

metadata.title: PCA Multidimensional Data
metadata.definition: apply Principal Components Analysis (PCA) to reduce the dimensionality of a multidimensional data set (e.g., images).

metadata.title: PageRank Algorithm
metadata.definition: Explain the PageRank algorithm and understand how it relates to eigenvector problems.

metadata.title: SVD vs PCA Geometry
metadata.definition: Explain the geometric differences between Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and Principal Component Analysis (PCA).

metadata.title: SVD Applications
metadata.definition: apply Separate Value Decomposition (SVD) to a concrete example (e.g., movie ratings).

metadata.title: Sequences

metadata.title: Series

metadata.title: Limits

metadata.title: Infinite Set vs Sequence

metadata.title: Formal Limit Definition
metadata.definition: Explain the exact mathematical definition of limit.

metadata.title: Sequence & Series Limits
metadata.definition: apply methods to find and prove limits for specific examples of sequences and strings.

metadata.title: Convergence & Divergence
metadata.definition: Explain the concept and criteria for determining convergence and divergence of sequences and series.

metadata.title: L'Hopital's Rule
metadata.definition: apply L'Hospital's rule and other methods to solve indeterminate limit types.

metadata.title: Limit Calculation Methods
metadata.definition: apply different methods (in addition to L'Hospital) to deal with indeterminate limit types.

metadata.title: Derivative Limit Definition
metadata.definition: Explain the definition of the derivative as a limit.

metadata.title: Derivative as Function

metadata.title: Basic Derivatives from Limit
metadata.definition: Perform basic derivative calculations based on limit definitions.

metadata.title: Sum, Product, Quotient Rule

metadata.title: Chain Rule

metadata.title: Special Function Derivatives
metadata.definition: Work with examples of derivatives of important functions (e.g., exponential, logarithmic, trigonometric).

metadata.title: Definite & Indefinite Integral
metadata.definition: Explain the definition and difference between definite and indefinite integrals.

metadata.title: Integration Rules
metadata.definition: apply the rules of integration to examples with important functions.

metadata.title: Special Function Integrals
metadata.definition: Calculate integrals of important functions (e.g. exponential, logarithmic, trigonometric).

metadata.title: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

metadata.title: Integral Applications
metadata.definition: apply integration to solve real-life problems.

metadata.title: Probability Integration

metadata.title: Parametric Curves
metadata.definition: apply parametric representations to important curves.

metadata.title: Polar Coordinates

metadata.title: Taylor Series

metadata.title: Taylor Series Approximation
metadata.definition: applying Taylor series to function approximation problems.

metadata.title: Partial Derivatives
metadata.definition: Calculate and understand the meaning of partial derivatives.

metadata.title: Gradient

metadata.title: Multivariable Chain Rule

metadata.title: Vector-valued Functions
metadata.definition: understand and work with vector-valued functions.

metadata.title: Convexity

metadata.title: Global & Local Minima

metadata.title: Gradient Descent
metadata.definition: understand and apply the gradient descent algorithm to find the minimum of a function.

metadata.title: Constrained Optimization
metadata.definition: Solve optimization problems when there are additional constraints.

metadata.title: Lagrange Multipliers
metadata.definition: apply the Lagrange multiplier method to solve constrained optimization problems.

metadata.title: ODE Definition
metadata.definition: understand the definition and classification of Ordinary Differential Equations.

metadata.title: Euler Method
metadata.definition: apply Euler's method to approximately solve Ordinary Differential Equations.

metadata.title: ODE Simulation
metadata.definition: applying Ordinary Differential Equations to simulation problems.

metadata.title: Monte Carlo Integration
metadata.definition: understand and apply the Monte Carlo integration method.

metadata.title: ML Gradient Descent
metadata.definition: apply gradient descent algorithm in machine learning problems.

metadata.title: Forward Kinematics
metadata.definition: understand and apply forward kinematics in mechanical and robotic systems.

metadata.title: Inverse Kinematics
metadata.definition: understand and apply inverse kinematics in mechanical and robotic systems.

metadata.title: Calculus in Probability
metadata.definition: Use calculus tools to solve problems related to probability.

metadata.title: Single-variable Derivative Apps
metadata.definition: apply derivatives of one variable to solve real-life problems.

metadata.title: Partial Derivative
metadata.definition: Concept and method of calculating the derivative of a multivariable function with respect to each independent variable.

metadata.title: Gradient
metadata.definition: The partial derivative vector of a function of many variables indicates the fastest increasing direction of the function.

metadata.title: Multivariable Chain Rule
metadata.definition: Rules for calculating the derivative of composite functions in the case of functions of many variables.

metadata.title: Vector-Valued Function
